questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the term used to describe an extra row of eyelashes behind the grey line?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Distichiasis

The extra row of eyelashes behind the grey line is called distichiasis.

Distichiasis can occur due to congenital or acquired causes. These lashes may irritate the cornea. Management is by lid splitting with cryotherapy to the base of the hair follicles.

Other options:

Option A: Trichiasis is inward misdirection of cilia, with the normal position of the lid margin.

Option C: Tylosis is the thickening of the tarsal plate.

Option D: Madarosis is the loss of eyelashes or eyebrows.
questions.learning: Distichiasis — The extra row of eyelashes behind the grey line is called distichiasis. Distichiasis can occur due to congenital or acquired causes.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text:
A child is brought to the casualty with a history of choking. On examination, there is decreased air entry in the left lung. What would be the correct management?

1. Bronchoscopy
2. Computed tomography scan
3. ICD insertion
4. Chest x-ray
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1 and 4

A history of choking and reduced breath sounds over the left lung in a child are suggestive of a foreign body lodged in the left bronchus. The next step in the management of this child is to obtain a chest x-ray, followed by bronchoscopic removal of the foreign body.

Food items (nuts, seeds hard candy, gum, bones raw fruits, and vegetables) account for the majority of choking cases in children. The most common site of foreign body lodging is the bronchus. Foreign body aspiration into the airway has three stages: immediate symptoms of coughing and choking, an asymptomatic interval, and later complications such as fever, atelectasis, and pneumonia.

When a child presents with a history of choking, detailed history taking and physical examination of the nose, oral cavity, pharynx, neck, and lungs are necessary.

The next step for suspected foreign body aspiration is to obtain a chest X-ray, including the abdomen, despite most foreign bodies being radiolucent. Secondary findings on the X-ray can indicate foreign body involvement, such as air trapping, atelectasis, obstructive emphysema, asymmetric hyperinflation, mediastinal shift, or consolidation. While a CT scan has high accuracy, it is not typically performed due to radiation risks.

The treatment of choice for a foreign body in the airway is its endoscopic removal with a rigid instrument, usually a bronchoscope, by a specialist otolaryngologist or pulmonologist. Bronchoscopy must be performed even if there is a high suspicion of an airway foreign body in spite of negative or inconclusive imaging.
questions.learning: 1 and 4 A history of choking and reduced breath sounds over the left lung in a child are suggestive of a foreign body lodged in the left bronchus. The next step in the management of this child is to obtain a chest x-ray, followed by bronchoscopic removal…

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Identify the true statement regarding the point marked on the myocardial action potential curve.
options: Due to opening of Na+ and closure of fast K+ channels
Due to slow but prolonged opening of Ca2+ channels
Due to closure of Na+ and opening of slow K+ channel
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Due to slow but prolonged opening of Ca2+ channels

The myocardial action potential curve marked above represents the plateau phase, which is due to the slower and prolonged opening of calcium channels.

Two types of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (T- and L-types) are present in myocardial cells. The opening of the slower L-type Ca2+ channels is mostly responsible for changes in the action potential. The action potential curve of cardiac muscles consists of 5 phases, as shown below.

Phase 0: Depolarization - Opening of voltage-gated sodium channels (fast sodium channels) leads to sodium influx.

Phase 1: Initial repolarization - Closure of Na+ channels and opening up of K+ channels leads to potassium efflux.

Phase 2: Plateau - Slower but prolonged opening of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, leading to calcium influx and reduced permeability of K+ channels, causes the graph to plateau

Phase 3: Rapid Repolarization - The closure of Ca2+ channels and opening of K+ at the end of the plateau phase causes repolarization.

Phase 4: Resting membrane potential - Is reached at the end of phase 3
questions.learning: Due to slow but prolonged opening of Ca2+ channels — The myocardial action potential curve marked above represents the plateau phase, which is due to the slower and prolonged opening of calcium channels.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the main role of Phase 1 in xenobiotic metabolism?
options: To make the compound more permeable across membranes
To extract functional proteins through oxidase/reductase reactions
To introduce or expose functional groups for further metabolism
To directly conjugate the compound and facilitate excretion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. To introduce or expose functional groups for further metabolism

Phase I reactions (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) introduce or expose polar functional groups on xenobiotics. These reactions are mainly mediated by CYP450 enzymes. The purpose is to prepare the molecule for Phase II conjugation. Thus, Phase I increases chemical reactivity for further metabolism.

| Reaction | Example

| -------- | -------

| Oxidation | CYP450 mediated

| Reduction | Nitro → amine

| Hydrolysis | Ester breakdown

| Feature | Phase I | Phase II

| ------- | ------- | --------

| Function | Functionalization | Conjugation

| Reaction | Oxidation, reduction | Glucuronidation, sulfation

| Enzymes | CYP450 | Transferases

| Result | Slightly polar | Highly water-soluble
questions.learning: To introduce or expose functional groups for further metabolism Phase I reactions (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) introduce or expose polar functional groups on xenobiotics.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with a history of a road traffic accident 2 hours ago was brought to the emergency department with an altered sensorium. His GCS was 10 and the CT scan is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Epidural hematoma

Axial CT shows a hyperdense lentiform (biconvex) opacity consistent with an epidural hematoma.

Extradural hematoma (EDH) is also known as an epidural hematoma. It is a collection of blood that forms between the inner surface of the skull and the outer layer of the dura, which is called the periosteal layer. It is commonly associated with a history of trauma and associated skull fracture.

The source of bleeding is usually a torn meningeal artery (most commonly the middle meningeal artery). It is associated with an underlying fracture of the squamous part of the temporal bone.

Investigations to be done include CT and MRI. It is seen as a biconvex lesion. It can cause a mass effect with herniation. They are usually limited by cranial sutures, but not by venous sinuses.

Swirl sign refers to the non-contrast CT appearance of acute extravasation of blood into a hematoma, for example, an extradural hematoma or subdural hematoma. It represents unclotted fresh blood which is of lower attenuation than clotted blood that surrounds it.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a radiological feature of hypothyroidism? (NEET Pg 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Beaking of vertebra

Beaking of vertebra is not associated with hypothyroidism. This vertebral finding is characteristic of mucopolysaccharidosis conditions, with central beaking observed in Morquio's disease and antero-inferior beaking seen in Hurler disease. Hypothyroidism has several skeletal manifestations, but vertebral beaking is not among them.

Other Options:

●        Option A. Wormian bones - These accessory sutural bones can be seen in various conditions including hypothyroidism\, especially in congenital hypothyroidism or cretinism.

●        Option B. Stipulated ribs - Rib abnormalities can occur in hypothyroidism as part of the broader skeletal manifestations of the disease.

●        Option D. Epiphyseal Dysgenesis - This is a recognized skeletal manifestation in hypothyroidism\, particularly in juvenile hypothyroidism\, affecting the growth plates.

Educational Objective:

Vertebal beaking is specifically associated with mucopolysaccharidosis conditions rather than hypothyroidism, which has its own distinct pattern of skeletal manifestations.
questions.learning: Beaking of vertebra Beaking of vertebra is not associated with hypothyroidism. This vertebral finding is characteristic of mucopolysaccharidosis conditions, with central beaking observed in Morquio's disease and antero-inferior beaking seen in Hurler disease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient was diagnosed with Ewing sarcoma with EWSR1 gene mutation. The technique shown in the image was performed to confirm the diagnosis. Identify the technique shown in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fluorescent in situ hybridisation

The technique shown in the image is FISH demonstrating a positive EWSR1 gene rearrangement, characteristic of Ewing sarcoma. The fused region denoted by Yellow corresponds to a normal intact gene, while a split signal pattern showing separate red and green signals is indicative of EWSR1 gene rearrangement.

Fluorescent In Situ Hybridisation (FISH) is a simple technique for the detection of specific genetic information on morphologically intact tissue using fluorescent probes. FISH can be performed on prenatal samples, peripheral blood cells, touch preparations from cancer biopsies, and even fixed archival tissue sections. It is used to detect

• numeric abnormalities of chromosomes (aneuploidy)
• subtle microdeletions and rearrangements.
• complex translocations that are not demonstrable by routine karyotyping
• gene amplification (e.g., HER2 in breast cancer or NMYC amplification in neuroblastomas)

Other options:

Option B: Karyotyping is the process by which chromosomes are isolated, stained, and examined to find chromosomal anomalies. It is used in prenatal diagnosis, investigation of repeat pregnancy loss, investigation of children and adults suspected of having a chromosomal disorder, and subtyping of lymphomas and leukemias for the purpose of exact diagnosis, giving a prognosis, and treatment.

Option C: IHC (Immunohistochemistry) is a staining method for histopathological specimens. It helps in the diagnosis and classification of tumors based on their distinct protein expression patterns. Eg: The expression of estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and HER2/neu in breast cancer cells is mainly assessed by immunohistochemistry.

Option D: Sanger's technique: This was the first technique used to determine the sequence of proteins. The first protein to be sequenced by this method was insulin. Sanger’s reagent is 1- Flouro 2,4 Dinitro benzene. Only dipeptides and tripeptides can be sequenced by this method.
questions.learning: Fluorescent in situ hybridisation — The technique shown in the image is FISH demonstrating a positive EWSR1 gene rearrangement, characteristic of Ewing sarcoma.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with a hard painless nodule on the upper eyelid. It was observed to be growing outwards, away from the lid margin. What could be the most probable diagnosis here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chalazion

The given clinical picture is suggestive of a chalazion (tarsal cyst/meibomian cyst). It has the malignant potential to become an adenocarcinoma of the meibomian gland.

It is the chronic lipogranulomatous inflammation of the meibomian gland. It presents as painless swelling of the eyelid. It is more common in adults than children. Treatment includes incision and curettage and intralesional injection of triamcinolone acetate.

Other options:

* Hordeolum externum or stye is the suppurative inflammation of the gland of Zeis. It is hard and painful, and there is a visible pus point on the lid margin.

* Entropion refers to the inward rolling and rotation of the lid margin towards the globe. It is more common in the lower lid

* Loss of eyelashes is seen in chronic blepharitis.

*
questions.learning: Chalazion — The given clinical picture is suggestive of a chalazion (tarsal cyst/meibomian cyst). It has the malignant potential to become an adenocarcinoma of the meibomian gland.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old female child is brought to the OPD with cramping abdominal pain. On examination, she is found to have rashes on the back of her legs, buttocks and the extensor surface of her forearms. Laboratory analysis reveals proteinuria and microscopic hematuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Henoch-Schönlein purpura

The diagnosis in this child with rash, abdominal pain and nephritis is Henoch-Schönlein purpura.

Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP), also known as IgA vasculitis, is a common small vessel vasculitis in childhood. It is a type III hypersensitivity reaction characterized by the deposition of IgA in the small vessels of the skin, joints, gastrointestinal tract, and kidney, resulting in vasculitis

Children usually present with the following features:

* Palpable purpura is symmetric and occurs in the lower extremities, extensor aspect of the upper limbs, and buttocks.

* Arthralgia and arthritis- commonly affecting hip, knee, or ankle joints.

* Gastrointestinal manifestations like abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, and intussusception.

* About 30% of the patients with HSP develop renal manifestations, presenting as microscopic hematuria, hypertension, and progressive glomerulonephritis.

Laboratory studies generally show mild leukocytosis, a normal platelet count, and occasionally eosinophilia. Serum complement components are normal.

Most clinical features of IgA vasculitis are self-limiting and resolve in a few days. Supportive management with the maintenance of hydration and pain relief is done. Patients developing nephritis due to IgA vasculitis may need aggressive management with immunosuppressants.

The image given below shows palpable purpura in the lower limbs seen in HSP.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In which of the following cases will gastric lavage be contraindicated?
options: Within one hour of consuming an unknown poison
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Strychnine poisoning

Gastric lavage will be contraindicated in a case of strychnine poisoning. Strychnine is a highly toxic substance that causes severe convulsions and muscle rigidity, which can lead to complications during the procedure, such as aspiration or further injury due to the patient's agitation or convulsions.

Contraindications of Gastric lavage:

* Corrosive poisonings like sulphuric acid and kerosene (except carbolic acid).

* Convulsants/CNS stimulants (Eg: Strychnine)

* Comatose patients

* Volatile poison

* Upper GI pathology (E.g: esophageal varices)

* Hypothermic patient

* Severe heart disease

* Advanced Pregnancy

Acts by the same mechanism as other strong acids, but also scavenges calcium ions, leading to hypocalcemia and Calcium oxalate renal stones.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Personal monitoring of radiation is done by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. TLD badge

Personal monitoring of radiation is done by a TLD badge.

The TLD badge (thermoluminescent dosimeter) should be positioned according to local or national practices. In India, one TLD badge has to be worn at the chest level inside the lead apron if the apron is used. An additional wrist badge has to be worn for procedures requiring hands close to the primary beam.

The thermoluminescent material used is calcium sulfate doped with dysprosium or lithium fluoride. Radiation exposure is monitored every three months. The maximum dose limit for occupational radiation workers is 30 mSv in a year, provided the cumulative dose in a block of 5 years does not exceed 100 mSv.

The given image shows a TLD badge.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 56-year-old patient suffering from alcoholic cirrhosis receives a healthy liver from his biological son. What is this type of transplant known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Allograft

Transplant of an organ/tissue from a son to a parent is an example of an allograft.

An allograft is transplant of cells/tissues/organs from a genetically non-identical donor of the same species.

Isografts are allografts in which cells/tissues/organs are transplanted from a donor to a genetically identical recipient. (monozygotic twins)

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The shelf life of copper T 380 A is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 10 years

Copper T-380A has a life span of 10 years.

Copper T-380A (Paraguard) is a second-generation intrauterine device(IUD) having 380 sq. mm of surface area of copper on the device. A higher surface area of copper results in higher contraceptive efficacy. It has a plastic T-shaped core with copper placed around the vertical stem and horizontal arms. The frame of the Copper T-380A is connected to a monofilament thread that protrudes into the upper vagina. This facilitates easy removal and allows the user to ensure that the IUD remains in the uterus.

It functions mainly by causing an inflammatory response within the uterus that impair the viability of the sperms and reduce its chances of fertilization. The same response also makes it difficult for blastocyst implantation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a normal distribution, what percentage of the data falls within one standard deviation of the mean?
questions.explanation: In a normal (Gaussian) distribution, the data are symmetrically distributed around the mean and follow the Empirical Rule, also known as the 68–95–99.7 rule. 1. Approximately 68% of the data lie within ±1 standard deviation (σ) of the mean. 2. About 95% of the data lie within ±2 standard deviations (2σ). 3. Nearly 99.7% of the data lie within ±3 standard deviations (3σ). Therefore, Option (A) 68% correctly represents the proportion of observations within one standard deviation of the mean. Why the other options are incorrect: 1. Option B (95%) corresponds to ±2 standard deviations, commonly used for 95% confidence intervals. 2. Option C (98%) is not a standard value in the empirical rule. 3. Option D (99%) approximates the ±3 standard deviation range but is not exact. Understanding this rule is fundamental in biostatistics, as it helps interpret variability, confidence intervals, and statistical significance in normally distributed data
questions.learning: In a normal (Gaussian) distribution, the data are symmetrically distributed around the mean and follow the Empirical Rule, also known as the 68–95–99.7 rule.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presented with low hemoglobin, platelet count of 25,000/mL, gum bleeding, and raised PT & aPTT. The image of his peripheral smear is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. AML with t(15;17)

The peripheral blood smear shows numerous Auer rods in the cytoplasm of progranulocytes, which are characteristic of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The presentation of the patient with gum bleeding points to the diagnosis of AML with t(15;17).

Auer rods (needle-like azurophilic granules) are predominantly seen in acute promyelocytic leukemia, which is a subtype of acute myeloid leukemia. It is associated with t(15;17), which results in the formation of the fusion gene called PML-RARA. The condition is associated with a high incidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Treatment includes the administration of all-trans retinoic acid.
questions.learning: AML with t(15;17) — The peripheral blood smear shows numerous Auer rods in the cytoplasm of progranulocytes, which are characteristic of acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is involved in recognition and clearance of necrotic cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inflammasome

Inflammasomes are involved in the recognition and clearance of necrotic cells.

Inflammasomes are involved in pyroptosis, a process of programmed cell death distinct from apoptosis and necrosis. This process is dependent on caspases 1, 4, and 5 and is responsible for killing of infected cells. It occurs in the following sequence:

• Activation of inflammasome complex by infected cells
• This causes activation of caspase-1
• This results in generation of IL-1, which is responsible for fever, inflammation, leukocyte recruitment

Option B: Toll-like receptors (TLR)- recognizes molecules shared by pathogens

Option C: P-selectins - an important role in the initial recruitment of WBCs at the site of inflammation & in platelet recruitment and aggregation at the site of injury.
questions.learning: Inflammasome Inflammasomes are involved in the recognition and clearance of necrotic cells. Inflammasomes are involved in pyroptosis, a process of programmed cell death distinct from apoptosis and necrosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the line depicted in the image given below?
questions.explanation: The image shows a dark, vertical hyperpigmented line extending along the midline of the pregnant abdomen. This is the Linea Nigra, a common physiological skin change during pregnancy caused by increased melanocyte-stimulating hormone. It usually develops from the pre-existing, faint "linea alba" (Option C), which is the fibrous structure where the abdominal muscle aponeuroses meet. Striae gravidarum (Option A), or stretch marks, appear as reddish or purplish linear streaks, typically found on the lower abdomen, breasts, or thighs, rather than a single midline dark line. Chloasma (Option B), also known as the "mask of pregnancy," refers to blotchy, brownish hyperpigmentation specifically on the face. The Linea Nigra is completely benign and typically fades several months after delivery as hormone levels return to baseline. Identification of this classic sign is a routine part of the obstetric physical examination

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An infant of 3 months presents with recurrent severe infections, including pneumonia, chronic diarrhea, and oral candidiasis. He has an absence of thymic shadow on chest X-ray. Laboratory tests reveal very low levels of adenosine deaminase (ADA). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)

Adenosine deaminase deficiency leads to accumulation of toxic purine metabolites causing lymphocyte apoptosis.

This results in combined deficiency of T cells, B cells, and NK cells.

Absent thymic shadow reflects severe T-cell depletion.

Early-onset recurrent infections, chronic diarrhea, and candidiasis are classic for severe combined immunodeficiency.

| Finding | Interpretation

| ------- | --------------

| 3 months age | Maternal IgG waning → immune defects become evident

| Recurrent severe infections | Combined immunodeficiency

| Chronic diarrhea + pneumonia | Opportunistic infections

| Oral candidiasis | T-cell deficiency (fungal infections)

| Absent thymic shadow | Thymic hypoplasia/aplasia → ↓ T cells

| ↓ ADA levels | Metabolic cause of SCID

When ADA is deficient:

• Deoxyadenosine accumulates
• Converted into dATP
• dATP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase

DNA synthesis stops

Lymphocyte proliferation fails

Massive loss of T cells, B cells, NK cells

| Disorder | Age of Onset | B cells | T cells | Key Feature

| -------- | ------------ | ------- | ------- | -----------

| Bruton’s | 6 months | ↓ | Normal | Recurrent bacterial infections

| Job syndrome | Childhood | Normal | Functional defect | ↑ IgE, abscess

| SCID | Early infancy | ↓ | ↓ | Severe infections, no thymus

| CVID | Adolescence | ↓ | Normal/slightly ↓ | Late onset
questions.learning: Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) Adenosine deaminase deficiency leads to accumulation of toxic purine metabolites causing lymphocyte apoptosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 36-year-old P2L2 woman with severe endometriosis is found to have pelvic adhesions on laparoscopy. She has a history of prior tubal ligation and adhesiolysis. What is the most appropriate management during laparoscopy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy

In this clinical scenario of a 36-year-old P2L2 woman with severe endometriosis and pelvic adhesions on laparoscopy, with a history of prior tubal ligation and adhesiolysis, the most appropriate laparoscopic management would be hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

The history of adhesiolysis indicates recurrence of endometriosis, while prior tubal ligation confirms that her family is complete. Therefore, in the setting of recurrent severe endometriosis with completed childbearing, the most appropriate laparoscopic management is hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

Endometriosis is the presence of endometrial tissue outside the uterus. The patient usually presents with symptoms of abdominal pain, dyspareunia, dysmenorrhea, and infertility. It is an estrogen-dependent disease of the childbearing age group. The most common site of occurrence is the ovary followed by the pouch of Douglas.

The gold standard for the diagnosis of endometriosis is visual inspection by laparoscopy, preferably with histological confirmation. Role of laparoscopy in endometriosis includes detection of pelvic endometriosis; location of the site of endometriosis and its staging, biopsy for histopathological confirmation and surgical treatment by ablation and / or removal.

Other investigations in endometriosis include:

* CA-125 levels : Raised

* Transvaginal ultrasound: Echo-free cysts or pelvic mass

* Colour doppler: Increased blood flow

* Anti-endometrial antibodies

Other options:

Option B: Total laparoscopic hysterectomy may not be the ideal option in this case, as the patient's childbearing is complete, symptoms are severe, and retaining the ovaries could increase the risk of developing chocolate cysts due to endometriosis.

Option C: Oophorectomy alone may not be the ideal option, as the presence of endometrial tissue in the uterus can still result in the recurrence of endometriosis.

Option D: GnRH antagonists may not be an ideal option for patients with severe symptoms and pelvic adhesions, as they may not provide sufficient relief or address the underlying structural issues.

Pearl PF1775: Endometriosis

Sites of Endometriosis:

* Pelvic endometriosis: Pelvic peritoneum, the pouch of Douglas, uterosacral ligament.

* Rectovaginal endometriosis.

* Ovarian endometriosis.

* Chocolate cyst of the ovary.

* Other sites—appendix, pelvic lymph nodes.

* Metastatic— lungs, umbilicus, scar endometriosis.

One pathology review revealed that endometriosis has been identified on all organs except the spleen.

Examination findings in endometriosis:

* Abdomen: Cystic swelling, fixed and tender.

* Pelvis: Cystic tender mass.

* Vaginal examination: Fixed, tender, retroverted uterus. Tenderness in the lateral fornices (indicative of endometriosis even if no mass).

* Speculum inspection of the Posterior fornix: Bluish/blackish puckered spots on speculum, tender to touch. The presence of puckered spots is pathognomonic of endometriosis.

* Posterior Fornix Palpation: Uterosacral ligaments & pouch of Douglas feel thickened and shotty with multiple small palpable nodules. This is called the cobblestone feel of uterosacral ligaments.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: What does the given image represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypnogram

The above image represents a hypnogram. It is a graph that depicts the stages of sleep as a function of time. It provides a visual representation of sleep structure and is useful in the diagnosis of various sleep disorders.

An electroencephalogram is the depiction of the electrical activity of the surface of the brain. Different waveforms (alpha, beta, theta, delta) are produced depending on the functional status of the brain.

Polysomnography is a multi parametric test that is considered the gold standard in the diagnosis of sleep disorders. It is a continuous recording of biophysiological changes that occur during sleep. It includes,

• Continuous EEG recording, from occipital and parietal leads
• Electro-oculography- to record eye movements
• Electromyography- for muscle potential and its activities
• ECG
• Multiple sleep latency tests- repeated measures of time taken to sleep
• Nasal-oral airflow, respiratory effort, oxyhemoglobin saturation, and leg movements during sleep are measured.

Epworth sleep assessment scale is a questionnaire used to quantify daytime sleepiness. It determines how frequently a patient is likely to doze off in 8 commonly encountered situations. It is a subjective assessment and hence less reliable.
questions.learning: Hypnogram — The above image represents a hypnogram. It is a graph that depicts the stages of sleep as a function of time.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Killian's dehiscence is seen between___?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cricopharyngeus and Thyropharyngeus

Killian's dehiscence is seen between the cricopharyngeus and thyropharyngeus muscles.

The inferior constrictor muscle is made up of 2 parts: The upper thyropharyngeus made of oblique fibres and the lower cricopharyngeus made of transverse fibres. Between the two muscles, there is a potential gap which is called as the pharyngeal dimple or Killian's dehiscence.

This is the site of weakness in the pharyngeal wall and therefore is the potential site for the development of the diverticula- Zenker's diverticula.

Another site of weakness in the pharyngeal wall is the Laimer's triangle, which is present between the cricopharyngeus and the circular muscle of the oesophagus.

Pearl PF0326: Zenker’s Diverticulum

* Hypopharyngeal diverticulum

* False diverticulum

* Pulsion diverticulum

* Acquired diverticulum, seen in the elderly (>60 years)

* Herniation is through the Killian’s triangle (a weak area between two parts of the inferior constrictor) in the posterior pharyngeal wall

* Clinical features:

* Dysphagia

* Regurgitation

* Halitosis

* Aspiration

* Gurgling sound during swallowing

* Investigation of choice: Barium swallow (Lateral X rays)

* Treatment

* Cricopharyngeal myotomy

* Surgical diverticulectomy

* Marsupialization

* Dohlman’s procedure

Zenker’s diverticulum

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In which condition is pulsus paradoxus observed?
options: Severe Asthma or Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
questions.explanation: Pulsus paradoxus is defined as an exaggerated drop in systolic blood pressure (>10 mmHg) during inspiration. While classically associated with cardiac tamponade, it is also frequently observed in severe obstructive airway diseases such as severe asthma or Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD). In these conditions, large negative intrathoracic pressures during inspiration increase venous return to the right heart, causing the interventricular septum to bulge into the left ventricle, which reduces stroke volume. Coronary artery disease (Option A) and atrial fibrillation (Option D) do not typically cause this inspiratory pressure drop. Right ventricular myocardial infarction (Option C) is more commonly associated with Kussmaul’s sign (lack of inspiratory fall in JVP). Recognizing pulsus paradoxus in a patient with asthma is a critical clinical indicator of severe respiratory distress and potential impending respiratory failure
questions.learning: Pulsus paradoxus is defined as an exaggerated drop in systolic blood pressure (>10 mmHg) during inspiration. While classically associated with cardiac tamponade, it is also frequently observed in severe obstructive airway diseases such as severe asthma or…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: According to the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), what does a verbal score of 1 indicate?
questions.explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is the global standard for assessing consciousness following head injuries. It measures three components: eye, motor, and verbal responses. For the verbal component, a score of 1 is the lowest possible rating and indicates that there is no verbal response at all. Incomprehensible sounds (Option C), such as moaning or groaning without words, receive a score of 2. Inappropriate words (Option B), where the patient speaks random words that do not form coherent sentences, score a 3. Confused conversation, where the patient forms sentences but is disoriented, scores a 4. An oriented response (Option D), indicating the patient knows their name, place, and date, receives the maximum verbal score of 5 . It is important to note that a GCS score is never 0; the minimum possible total score is 3. Identifying a verbal score of 1 is critical for determining a patient’s risk of airway compromise
questions.learning: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is the global standard for assessing consciousness following head injuries. It measures three components: eye, motor, and verbal responses.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is associated with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gilbert syndrome

Gilbert syndrome is associated with Inherited unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

Inherited unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia:

* Gilbert syndrome

* Crigler Najjar type 1

* Crigler Najjar type 2

Inherited conjugated hyperbilirubinemia

* Dubin Johnson syndrome (Option B)

* Rotor syndrome (Option C)

Gilbert syndrome is a benign, familial disorder inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern characterized by mild intermittent jaundice usually seen during stress, illnesses, or any other precipitating factors. There is no hemolysis or underlying liver disease. The condition is recognized to arise from a mutation in the promoter region of the UGT1A1 gene, which results in mildly decreased UDP - glucuronoyl transferase production. UGT1A1 activity is reduced to 10-33% of normal.

It presents with mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with other liver function tests being normal. The disorder is precipitated by stress, alcohol, and reduced caloric intake.

Liver histology shows increased lipofuscin pigment. It responds well to phenobarbitone.

Gilbert's syndrome does not require treatment. The bilirubin levels may fluctuate over time, and patients may occasionally have jaundice, which usually resolves on its own with no ill effects.

UDP-Glucoronyltransferase is required for the conjugation of bilirubin.

Option B: Dubin-Johnson syndrome is a benign autosomal recessive disease that is characterized by chronic conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and conspicuous brown-black melanin-like pigment deposition in the liver. The disease is caused by mutation in multidrug resistance protein 2 (MRP-2) in hepatocytes, which is required for the transport of non-bile salt organic anions at the canalicular membranes. Liver biopsy shows characteristic deposition of black-coloured pigment.

Option C: Rotor syndrome: similar to Dubin-Johnson syndrome but with a milder presentation and increased conjugated bilirubin levels. The liver biopsy does not show a black-coloured liver.

Option D: Biliary atresia presents with clay-coloured stools, progressive jaundice, persistent acholic stools, and hepatomegaly. Laboratory investigations show conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT). Ultrasonography reveals a triangular cord sign (a hyperechoic area corresponding to the fibrous portion of the bile duct) and a small or absent gallbladder.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is associated with Vitamin A deficiency?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency is a leading cause of preventable blindness worldwide and manifests through a spectrum of ocular changes known as xerophthalmia. One of the most characteristic early clinical signs is the appearance of Bitot’s spots. These are dry, foamy, white or greyish patches that typically form on the bulbar conjunctiva, often in a triangular shape lateral to the limbus. They represent areas of squamous metaplasia and keratinization. Pinguecula (Option A) and Pterygium (Option C) are common degenerative growths related to chronic UV exposure and wind irritation, not nutritional deficiency. Stocker’s line (Option D) is a brownish iron deposit found at the leading edge of a pterygium. If left untreated, Vitamin A deficiency can progress from night blindness and Bitot’s spots to corneal drying (xerosis), ulceration, and eventually total melting of the cornea (keratomalacia). Supplementation programs and dietary education are critical public health interventions to combat this deficiency
questions.learning: Vitamin — A deficiency is a leading cause of preventable blindness worldwide and manifests through a spectrum of ocular changes known as xerophthalmia. One of the most characteristic early clinical signs is the appearance of Bitot’s spots.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 42-year-old man sustains a head injury following which blood accumulates around his eyes, leading to periorbital swelling. This presentation is due to disruption of a specific anatomical attachment. Which structural attachment is responsible for this condition??
questions.explanation: The condition described is "raccoon eyes" (periorbital ecchymosis), which often follows a head injury involving the scalp's loose areolar tissue layer. The scalp has five layers: Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica), Loose areolar tissue, and Periosteum. When bleeding occurs in the loose areolar tissue, the blood can track anteriorly into the eyelids. This happens because the epicranial aponeurosis has no bony attachment anteriorly; its fibers instead blend with the orbicularis oculi muscle. Conversely, the periosteum (Option B) is firmly attached at the sutures, which would prevent such extensive tracking of fluid. Cellulitis (Option C) is a bacterial skin infection that presents with warmth, redness, and fever, rather than immediate post-traumatic blood collection. The "raccoon eyes" sign is a critical clinical indicator of a basal skull fracture or severe scalp trauma, facilitated specifically by the lack of an anterior bony attachment of the aponeurosis
questions.learning: The condition described is "raccoon eyes" (periorbital ecchymosis), which often follows a head injury involving the scalp's loose areolar tissue layer.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the most effective method for locating an extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma?
questions.explanation: Pheochromocytomas are catecholamine-secreting tumors. While 90% are in the adrenal medulla, "extra-adrenal" types (paragangliomas) can occur anywhere along the sympathetic chain. The most effective method for locating these ectopic tumors is a nucleotide scan (Option C), specifically the MIBG (Meta-iodobenzoguanidine) scan. MIBG is a catecholamine precursor that is taken up by chromaffin tissue, allowing the scan to "light up" the tumor anywhere in the body. VMA excretion (Option B) (urinary vanillylmandelic acid) is a biochemical test used to diagnose the presence of a tumor but cannot locate it. X-rays (Option A) are not sensitive enough to detect these soft-tissue masses. Clinical examination (Option D) may detect hypertension or a rare abdominal mass but is not an accurate localization tool . MIBG scans are superior to CT/MRI for extra-adrenal cases because they identify functionally active tumors across a whole-body survey. Therefore, functional imaging via nucleotide scanning is the gold standard for localization
questions.learning: Pheochromocytomas are catecholamine-secreting tumors. While 90% are in the adrenal medulla, "extra-adrenal" types (paragangliomas) can occur anywhere along the sympathetic chain.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are the consequences of a deficiency in Vitamin A?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A is essential for vision and the maintenance of epithelial tissues. A severe deficiency leads to Xerophthalmia, a spectrum of ocular changes ranging from night blindness (nyctalopia) to conjunctival xerosis, Bitot's spots, and eventually keratomalacia (total melting of the cornea), which results in irreversible blindness. Beriberi (Option A) is caused by a deficiency of Vitamin B1 (Thiamine). Pellagra (Option B) results from a deficiency of Vitamin B3 (Niacin). Neuropathy (Option D) can be caused by various B-vitamin deficiencies (B1, B6, B12) or Vitamin E deficiency, but is not the hallmark of Vitamin A lack. Vitamin A is a critical component of rhodopsin in the retina, allowing for low-light vision. It also regulates the differentiation of mucus-secreting goblet cells; without it, the ocular surface becomes dry and keratinized. Universal Vitamin A supplementation for children in endemic areas is a major global health priority for preventing childhood blindness and reducing mortality from infections

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman presents with difficulty reading and eye strain while focusing on near objects. She has a known history of myopia and has recently developed these new symptoms. On detailed ophthalmic evaluation, she is found to have an atypical form of presbyopia in which the horizontal meridian is more powerful than the vertical meridian. Which combination of cylindrical lenses would be most suitable to correct her refractive error?
questions.explanation: The question describes an atypical presbyopia with astigmatism, where the horizontal meridian is more powerful than the vertical meridian. This means the eye has greater refractive power in the horizontal (180°) meridian, so it requires less plus (or more minus) correction compared to the vertical meridian. In cylindrical lens notation: 1. Axis 180° corrects the horizontal meridian 2. Axis 90° corrects the vertical meridian Since the horizontal meridian is already more powerful, it needs relatively less convex (+) correction or more concave (−) effect. The vertical meridian, being weaker, needs more plus power. Option (A) provides: 1. +5.00 DC × 180 (moderate correction for horizontal meridian) 2. −3.00 DC × 90 (effectively increases power difference between meridians) This combination creates the appropriate power difference between the two principal meridians, correcting the astigmatic imbalance. Other options: (B) Both positive → no differential correction (C) Both negative → incorrect for presbyopia (D) Insufficient correction

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Considering the structural organization of the esophageal wall, which consists of several distinct layers, which of the following is NOT a recognized layer of the esophagus?
questions.explanation: The esophagus is unique among the organs of the gastrointestinal tract because it lacks a true serosa. Most other abdominal digestive organs are covered by a serous membrane (visceral peritoneum). Instead, the outermost layer of the esophagus is the adventitia, which consists of loose connective tissue that anchors the esophagus to surrounding structures in the mediastinum. The other listed layers are standard components of the esophageal wall: the mucosa (Option A), which is the innermost lining; the submucosa (Option B), which contains glands and blood vessels; and the muscularis externa (Option D), which consists of both skeletal and smooth muscle layers to facilitate peristalsis. The absence of a serosa is clinically important because it allows esophageal infections and tumors to spread more easily into the surrounding mediastinal space, often leading to more rapid complications compared to organs with a protective serous layer
questions.learning: The esophagus is unique among the organs of the gastrointestinal tract because it lacks a true serosa. Most other abdominal digestive organs are covered by a serous membrane (visceral peritoneum).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: One week after having unprotected sexual intercourse, a 25-year-old male develops urethral discharge as shown in the image below. What is the most likely causative organism for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neisseria gonorrheae

The given image shows purulent urethral discharge that developed one week after unprotected sexual intercourse is suggestive of acute urethritis. The most likely causative organism for acute urethritis in males is Neisseria gonorrheae.

Purulent urethral discharge can be seen in gonorrhea caused by Neisseria gonorrhea or lymphogranuloma venerum caused by Chlamydia trachomatis.

Gonorrhea:

Gonorrhea is a disease acquired by sexual contact. The first step in infection is the infection of gonococci to the urethra or other mucosal surfaces. Pilli is involved in this adhesion. The cocci penetrate the intracellular spaces and reach subepithelial tissue by the third day of infection. The incubation period is 2-8 days. The major symptoms include urethral discharge and dysuria, usually without urinary frequency or urgency. The specific symptoms seen in males and females are as follows:

In males :

• The disease starts as acute urethritis. This infection may extend along the urethra to involve the prostate, seminal vesicles, and epididymis.
• Chronic urethritis may lead to stricture formation.
• The infection may spread to the periurethral tissues causing abscesses and multiple discharging sinuses (watercan perineum).

In females :

• The initial infection involves the cervix uteri and urethra which may extend to Bartholin glands, endometrium, and fallopian tubes.
• The vaginal mucosa is not usually affected in adults because the stratified squamous epithelium is resistant to infection by the cocci, and also because of the acidic pH of vaginal secretions.
• Pelvic inflammatory disease and salpingitis may lead to sterility.
• Rarely peritonitis may develop with perihepatic inflammation (Fitz Hugh Curtis syndrome)

Lab diagnosis:

The discharge is collected and subjected to Gram's stain which reveals gram‐negative intracellular diplococci within phagocytes. Stuart's transport medium is used. Cultures can be obtained from chocolate agar or Mueller-Hinton agar. Specifically, Thayer-Martin agar is used to isolate Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

Treatment: Ceftriaxone (250mg, IM) single-dose + azithromycin 1 g PO, single-dose, or doxycycline 100 mg PO BD for 7 days

The image below shows the Gram-stain of a urethral exudate showing typical intracellular gram-negative diplococci and pleomorphic extracellular gram-negative organisms

Non-gonococcal urethritis is caused by:

• Chlamydia trachomatis
• Ureaplasma urealyticum (Option-B)
• Mycoplasma genitalium
• Trichomonas vaginalis (Option-D)
• Herpes simplex virus (rare)
• Adenovirus
• Haemophillus vaginalis
• Mycoplasma genitalium

Other options:

Option B: Ureaplasma urealyticum is the second most common cause of non-gonococcal urethritis next to chlamydia. That is why the initial etiological agent under suspicion always remains gonorrhea.

Option C: Herpes Simplex will be associated with vesicular lesions.

Option D: Trichomonas vaginalis generally presents with a frothy discharge.
questions.learning: Neisseria gonorrheae — The given image shows purulent urethral discharge that developed one week after unprotected sexual intercourse is suggestive of acute urethritis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A hospital is comparing two treatment strategies for the same disease. Treatment A costs ₹5,000 and has a 70% success rate, whereas Treatment B costs ₹8,000 with an 85% success rate. Which of the following economic evaluation methods is most appropriate for comparing these interventions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cost-effectiveness analysis

Cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) is used when interventions are compared based on cost (monetary units) and clinical outcomes measured in natural units, such as treatment success, life-years gained, cases prevented, or blood pressure reduction. Since the outcome here is success rate (%), CEA is the appropriate method.

Why not the other options?

• A. Cost-benefit analysis: Both costs and benefits are expressed in monetary terms (e.g., ₹ saved), which is not the case here.
• C. Cost-utility analysis: Outcomes are measured in quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) or disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), not simple treatment success.
• D. Cost-minimization analysis: Applicable only when both interventions have equivalent clinical effectiveness, which is not true here.

High-Yield Pearl:

The Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio (ICER) is calculated as: ICER = (Cost₂ − Cost₁) ÷ (Effect₂ − Effect₁)

In this example:

• Additional cost = ₹8,000 − ₹5,000 = ₹3,000
• Additional effectiveness = 85% − 70% = 15%

ICER = ₹3,000 ÷ 15 = ₹200 per 1% additional treatment success, making this a classic example of cost-effectiveness analysis.
questions.learning: Cost-effectiveness analysis Cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) is used when interventions are compared based on cost (monetary units) and clinical outcomes measured in natural units, such as treatment success, life-years gained, cases prevented, or blood…

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following topical local anesthetics is commonly used in cataract surgery?
questions.explanation: In modern ophthalmic practice, particularly for small-incision cataract surgery, topical anesthesia is frequently used. Proparacaine 0.5% is the most common topical local anesthetic applied to the corneal surface. It provides rapid, effective surface anesthesia with a fast onset (within 30 seconds) and minimal corneal irritation. Bupivacaine 0.5% (Option B) is a long-acting anesthetic typically used for regional nerve blocks (like retrobulbar or peribulbar blocks) but is not the standard agent for purely topical application. Halothane (Option C) and Nitrous Oxide (Option D) are inhalation anesthetics used for general anesthesia, not for topical numbing. Topical anesthesia is preferred for its safety, immediate visual recovery, and avoidance of the risks associated with needle-based blocks, such as globe perforation or retrobulbar hemorrhage. It is often supplemented with intracameral lidocaine to ensure patient comfort during manipulation of the lens and iris
questions.learning: In modern ophthalmic practice, particularly for small-incision cataract surgery, topical anesthesia is frequently used. Proparacaine 0.5% is the most common topical local anesthetic applied to the corneal surface.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: All of the following can activate Hormone- sensitive lipase. Except?
questions.explanation: Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) is a key enzyme in adipocytes responsible for the breakdown of stored triacylglycerols into free fatty acids and glycerol (lipolysis). It is activated by phosphorylation in response to hormones that signal a need for energy. Glucagon (Option A), Epinephrine (Option B), and ACTH (Option C) all bind to G-protein coupled receptors that increase intracellular cAMP, thereby activating HSL. Insulin, conversely, is the primary inhibitor of HSL. When blood glucose is high, insulin is secreted to promote fat storage (lipogenesis) and inhibit the breakdown of fat. It acts by activating a phosphatase that dephosphorylates and inactivates HSL, effectively shutting down lipolysis. This regulatory mechanism ensures that fat stores are mobilized only when other energy sources are low. Therefore, insulin is the exception among the hormones listed, as its role is to suppress rather than activate this enzyme
questions.learning: Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) is a key enzyme in adipocytes responsible for the breakdown of stored triacylglycerols into free fatty acids and glycerol (lipolysis).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following CT findings is not an indication to perform angiography in a splenic trauma patient under conservative management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Subcapsular hematoma covering 40% surface area

In a splenic trauma patient under conservative management, angiography is indicated if the CT shows a high-grade injury rather than a low-grade injury (subcapsular hematoma covering 40% surface area is a grade II injury).

In splenic trauma patients that are managed conservatively, angiography is indicated if there is the presence of the following CT findings:

* Contrast extravasation

* Presence of pseudoaneurysm

* Significant hemoperitoneum

* High-grade injury

* Evidence of vascular injury

Management of Splenic trauma:

Grade I and II injuries:

* They are usually hemodynamically stable and are managed non-operatively.

* Initially, these patients are managed conservatively with regular monitoring of vitals and serial CECT.

* If the grade of injury is found to increase, then angiography and embolization of the bleeding vessel are done to achieve hemostasis.

* If angiography and embolization fail to achieve hemostasis, or if the patient becomes hemodynamically unstable or if there is a contrast blush, then a splenorrhaphy is done.

Grade III injuries that are hemodynamically stable are managed like that of Grades I and II, while those that are hemodynamically unstable are managed like that of Grades IV and V.

Grade IV and V injuries: These patients are usually hemodynamically unstable and splenectomy is done.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old man presents with gynecomastia. Ultrasonography (USG) reveals a 1-cm solid mass within the body of the testis. His serum testosterone is 600 ng/dL and estradiol is 35 pg/mL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Leydig cell tumour

A 40-year-old man presenting with gynecomastia, testicular mass, and increased sex hormones is most likely to have  Leydig cell tumor of the testis.

Leydig cell tumor:

* It is the most common sex-cord stromal type of testicular neoplasm.

* It is mostly benign and invariably unilateral.

* Most cases occur between 20 and 60 years of age; however, it can present at any age.

* The most common presenting feature is testicular swelling or gynecomastia (~15% of cases).

* In children, hormonal effects manifested primarily as sexual precocity, are the dominant features.

* Tumors of Leydig cells may secrete androgens and estrogens, and even corticosteroids.

Grossly: Golden brown, homogeneous circumscribed nodules <5 cm in diameter.

Histologically:

* large, round, or polygonal cells

* round central nucleus and prominent nucleoli

* abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm containing lipid droplets, vacuoles, or lipofuscin pigment

* crystalloids of Reinke, rod-shaped eosinophilic cytoplasmic bodies are seen in about 25% of the tumors

Other options:

* Sertoli cell tumor mostly presents as a painless testicular mass. They are usually hormonally silent but sometimes produces estrogen. In this patient, increased testosterone along with gynaecomastia make Leydig cell more likley.

* Spermatocytic tumor mainly occurs in older adults as a slow-growing testicular mass. They do not secrete any hormones.

* Granulosa cell tumor usually presents as a slow-growing and non-functioning testicular mass. Gynecomastia is rare.
questions.learning: Leydig cell tumour — A 40-year-old man presenting with gynecomastia, testicular mass, and increased sex hormones is most likely to have Leydig cell tumor of the testis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 5-year-old child was brought by her mother to the outpatient department with an abdominal swelling. She has mild discomfort but no other symptoms of pain or vomiting. On examination, the swelling is fluctuant, soft in consistency, and moves freely in a plane perpendicular to the attachment of mesentery. What is the most likely diagnosis here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chylolymphatic cyst

The given clinical scenario is typical of the mesenteric cyst with a positive Tillaux sign. The most common type of cyst is chylolymphatic cyst.

In chylolymphatic cyst there is congenitally misplaced lymphatic tissue which has no efferent communication with the lymphatic system.The thin wall of the cyst, is composed of connective tissue, lined by flat endothelium, and is filled with clear lymph or chyle.

Mesenteric cyst:

* Cysts may occur in the mesentery of the small intestine or the colon and can be of different types:

* Chylolymphatic

* Enterogenous

* Urogenital remnant

* Dermoid.

* Most commonly presents as painless abdominal swelling with the following characteristic physical signs,

* Fluctuant swelling near the umbilicus

* Swelling moves freely in a plane at right angles to the attachment of the mesentery (Tillaux’s sign)

* Presence of zone of resonance around the cyst

* Investigations- USG and CT scan demonstrate the type of cyst.

* Treatment of choice is enucleation with or without resection of the bowel.
questions.learning: Chylolymphatic cyst — The given clinical scenario is typical of the mesenteric cyst with a positive Tillaux sign. The most common type of cyst is chylolymphatic cyst.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient presents with excessive thirst and markedly increased urine output of about 6–7 liters per day, with a history of cerebral trauma one month earlier. What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: Post-traumatic polyuria (6–7 L/day) and polydipsia after head injury are hallmark signs of Central Diabetes Insipidus (CDI). CDI results from damage to the posterior pituitary or hypothalamus, leading to a deficiency of Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH). The most appropriate and first-line treatment is Desmopressin (DDAVP), a synthetic vasopressin analog. Desmopressin binds to renal V2 receptors, promoting water reabsorption and correcting the fluid imbalance. Hydrochlorothiazide (Option A) is used for nephrogenic DI, where the kidneys are resistant to ADH, but is not first-line for CDI. Tolvaptan (Option C) is a V2 receptor antagonist used to treat SIADH (fluid overload), which would worsen DI. Insulin (Option D) is for diabetes mellitus, which is an unrelated disorder of glucose metabolism. Therefore, replacing the missing hormone with desmopressin is the correct clinical intervention
questions.learning: Post-traumatic polyuria (6–7 L/day) and polydipsia after head injury are hallmark signs of Central Diabetes Insipidus (CDI). CDI results from damage to the posterior pituitary or hypothalamus, leading to a deficiency of Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Safety pin appearance is seen in -
questions.explanation: In microbiology, the term "safety pin appearance" refers to bipolar staining, where the ends of the bacterium stain more intensely than the center. This characteristic is famously seen in Burkholderia pseudomallei, the causative agent of Melioidosis. It is also classically associated with Yersinia pestis (the plague bacillus). Haemophilus influenzae (Option A) is a pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacillus but does not characteristically show this bipolar pattern. Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Option C) and Burkholderia cepacia (Option D) are typical Gram-negative rods without the distinct safety pin morphology. Burkholderia pseudomallei is an environmental saprophyte common in soil and water in Southeast Asia and Northern Australia. Melioidosis can present as acute pneumonia, localized abscesses, or overwhelming septicemia. Recognizing this specific staining pattern on a Gram or Wayson stain can provide a critical early diagnostic clue for this potentially biothreat agent
questions.learning: In microbiology, the term "safety pin appearance" refers to bipolar staining, where the ends of the bacterium stain more intensely than the center. This characteristic is famously seen in Burkholderia pseudomallei, the causative agent of Melioidosis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A lady developed a skin reaction as shown in the image after using a hair dye. Which of the following chemicals is responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. p-Phenylenediamine

This is most likely a case of hypersensitivity reaction caused by p-phenylenediamine (PPD), which is present in hair dyes.

Hair dyes such as PPD have the potential to cause contact dermatitis. 10% of PPD users tend to develop contact dermatitis. A patch test is recommended 24-48 hours before its usage either on the forearm or behind the ear. The appearance of any redness, blistering, or swelling implies allergy;  therefore, the application of dye is not recommended. Cross-sensitization with other aromatic benzenes is also noted, which needs to be avoided.

Hair dyes can trigger acute edema and intense pruritus, followed by desquamation. Hair dye can elicit an allergic reaction on the forehead. PPD in the hair dye can also cause an erythema multiforme–like reaction.

In PPD-associated allergies, there is edema and weeping of the scalp margins, eyes, and ears. There may be relative sparing of the scalp. Immediate hypersensitivity reactions present as urticaria, and contact anaphylaxis have also been noted to occur in patients using PPD.  To minimize the risk of an allergic reaction to hair dye, individuals should follow the manufacturer's instructions, perform a patch test, and avoid over-processing the hair. Treatment for PPD-induced contact dermatitis may include topical corticosteroids, oral antihistamines, and in severe cases, oral corticosteroids.

Other options:

Option A: Pollen is not typically found in hair dyes and is not responsible for this condition. Pollen allergies usually present as hay fever or seasonal allergic rhinitis.

Option B: Chromates, which can be found in cement, leather, and paints, are not typically present in hair dyes and are not responsible for this skin reaction.

Option C: Balsam of Peru, a fragrant resin, is found in various cosmetic and food products but is not a common component of hair dyes. It is less likely to be responsible for this condition compared to PPD.
questions.learning: p-Phenylenediamine This is most likely a case of hypersensitivity reaction caused by p-phenylenediamine (PPD), which is present in hair dyes. Hair dyes such as PPD have the potential to cause contact dermatitis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: How long does lochial discharge typically last in a woman after childbirth?
questions.explanation: Lochia is the physiological vaginal discharge following delivery, consisting of blood, mucus, and placental tissue. It progresses through three stages: lochia rubra, serosa, and alba. While the initial heavy red discharge (rubra) lasts only a few days, the entire process of uterine involution and shedding typically results in a discharge that persists for 24 to 36 days (roughly 4 to 5 weeks). Option A and B are too short, representing only the initial inflammatory stages. Option D (up to 42 days or 6 weeks) is the absolute upper limit of the puerperium, but most women find that the discharge tapers off before this point. Clinical monitoring of lochia is essential to identify secondary postpartum hemorrhage or endometritis (infection) if the discharge becomes foul-smelling or remains bright red after the first week. Therefore, the average clinical duration for standard lochial discharge is recognized as the 4-week window
questions.learning: Lochia is the physiological vaginal discharge following delivery, consisting of blood, mucus, and placental tissue. It progresses through three stages: lochia rubra, serosa, and alba.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old primigravida presents with painful vaginal bleeding during the first trimester. Ultrasonography shows a well-formed gestational sac with central embryonic echoes and visible fetal cardiac activity, indicating a viable fetus. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario of vaginal bleeding in the first trimester with a confirmed viable fetus (fetal cardiac motion) and an intrauterine gestational sac on ultrasound is diagnostic of a threatened abortion. In this condition, the internal cervical os remains closed, and the pregnancy has a high chance of continuing successfully with conservative management. In an inevitable abortion (Option A), the cervical os is open, and miscarriage is certain. Incomplete abortion (Option C) involves the partial expulsion of products of conception through an open os. A complete abortion (Option D) is characterized by the total expulsion of products followed by os closure. Since the ultrasound confirms a healthy, living embryo despite the bleeding, the diagnosis remains "threatened" rather than inevitable or complete
questions.learning: The clinical scenario of vaginal bleeding in the first trimester with a confirmed viable fetus (fetal cardiac motion) and an intrauterine gestational sac on ultrasound is diagnostic of a threatened abortion.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A maid is playing with a child by spinning him while holding his hands. A few hours later, the child starts crying, does not use his arm, and does not let anybody touch him. What is the possible diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pulled elbow

The given scenario of spinning the child by holding his hands, followed by features suggesting pain and inability to use the arm, points to a diagnosis of pulled elbow.

Pulled elbow or nursemaid's elbow refers to the dislocation of the radial head over the annular ligament, commonly seen in children under the age of 6 years. The mechanism of injury is through axial traction on the extended and pronated forearm. This happens when a child is pulled, lifted, or swung by the arm.

Following the dislocation, the child holds the arm relatively immobile, with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated, and resists supination.

The diagnosis is primarily clinical, though X-rays are usually obtained to exclude a fracture.

To treat the condition, simple analgesia is administered, and while the child's attention is diverted, the elbow is extended and pronated to relocate the radial head with a snap. This technique is preferred over the alternative method of supination and flexion, which tends to be more painful and less successful.
questions.learning: Pulled elbow — The given scenario of spinning the child by holding his hands, followed by features suggesting pain and inability to use the arm, points to a diagnosis of pulled elbow.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is found to have a ring-shaped lytic lesion in the bone on imaging. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A ring-shaped lytic lesion surrounded by a thick, reactive sclerotic rim is the classic radiographic appearance of a Brodie's abscess. This is a localized, subacute or chronic form of osteomyelitis, most often found in the metaphysis of long bones like the tibia. The central lytic area represents pus, while the sclerotic rim is new bone laid down in response to the infection. A simple bone cyst (Option B) appears as a lucent area but typically lacks the thick sclerotic border. An aneurysmal bone cyst (Option C) is characterized by an expansile "soap bubble" appearance and internal fluid levels, not a simple ring shape. An osteoid osteoma (Option D) involves a very small radiolucent "nidus" within a massive area of cortical sclerosis, differing from the balanced ring lesion seen here. Therefore, Brodie's abscess is the most accurate diagnosis

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 28-year-old patient presents with severe ear pain and unilateral facial weakness. Examination reveals vesicular lesions in the external auditory canal and on the tympanic membrane, along with inability to smile or close the eye on the affected side. What is the most likely diagnosis, and which part of the nervous system is involved?
options: Ramsay Hunt syndrome and basal ganglion
Ramsay Hunt syndrome and geniculate ganglion
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of facial nerve palsy (difficulty smiling/closing eyelids), severe ear pain, and vesicular eruptions in the external ear canal is pathognomonic for Ramsay Hunt syndrome (Herpes Zoster Oticus). This condition results from the reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus specifically within the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve (Cranial Nerve VII). Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome (Options C and D) is a rare neurological disorder characterized by a triad of recurrent facial paralysis, swelling of the face and lips, and a fissured tongue, but it does not involve painful vesicles. The basal ganglion (Option A) is involved in movement disorders like Parkinson's, not peripheral nerve palsies. Management of Ramsay Hunt syndrome requires urgent initiation of antiviral medications (acyclovir) and oral corticosteroids to reduce nerve inflammation. Early treatment is critical, as the prognosis for facial nerve recovery in Ramsay Hunt is generally poorer than in standard Bell's palsy
questions.learning: The clinical triad of facial nerve palsy (difficulty smiling/closing eyelids), severe ear pain, and vesicular eruptions in the external ear canal is pathognomonic for Ramsay Hunt syndrome (Herpes Zoster Oticus).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most effective approach to managing mild nausea and vomiting in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: For the management of mild nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (morning sickness), lifestyle and dietary modifications are the recommended first-line treatments. This includes eating small, frequent meals throughout the day to avoid an empty stomach, which can trigger nausea. High-protein snacks and avoiding greasy or spicy foods are also beneficial. Increasing fluid intake (Option C) is important to prevent dehydration, but fluids should be taken between meals rather than with them to avoid over-distension of the stomach. Domperidone (Option B) and metoclopramide (Option D) are prokinetic medications that may be used in more persistent or severe cases (Hyperemesis Gravidarum), but they are not the "initial" approach for mild symptoms. Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) alone or in combination with doxylamine is the preferred first-line pharmacological agent if dietary changes are insufficient. Thus, simple behavioral and dietary adjustments remain the most effective starting point for mild symptoms
questions.learning: For the management of mild nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (morning sickness), lifestyle and dietary modifications are the recommended first-line treatments.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Conjunctival xerosis is caused by which vitamin deficiency?
questions.explanation: Conjunctival xerosis (drying of the conjunctiva) is one of the earliest clinical manifestations of Vitamin A deficiency and is a component of the xerophthalmia spectrum. Vitamin A is essential for maintaining the health of the epithelial surfaces and the function of the goblet cells that produce the lubricating mucus layer of the tear film. Without it, the conjunctiva becomes dry, dull, and loses its luster. This can progress to Bitot's spots—foamy white patches on the bulbar conjunctiva. Vitamin C deficiency (Option C) causes scurvy, which results in hemorrhages but not primary xerosis. Deficiencies in Vitamins K and D (Options B and D) do not have direct primary manifestations as ocular surface drying. Severe Vitamin A deficiency eventually leads to corneal xerosis and keratomalacia (total melting of the cornea), resulting in irreversible blindness. This is a major preventable public health problem in many developing nations. Prevention involves dietary diversification and national Vitamin A supplementation programs for young children
questions.learning: Conjunctival xerosis (drying of the conjunctiva) is one of the earliest clinical manifestations of Vitamin A deficiency and is a component of the xerophthalmia spectrum.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the mean pH of the vagina during pregnancy? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 4

During pregnancy, the vaginal pH becomes more acidic, with a mean pH of approximately 4.

• Increased estrogen causes accumulation of glycogen in vaginal epithelial cells
• Lactobacilli metabolize glycogen to lactic acid
• This lowers vaginal pH

Functions of acidic vaginal pH:

• Inhibits growth of pathogenic organisms
• Maintains normal vaginal flora
• Protects against ascending infections

Normal vaginal pH in reproductive-age women: Approximately 3.8–4.5

Despite acidic pH, pregnancy increases susceptibility to candidal infection due to high glycogen content.
