questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding at 12 weeks of gestation, diagnosed with a complete hydatidiform mole. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Suction and Evacuation

Suction evacuation (vacuum aspiration) is the treatment of choice for a hydatidiform mole, particularly in women who wish to preserve fertility, as it provides rapid and complete evacuation of molar tissue with minimal complications.

Why not the other options?

• B. Dilatation and Curettage (D&C): Less effective for complete molar evacuation and associated with greater blood loss; suction evacuation is preferred.
• C. Inj. Methotrexate: Not used for initial treatment; reserved for persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) or selected high-risk cases.
• D. Hysterectomy: Considered only in women who have completed childbearing or have uncontrolled bleeding/high risk of persistent disease; β-hCG surveillance is still required.
questions.learning: Suction and Evacuation Suction evacuation (vacuum aspiration) is the treatment of choice for a hydatidiform mole, particularly in women who wish to preserve fertility, as it provides rapid and complete evacuation of molar tissue with minimal complications.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with fatigue and pallor. Laboratory investigations reveal a hemoglobin level of 9.8 g/dL with a markedly increased MCV of 160 fL, while serum methylmalonyl-CoA levels are normal. Based on these findings, which treatment should be given?
questions.explanation: The patient has macrocytic anemia, as evidenced by the high MCV (160 fl; normal is 80-100 fl) and low hemoglobin. The two primary causes of megaloblastic macrocytic anemia are Vitamin B12 deficiency and Folic acid deficiency. To differentiate between them, serum methylmalonic acid (MMA) levels are used. Vitamin B12 is a cofactor for the conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA; thus, B12 deficiency results in "elevated" MMA. Since this patient’s MMA levels are "normal," a Vitamin B12 deficiency is ruled out, leaving "Folic acid deficiency" as the most likely cause. Folic acid (Option D) should be administered to correct the anemia. Administering B12 (Option A) would not be targeted. Iron (Option B) is used for microcytic anemia, and Vitamin C (Option C) for scurvy. Distinguishing these deficiencies is critical because treating a B12 deficiency with folic acid alone can mask the anemia while allowing irreversible neurological damage to continue
questions.learning: The patient has macrocytic anemia, as evidenced by the high MCV (160 fl; normal is 80-100 fl) and low hemoglobin. The two primary causes of megaloblastic macrocytic anemia are Vitamin B12 deficiency and Folic acid deficiency.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A female died due to an unnatural cause within 7 years of marriage, and allegations have been raised. Under which section will the inquest be conducted? BNS - Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 176 CrPC/196 BNSS

The given clinical scenario of a female who died due to an unnatural cause within 7 years of marriage suggests a possibility of dowry death. A magistrate inquest is done under BNSS Section 196 (Section 176 CrPC).

BNSS 196 (Section 176 CrPC) deals with magistrate inquest in which the cause of death is not under natural circumstances. Magistrate inquest may be conducted by the District Magistrate, Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Tahsildar, or any other Executive Magistrate empowered by the State Government.

Indications for Magistrate Inquest:

* Dowry death

* Custodial rape

* Death in police custody or police interrogation

* Death in police firing

* Death in prison, reformatories, Borstal school

* Death in a psychiatric hospital

* Cases of exhumation.

Other options:

Option A: Section 106 BNS (304A IPC) defines the punishment for causing the death of a person by any rash or negligent act, not amounting to culpable homicide, the punishment is imprisonment for up to 2 years, and a fine.

Option B:  BNSS Section 194 (Section 174 CrPC) deals with the police inquest. It is done in suicide, homicide, killing by any animal or machinery or accident, and death under circumstances that raise suspicion of another person committing the offence.

Option D: BNS Sec 89 (IPC 313) deals with the causation of miscarriage of a woman with child (and/or quick with child) without her consent. Only the person causing the abortion is liable to punishment.
questions.learning: 176 CrPC/196 BNSS The given clinical scenario of a female who died due to an unnatural cause within 7 years of marriage suggests a possibility of dowry death.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman comes to the OPD due to moderate pain in her lower back, hips, and knees for the past several weeks. She has no associated morning stiffness. The patient has end-stage renal disease due to diabetic nephropathy and has been on Hemodialysis for the past 2 years. Her other medical problems include type 1 diabetes mellitus diagnosed 20 years ago and sarcoidosis diagnosed 8 years ago. Physical examination shows no obvious bone or joint deformity, and she has full range of motion in all joints. Laboratory results are as follows: Sodium-136 mEq/L Potassium-3.9 mEq/L Bicarbonate-23 mEq/L Creatinine-3.1 mg/dL Calcium-7.9 mg/dL (N-8.5 to 10.5 mg/dl) Phosphorus-6.1 mg/dL (N-2.8 to 4.5 mg/dL) Albumin-4.1 g/dL (N-3.4 to 5.4 g/dL) Which of the following is the most likely histopathological abnormality underlying this patient's current symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. PTH hyperplasia

Chronic kidney disease (CKD) leads to secondary hyperparathyroidism due to disturbances in calcium-phosphate metabolism.

Mechanism:

• ↓ Renal phosphate excretion → Hyperphosphatemia
• ↓ Renal 1α-hydroxylase activity → ↓ calcitriol (active vitamin D)
• ↓ Intestinal calcium absorption → Hypocalcemia

These changes chronically stimulate the parathyroid glands, causing diffuse parathyroid hyperplasia and increased parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Infusion of which one of the following antibacterial agents may cause the ‘Red Man Syndrome’ characterized by rapid onset of erythematous rash and pruritus on the head, face, neck and upper trunk?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vancomycin

Red Man Syndrome is an infusion-related reaction caused by rapid IV administration of vancomycin. It is due to non-IgE-mediated histamine release from mast cells, producing:

• Rapid-onset flushing and erythema
• Pruritus
• Predominantly involving the face, neck, and upper trunk
• Sometimes hypotension and tachycardia

Why not other options?

• A. Vancomycin: Correct. Classic cause of Red Man Syndrome.
• B. Minocycline: Can cause dizziness, pigmentation, and hypersensitivity reactions, but not the classic Red Man Syndrome.
• C. Levofloxacin: Can cause QT prolongation, tendinopathy, CNS effects, and dysglycemia.
• D. Metronidazole: Common adverse effects include GI symptoms and a metallic taste; prolonged use can cause peripheral neuropathy.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 14-year-old male presented with a mushroom-like tumor in the distal femur for the past 2 years. Which of the following features will help the clinician to identify a malignant transformation?
options: Initially growth of the tumor was away from the joint, now the growth of tumor is towards the joint.
Tumor does not have malignant transformation potential.
Tumor is in continuation with bone marrow cavity of the normal bone.
Hyaline cap thickness on MRI is 2cms.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hyaline cap thickness on MRI is 2cms.

The given X-ray shows a well-defined exostosis pointing to the diagnosis of osteochondroma. 2cms thickness of hyaline cap thickness on MRI is suggestive of malignant transformation.

Osteochondroma can turn into low-grade chondrosarcoma but the malignant transformation is extremely rare(Option B). It should be suspected in the following cases:

1. Growth after skeletal maturity
2. Lucency in the bone
3. Additional scintigraphic activity
4. Cortical destruction
5. Pain after puberty
6. Soft tissue mass
7. Thickened cartilage cap >2 cm

Osteochondromas are common benign bone tumors mostly arising from the metaphysis of long bones. The cortical and medullary continuity of the tumor with the underlying bone is a pathognomonic feature that establishes the diagnosis. (Option C). The lesions consist of a bony mass, often in the form of a stalk, produced by endochondral ossification of a growing cartilaginous cap. Most of these lesions are asymptomatic and are discovered incidentally.

These are of two types: Pedunculated and sessile, pedunculated types are more common. The definite stalk is directed away from the physis(Option A). The lesions are usually covered with a cartilaginous cap which cannot be seen radiologically and hence the lesions are larger clinically than what their X-Ray appearance suggests. The important feature is that the host bone flares from the cortex into the osteochondroma.

Most patients are asymptomatic and never seek medical attention. However, symptomatic people may undergo resection.
questions.learning: Hyaline cap thickness on MRI is 2cms. The given X-ray shows a well-defined exostosis pointing to the diagnosis of osteochondroma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which cells, apart from natural killer (NK) cells, are capable of recognizing and destroying target cells bearing antibody-coated surface antigens through their effector functions?
questions.explanation: The process described is Antibody-Dependent Cellular Cytotoxicity (ADCC), an effector mechanism where immune cells actively lyse target cells that have been "tagged" by specific antibodies (usually IgG). While Natural Killer (NK) cells (Option A) are the most well-known mediators of ADCC, several other myeloid cells also possess the necessary Fc receptors to perform this task. Specifically, neutrophils, eosinophils, and macrophages (Option B and D) are all equipped to recognize antibody-bound targets and release cytotoxic granules to destroy them. Eosinophils are particularly famous for utilizing ADCC to kill large parasites like helminths. Because both neutrophils and eosinophils are listed together in Option C as additional cells capable of this function, it is the most complete and accurate choice. This mechanism bridges the innate and adaptive immune systems, allowing non-specific effector cells to target specific pathogens marked by antibodies
questions.learning: The process described is Antibody-Dependent Cellular Cytotoxicity (ADCC), an effector mechanism where immune cells actively lyse target cells that have been "tagged" by specific antibodies (usually IgG).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following statements accurately describes the Little's area?
options: Keisselbach's plexus is present in the Little' area
It is situated at the postero-inferior part of the nasal septum
Anastomoses of 7 major arteries occur here
questions.explanation: Little's area is a clinically significant region located on the antero-inferior part of the nasal septum (Option B is incorrect). It is famous for the presence of Kiesselbach’s plexus (Option A), which is a dense network of anastomosing vessels. This area is the most common site for epistaxis (nosebleeds), accounting for approximately 90% of cases, due to its vascularity and exposure to trauma and dry air (Option C is incorrect). The plexus is formed by the anastomosis of four (not seven) major arteries: the Anterior ethmoidal, Sphenopalatine, Greater palatine, and Superior labial arteries. Recognizing Little's area is essential for clinicians as it is the primary target for anterior nasal packing or chemical cautery with silver nitrate to stop common nosebleeds. Therefore, the presence of the Kiesselbach's plexus is the definitive anatomical hallmark of this region. Accurate localization helps in directing effective emergency treatment for pediatric and adult patients alike
questions.learning: Little's area is a clinically significant region located on the antero-inferior part of the nasal septum (Option B is incorrect). It is famous for the presence of Kiesselbach’s plexus (Option A), which is a dense network of anastomosing vessels.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Please determine the size of the thyroid gland based on the provided image.
questions.explanation: The thyroid gland extends from C5 to T1 vertebral levels, which corresponds to: 1. A = C5 (upper limit) 2. D = T1 (lower limit) 3. So, the correct range is A to D. The thyroid gland is located in the anterior neck, just below the larynx, and lies opposite the C5 to T1 vertebrae. It consists of two lateral lobes connected by an isthmus that lies anterior to the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th tracheal rings. The superior poles of the thyroid reach up to the level of the thyroid cartilage (around C5), while the inferior poles extend downward to approximately the C7–T1 level. Radiologically, especially in lateral neck X-rays, these vertebral landmarks are used to estimate the size and extent of the thyroid gland. Since the gland spans from C5 (A) to T1 (D), the correct option is A to D. Other options are incorrect because: 1. B to D misses the upper limit (C5) 2. A to C misses the lower extension (T1) 3. C to D includes only the lower portion of the gland
questions.learning: The thyroid gland extends from C5 to T1 vertebral levels, which corresponds to: 1. The thyroid gland is located in the anterior neck, just below the larynx, and lies opposite the C5 to T1 vertebrae.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In the adjacent graph, plateau phase represents which one of the following properties?
questions.explanation: The provided graph is a cystometrogram, which plots intravesical pressure against volume during bladder filling. The plateau phase (Phase II) of this curve represents the property of plasticity (also known as accommodation). During this phase, the bladder volume increases significantly with only a minimal rise in pressure. This is due to the inherent ability of the smooth muscle (detrusor) to relax and reorganize its fibers as it stretches, allowing the bladder to store large amounts of urine without reaching the micturition threshold prematurely. Elasticity (Option A) refers to the immediate return to original shape after stretching, but plasticity describes the sustained adaptation to new volumes. Contractility (Option C) is the active phase (Phase III) where the muscle shortens to expel urine, resulting in a sharp pressure rise. Automaticity (Option D) refers to self-initiated contraction, which is generally not a feature of a normal bladder under this filling test. Thus, plasticity is the specific physiological property illustrated by the long plateau
questions.learning: The provided graph is a cystometrogram, which plots intravesical pressure against volume during bladder filling. The plateau phase (Phase II) of this curve represents the property of plasticity (also known as accommodation).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 70 kg elderly athlete undergoes surgery and is administered succinylcholine due to the unavailability of vecuronium. A total of 640 mg of succinylcholine is given intermittently. During recovery, the patient is unable to breathe spontaneously or move limbs. What is the explanation?
options: Pseudocholinesterase deficiency increasing action of succinylcholine
Undiagnosed muscular dystrophy and muscular weakness
Muscular weakness due to fasciculation produced by succinylcholine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phase 2 blockade produced by succinylcholine

A total dose of 640 mg succinylcholine in a 70-kg patient is excessive and can convert the usual phase I depolarizing block into a phase II (desensitizing) block. Phase II block resembles a non-depolarizing neuromuscular block, with flaccid paralysis, TOF fade, and prolonged apnea, explaining the inability to breathe or move during recovery.

Why others are incorrect:

• A. Pseudocholinesterase deficiency increasing action of succinylcholine: Causes prolonged block after normal doses, not massive cumulative dosing.
• C. Undiagnosed muscular dystrophy and muscular weakness: Would cause hyperkalemia and cardiac issues, not isolated prolonged paralysis.
• D. Muscular weakness due to fasciculations produced by succinylcholine: Cause transient myalgia, not prolonged apnea or paralysis.
questions.learning: Phase 2 blockade produced by succinylcholine — A total dose of 640 mg succinylcholine in a 70-kg patient is excessive and can convert the usual phase I depolarizing block into a phase II (desensitizing) block.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Identify A and B in the image of the mosquito larvae given.
questions.explanation: Mosquito larvae are identified by their resting position and breathing structures. Larva A rests horizontally parallel to the water surface and lacks a respiratory siphon, which is characteristic of Anopheles. Larva B rests at a 45-degree angle to the surface and possesses a long respiratory siphon, identifying it as Culex. Aedes larvae (Option A) also rest at an angle but have a much shorter, barrel-shaped siphon. Mansonia larvae (Option D) have a specialized siphon used to attach to the roots of aquatic plants for breathing. Anopheles is the vector for malaria, while Culex transmits filariasis and Japanese encephalitis. Thus, the horizontal versus angled resting positions are the primary visual cues for distinguishing these two common genera
questions.learning: Mosquito larvae are identified by their resting position and breathing structures. Larva A rests horizontally parallel to the water surface and lacks a respiratory siphon, which is characteristic of Anopheles.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Primary level of prevention for specific protection includes all of the following except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hand washing

Handwashing is not a specific protection measure under primary prevention. All other options are protection measures against specific diseases.
questions.learning: Hand washing Handwashing is not a specific protection measure under primary prevention. All other options are protection measures against specific diseases.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 27-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a history of eye trauma caused by vegetative matter. He complains of mild ocular pain, photophobia, and redness. On examination, a corneal ulcer is seen along with hypopyon and characteristic satellite lesions surrounding the ulcer. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The history of ocular trauma involving vegetative matter (like a branch or leaf) is the classic predisposing factor for fungal keratitis. The examination findings of a corneal ulcer accompanied by a hypopyon (pus in the anterior chamber) and, most significantly, satellite lesions (small infiltrates separate from the main ulcer), are diagnostic hallmarks of a fungal etiology. Acanthamoeba keratitis (Option B) typically presents in contact lens wearers with severe pain and a ring infiltrate. Viral keratitis (Option C) classically shows a dendritic or geographic ulcer pattern. Bacterial keratitis (Option D) usually has a more rapid, suppurative onset and lacks satellite lesions. Diagnosis should be confirmed by corneal scraping for KOH mount or culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar. Therefore, given the specific trauma history and pathognomonic satellite lesions, fungal keratitis is the most likely diagnosis

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient post-tonsillectomy in the recovery room starts bleeding from the operative site. On examination, blood clots are seen. What will be your immediate management?
options: Shift to OT, remove the clots, and cauterize/ligate the vessel
Shift to OT, start IV antibiotics, and pack the tonsillar fossa
Give anticoagulants, repeated gargling, and wait for 24 hours
Do blood transfusion and wait and watch
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Shift to OT, remove the clots, and cauterize/ligate the vessel

The given clinical picture suggests reactionary hemorrhage post-tonsillectomy. The immediate management is to shift the patient to OT, remove the clots, and cauterize/ligate the bleeding vessel.

Hemorrhage is a common complication of tonsillectomy. It can be primary, reactionary, or secondary.

Primary hemorrhage occurs at the time of operation. It can be controlled by pressure, ligation, or electrocoagulation of the bleeding vessels.

Reactionary hemorrhage occurs within 24 hours. It may be due to improper clipping action of the superior constrictor muscle.

The tonsillar artery perforates the superior constrictor and ramifies in the tonsil. Therefore, the presence of a clot can hinder the clipping action of the superior constrictor muscle, leading to hemorrhage. Slippage of ligature, or blood pressure returning to normal are other causes.

It is managed by removing the clot and application of pressure or vasoconstrictor. Ligation or electrocoagulation of the bleeding vessels is done under anesthesia if the above measures fail.

The image below shows the relation between the superior constrictor muscle and the tonsillar artery at the tonsillar bed.

Secondary hemorrhage is usually seen between the 5th to 10th postoperative day, due to sepsis and premature separation of the membrane. Clots are removed, IV antibiotics are given and the bleeding vessel is electrocoagulated or ligated if bleeding continues.
questions.learning: Shift to OT, remove the clots, and cauterize/ligate the vessel The given clinical picture suggests reactionary hemorrhage post-tonsillectomy. The immediate management is to shift the patient to OT, remove the clots, and cauterize/ligate the bleeding vessel.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 75-year-old man presented with temporal headache, jaw pain, exacerbated by chewing and talking. Which one of the following investigations will most likely help in diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Temporal artery biopsy

Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis) is a granulomatous vasculitis of medium- and large-sized arteries, classically affecting individuals >50 years of age. It presents with new-onset temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, and visual symptoms. Temporal artery biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis and should be performed promptly, although high-dose corticosteroids must be started immediately if the diagnosis is suspected to prevent irreversible blindness.

• A. Temporal artery biopsy:

• Gold standard investigation for Giant Cell Arteritis.
• Shows granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells, disruption of the internal elastic lamina, and intimal thickening.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Electromyography: Used to evaluate neuromuscular disorders, not vasculitis.
• C. MRI of the brain: May exclude intracranial pathology but does not diagnose Giant Cell Arteritis.
• D. Carotid colour Doppler: Evaluates carotid artery disease and stroke risk, but is not the diagnostic test for temporal arteritis.
questions.learning: Temporal artery biopsy Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis) is a granulomatous vasculitis of medium- and large-sized arteries, classically affecting individuals >50 years of age.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes are affected during the process of collagen synthesis due to vitamin C deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Prolyl hydroxylase

Deficiency of vitamin C results in a defective prolyl hydroxylase activity, leading to defective collagen formation.

Collagen is synthesized intracellularly in fibroblasts. Each polypeptide chain of collagen has about 1000 amino acid residues composed of Glycine-X-Y repeats, where X and Y are proline and hydroxyproline predominantly.

Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues takes place intracellularly as a part of post-translational modification with the help of prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase. This is a critical step in stabilizing the collagen triple helix. These enzymes require iron in a reduced state in its active site. Vitamin C/ascorbic acid keeps iron in a reduced state in these enzymes and thus helps in the maturation of collagen. Deficiency of vitamin C leads to scurvy which is characterized by bleeding tendencies, anemia, and skeletal abnormalities due to defective collagen in the connective tissue.

Steps of post-translational modification of collagen include:

* Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues.

* Glycosylation of hydroxylysine residues.

* Formation of intrachain and interchain disulfide bonds.

* Triple helix formation.

* Cleavage of 25–35 kDa portions at both carboxy and amino-terminal end.

* Quartered staggered arrangement.

* Oxidative deamination of lysine and hydroxylysine residues.

* Formation of intrachain and interchain crosslinks.

Other options:

Option B: Prolyl oxidase is an enzyme involved in oxidative reactions of proline metabolism, contributing to cellular redox balance. It plays a role in processes like collagen biosynthesis and amino acid catabolism.

Option D: Lysyl oxidase is a copper-containing enzyme that helps in covalent crosslinking collagen fibers. Deficiency of copper results in defective function of lysyl oxidase, and reduced cross-linkage of collagen leading to a condition called Menke's disease. Zinc has no role in collagen maturation.

Pearl PF0669: Synthesis of collagen and its disorders

1. Collagen backbone
Preprocollagen - Glycin-proline-lysine

2. Hydroxylation

Of proline and lysine in the presence of Vit C.

Deficiency of Vit C causes Scurvy.

3. Glycosylation
Formation of procollagen and resulting triple helix

4. Cleavage of terminals of procollagen
Resulting in the formation of tropocollagen

5. Cross-linking by lysyl oxidase (copper-containing enzyme)

Formation of mature collagen.

Defect causes Menkes disease and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 29-year-old man presents with coarse facial features and progressive enlargement of the hands and feet over the past 10 years. Investigations show elevated IGF-1 levels and failure of growth hormone suppression after a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test, confirming acromegaly. Which drug is recommended for the treatment of this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical description of coarse features and extremity enlargement in an adult is pathognomonic for Acromegaly, usually caused by a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma. When surgical resection is not feasible or curative, medical management is required. Lanreotide (or Octreotide) is a long-acting somatostatin analog and is the primary recommended pharmacological treatment. These drugs work by binding to somatostatin receptors on the pituitary tumor to directly inhibit the secretion of growth hormone. Terlipressin (Option B) is a vasopressin analog used for esophageal varices. Leuprolide (Option C) is a GnRH agonist used for prostate cancer or endometriosis. Ketoconazole (Option D) can inhibit steroid synthesis and is sometimes used for Cushing syndrome, not primarily for acromegaly. Somatostatin analogs not only lower GH and IGF-1 levels but can also lead to tumor shrinkage in some patients. They are typically administered as monthly depot injections. Precise hormonal control is vital to prevent the long-term cardiovascular and metabolic complications associated with excess growth hormone
questions.learning: The clinical description of coarse features and extremity enlargement in an adult is pathognomonic for Acromegaly, usually caused by a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: All the following are functions of the superior oblique muscle except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Adduction

The superior oblique muscle has three primary actions:

• Intorsion (primary action)
• Depression (especially in adducted eye)
• Abduction

Why A is correct (NOT a function):

• Adduction is NOT a function of the superior oblique
• Adduction is mainly performed by the medial rectus

Superior oblique passes through the trochlea, giving it a unique action:

• Pulls the eye downward and outward
• Rotates the top of the eye inward (intorsion)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text:
Inferior thyroid artery supplies which of the following structures?

1. Thyroid
2. Parathyroid
3. Esophagus
4. Thymus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3, and 4

All the given 4 structures are supplied by the Inferior thyroid artery.

Inferior thyroid artery is a branch of the thyrocervical trunk, which in turn, is a branch of the first part of the subclavian artery. The inferior thyroid artery loops upwards anterior to the medial border of the scalenus anterior, turns medially just below the sixth cervical transverse process, and then descends on longus colli to the lower border of the thyroid gland.

Branches:

• Pharyngeal branches: These supply the lower part of the pharynx.

• Tracheal branches supply the trachea and anastomose with the bronchial arteries;
• Oesophageal branches supply the oesophagus and anastomose with the oesophageal branches of the thoracic aorta; and
• Inferior and ascending glandular branches supply the posterior and inferior regions of the thyroid gland, and anastomose with the contralateral inferior and ipsilateral superior thyroid arteries.
• The ascending branch also supplies the parathyroid glands.

• Ascending cervical artery
• Inferior laryngeal
• Muscular branches

Note: Thymic branches originating from the internal thoracic, inferior thyroid artery, and sometimes superior thyroid arteries supply the thymus and the surrounding mediastinal connective tissue.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3, and 4 All the given 4 structures are supplied by the Inferior thyroid artery. Inferior thyroid artery is a branch of the thyrocervical trunk, which in turn, is a branch of the first part of the subclavian artery.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Xray of a 2 year old child is given, what is the possible diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pneumoperitoneum

The X-ray shows "football sign" which is seen in the pneumoperitoneum.

Football sign-the abdominal cavity is outlined by gas from a perforated viscus, seen in massive pneumoperitoneum.

Causes of pneumoperitoneum include:

* Bowel perforation

* Peptic ulcer

* Ischemic bowel

* Necrotizing enterocolitis

* Small bowel perforation

* Trauma

* Penetrating injuries

* During surgery/laparoscopy

Radiological signs in pneumoperitoneum include:

* Bowel related signs

* Double-wall sign (also known as Rigler's sign): Both the outer and inner walls of the bowel are visible.

* Telltale triangle sign (also known as triangle sign): A radiolucent triangle of gas between three loops of bowel or between two loops of bowel and the abdominal wall.

* Peritoneal ligament related signs

* Football sign -the abdominal cavity is outlined by gas from a perforated viscus, seen in massive pneumoperitoneum.

* Falciform ligament sign - Falciform or medial umbilical ligaments may be seen due to free gas on either side of the ligaments.

* Lateral umbilical ligament sign (also known as inverted "V" sign) - Free gas routines the lateral umbilical ligament.

* Urachus sign

* Right upper quadrant signs

* Morison's pouch sign - a triangular area of gas in the right upper quadrant, usually bound by the 11th rib in the right upper quadrant in the area of Morrison's pouch.

* Cupola sign - Gas under the right and left hemidiaphragm joining in the midline. Seen on chest X-ray.

* Fissure for ligamentum teres sign

* Hepatic edge sign

* Lucent liver sign

* Periportal free gas sign

Rigler's sign-

Falciform ligament sign.

Cupola sign-
questions.learning: Pneumoperitoneum — The X-ray shows "football sign" which is seen in the pneumoperitoneum. Football sign-the abdominal cavity is outlined by gas from a perforated viscus, seen in massive pneumoperitoneum.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The present day strategy of initial screening of women for cervical cancer in a primary health centre is:
options: Visual inspection after application of freshly prepared solution 5% acetic acid solution
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Visual inspection after application of freshly prepared solution 5% acetic acid solution

The present day strategy of initial screening of women for cervical cancer is by visual inspection after application of freshly prepared solution 5% acetic acid solution.

Visual inspection with acetic acid is naked-eye examination of the uterine cervix, after application of 5% acetic acid and interpreting the result after one minute. This is a simple and inexpensive test for the detection of cervical precancerous lesions and early invasive cancer.

* Detection of well defined circum- orificial acetowhite areas or ulceroproliferative growth on the cervix will provide VIA or VIAM positive.

* In the district hospital treatment should be based on single visit colposcopy approach.

* Biopsy and Colposcopy are done to ensure that there are cytological and histological backup for the interventions.
questions.learning: Visual inspection after application of freshly prepared solution 5% acetic acid solution The present day strategy of initial screening of women for cervical cancer is by visual inspection after application of freshly prepared solution 5% acetic acid solution.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following drug is not given in endometrosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Estradiol

Estradiol is not used in the treatment of endometriosis as estrogen administration leads to further development of endometriotic lesions.

Treatment of endometriosis:

1. Medical management:

For minimal disease, the drug of choice is NSAIDs. Oral contraceptive pills are given if associated menstrual complaints are present. OCPs inhibit gonadotropin release and decrease the menstrual flow.

For moderate to severe diseases, oral progestogens are the first drugs to be started. They antagonize estrogenic effects on the endometrium, causing endometrial atrophy. The drug of choice is GnRH agonist.

Endometriosis requires angiogenesis.Cabergoline, a vascular endothelial growth factor pathway inhibitor, is an effective therapeutic option for women with chronic pain due to endometriosis. (Option B)

Mnemonic to remember drugs used: GOLD GAP

• G: GnRH analog(Leuprolide)
• O: Oral contraceptive pills
• L: Letrozole(Option D)
• D: Danazol
• G: Gestrinone
• A: Antiprogesterone-Mifepristone
• P: Progesterone(Medroxyprogesterone acetate)(Option A)

2. Surgical management:

Primary surgery is preferred in infertile women because hormonal treatment would delay pregnancy.

• Conservative surgery: Endometrial deposits are destroyed by electrocautery/laser.
• Laparoscopic uterosacral nerve ablation (LUNA)
• Radical surgery: Total hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy.

Endometriosis is the presence of endometrial tissue (glands and stroma) outside the uterus.

Risk factors for the development of endometriosis

• Family history
• Nulliparity
• Prolonged exposure to endogenous estrogen (early menarche, late menopause)
• Estrogen therapy
• In utero exposure to diethylstilbesterol (DES)

Key clinical features

• Dysmenorrhea
• Lower abdominal pain
• Infertility
• Pain during urination or defecation
• Constipation or diarrhea
• Irregular bleeding

The gold standard for the diagnosis of endometriosis has been a visual inspection by laparoscopy, preferably with histological confirmation. Laparoscopy helps detect and diagnose pelvic endometriosis, locate the site of endometriosis and staging, take a biopsy, and perform surgical ablation as a part of treatment.

Other investigations:

• CA-125 levels: raised in endometriosis.
• Monocyte chemotactic protein (MCP-1) levels: raised in the peritoneal fluid
• MRI
• Color Doppler
• Anti-endometrial antibodies
questions.learning: Estradiol Estradiol is not used in the treatment of endometriosis as estrogen administration leads to further development of endometriotic lesions. Medical management: For minimal disease, the drug of choice is NSAIDs.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A gentleman of 60 years presented with a brawny swelling of the submandibular region with inflammatory oedema of mouth and putrid halitosis. Most likely he is suffering from:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ludwig’s angina

Ludwig’s angina is a rapidly progressive cellulitis involving the bilateral submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces, most commonly arising from an infected mandibular second or third molar tooth. It is a surgical emergency because of the risk of airway obstruction.

Why not other options?

• A. Tubercular adenitis: Presents as chronic, painless cervical lymph node enlargement, often with matted nodes and cold abscesses, not acute brawny swelling.
• B. Chronic lymphadenitis: Causes chronic lymph node enlargement without diffuse floor-of-mouth cellulitis or putrid halitosis.
• C. Acute lymphadenitis: Produces tender enlarged lymph nodes but does not cause the characteristic brawny submandibular swelling with floor-of-mouth edema.
questions.learning: Ludwig’s angina Ludwig’s angina is a rapidly progressive cellulitis involving the bilateral submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces, most commonly arising from an infected mandibular second or third molar tooth.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Feeding is done through the given method. Which of the following is not a complication of this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Aspiration pneumonia

The given image shows a central line. Pneumothorax, osteoporosis, and refeeding syndrome are likely complications in patients receiving total parenteral nutrition through a central line. Aspiration pneumonia is more common in enteral feeding and can be prevented by placing the patient in a semi-recumbent position while feeding.

Complications of enteral nutrition are as follows:

1. Tube-related (most common): Malposition, displacement, blockage, breakage/leakage, local complications (e.g. erosion of skin/mucosa)
2. Gastrointestinal: Diarrhoea, bloating, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, aspiration, constipation
3. Metabolic/biochemical: Electrolyte disorders, vitamin, mineral, and trace element deficiencies, drug interactions
4. Infective: Exogenous (handling contamination) and endogenous (patient)

Other options:

Option A: Refeeding syndrome is a significant metabolic complication of both parenteral and enteral feeding. It occurs days after feeding is commenced in patients who have been severely malnourished. The major pathological process is hypophosphatemia which causes fluid and electrolyte shifts between the intra- and extracellular compartments.

Option B: Osteoporosis and osteomalacia are complications of long-term parenteral nutrition and may lead to fractures or kidney stones. Calcium, phosphate, vitamin D supplementation, and bisphosphonates can help prevent as well as treat this complication.

Option C: Pneumothorax is the most common complication of line insertion and most commonly occurs during the insertion of subclavian lines. It is managed by insertion of a chest drain.
questions.learning: Aspiration pneumonia — The given image shows a central line. Pneumothorax, osteoporosis, and refeeding syndrome are likely complications in patients receiving total parenteral nutrition through a central line.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 24-month-old child weighing 11 kg was brought to the pediatric OPD. He had a respiratory rate of 38/min. On examination, chest indrawing was observed. What is the next step of management?
options: Urgent referral to the tertiary care centre immediately
Administer IV antibiotics and ask the patient to be brought after 24 hours
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Oral amoxicillin for five days

From the given clinical picture, it appears that the child has pneumonia as diagnosed from the presence of chest indrawing. The next best step of management is to give oral amoxicillin for five days and send the child home.

This is based on the revised WHO classification and treatment of childhood pneumonia at health facilities. Pneumonia with general danger signs like inability to drink, persistent vomiting, convulsions, lethargic or unconscious, stridor in a calm child or severe malnutrition needs antibiotics with urgent referral to higher centre.

The following image distinguishes the previous and revised classification and treatment of the childhood pneumonia.
questions.learning: Oral amoxicillin for five days From the given clinical picture, it appears that the child has pneumonia as diagnosed from the presence of chest indrawing.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the vector responsible for transmitting the Zika virus among the options listed?
questions.explanation: The Zika virus (ZIKV) is a single-stranded RNA arbovirus from the Flaviviridae family. It is primarily transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected mosquito. The two most significant vectors responsible for its spread are Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus (the Asian tiger mosquito). These species also transmit other viral infections like dengue and chikungunya. While vertical transmission from mother to child (especially in the first trimester) and sexual contact can occur, mosquito-borne transmission remains the most common route. Options A, C, and D are incorrect as these species are not the primary vectors involved in Zika virus epidemics. Laboratory diagnosis relies on RT-PCR for viral RNA or IgM antibody detection after the first week of symptoms
questions.learning: The Zika virus (ZIKV) is a single-stranded RNA arbovirus from the Flaviviridae family. It is primarily transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected mosquito.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is considered a contraindication to the use of bi-level positive airway pressure (BiPAP)?
questions.explanation: Bi-level Positive Airway Pressure (BiPAP) is a form of non-invasive ventilation (NIV) that requires the patient to be alert, cooperative, and able to protect their own airway. Therefore, being unconscious or heavily sedated is an absolute contraindication for its use. In such patients, BiPAP carries a high risk of aspiration and gastric insufflation; they require invasive endotracheal intubation instead. Obstructive sleep apnea (Option A) is a primary indication for positive pressure therapy (usually CPAP or BiPAP). Low oxygen levels (hypoxia) (Option D) are often the very reason BiPAP is initiated (e.g., in COPD or heart failure). High oxygen levels (Option C) are not a direct contraindication, although therapy would be unnecessary if oxygenation is normal. Other contraindications for BiPAP include severe facial trauma, vomiting, or excessive secretions. The success of BiPAP depends heavily on the patient's ability to synchronize with the machine and maintain their airway reflexes. Clinicians must meticulously screen patients before initiating non-invasive support
questions.learning: Bi-level Positive Airway Pressure (BiPAP) is a form of non-invasive ventilation (NIV) that requires the patient to be alert, cooperative, and able to protect their own airway.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A neonate is found to have increased irritability, poor feeding, and 2 episodes of seizures. Lumbar puncture was done and the findings were suggestive of meningitis. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Escherichia coli

The given clinical scenario describes neonatal meningitis. E. coli > Streptococcus agalactiae, part of group B streptococci, are the most likely causative organism of neonatal meningitis.

Early features of meningitis include temperature instability (hypo or hyperthermia), lethargy, bradycardia, and feed intolerance. Late features include seizures, bulging fontanelle, and nuchal rigidity.

The most common cause of bacterial meningitis in a 0 to 2-month baby is group B streptococci (Option B) worldwide and gram-ve bacteria like E.coli and Klebsiella (option A) in India. In babies aged 2 to 24 months, pneumococci are the primary causative pathogens, followed by H. influenzae. For children older than 2 years, pneumococci remain a prominent cause of meningitis, with Neisseria meningitidis being the second most common pathogen.

The most common etiological agents of neonatal meningitis and sepsis are listed in the table below:

India
Worldwide

Neonatal meningitis
E. coli, Klebsiella
Group B Streptococci

Neonatal sepsis
Klebsiella, S. aures, E. coli
Group B Streptococci

Neonates have immature cellular and humoral immunity. This makes them prone to meningitis and sepsis. Thus, an infant with a fever who is 28 days or younger, should be evaluated for sepsis.

Option C: Meningococcal infections are usually asymptomatic. If invasive disease occurs, then the clinical spectrum varies widely from meningococcal meningitis (highest proportion) to bacteremia without sepsis, meningococcal septicemia with or without meningitis, pneumonia, chronic meningococcemia, and occult bacteremia.

Option D: Meningitis caused by Listeria monocytogenes is rare but clinically significant. Infants can acquire the infection in utero or through an infected birth canal. Neonatal listeriosis can manifest as early-onset disease, typically within 1-2 days of birth, primarily as a septicemic form. Alternatively, it can present as a late-onset disease in infants older than 5 days, predominantly as a meningitic form.
questions.learning: Escherichia coli — The given clinical scenario describes neonatal meningitis. E. coli > Streptococcus agalactiae, part of group B streptococci, are the most likely causative organism of neonatal meningitis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The test given below in the image is used for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stereopsis test

The given image is of Titmus stereotest, which is done for the assesment of stereopsis (perception of depth).

• The pictures consist of a housefly for children and circular patterns for adults.
• The picture is held in front of the eyes of the patient at a distance of about 16 inches and the patient is asked to wear polarized glasses.
• If the patient's perception of the depth is normal, the housefly appears to rise above the plane, like a 3D image. If the patient is asked to pinch the wings of the housefly, he/she will try to pinch in the air, above the plane of the image.
• If the patient's perception of depth in either eye is defective, then the image appears just like normal 2D image.

Option A: Tests for ocular deviation include

• Cover tests
• Prism cover test- This will tell the amount of deviation in prism dioptres.
• Maddox rod test
• Hirschberg corneal reflex test

The below given image shows Maddox rod test.

Option C: Test for refractive error includes

• Retinoscopy
• Auto refractometry

The below given image shows the findings of Retinoscopy in different refractive errors.

Option D: Tests for colour blindness include

• Ishihara test: It is frequently used to screen for a red–green colour vision deficit. It consists of a test plate followed by 16 plates, each with a series of dots arranged to show a shape or number that the subject is asked to identify.
• Hardy–Rand–Rittler test: It is similar to ishihara test but is used to detect all three color vision defect.
• Farnsworth–Munsell 100-hue test: Is the most sensitive test for both acquired and congenital colour blindness. It consists of 85 caps of different hue that needs to be rearranged.

The below given image depicts the ishihara test.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct with regard to clubbing? 1. It usually affects the fingers symmetrically. 2. It does not involve the toes. 3. It may be associated with malignant lung conditions. 4. It may recede following lung transplantation in cystic fibrosis. Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3 and 4

Clubbing is a bulbous enlargement of the distal phalanges caused by proliferation of connective tissue beneath the nail bed. It is commonly associated with chronic pulmonary, cardiac, gastrointestinal, and hepatobiliary diseases.

Explanation of the statements:

• Statement 1. It usually affects the fingers symmetrically: Correct. Clubbing usually affects the fingers symmetrically and often involves both hands.
• Statement 2. It does not involve the toes: Incorrect. Clubbing commonly involves both the fingers and toes, not just the fingers.
• Statement 3. It may be associated with malignant lung conditions: Correct. Clubbing is associated with malignant lung diseases, especially bronchogenic carcinoma, as well as chronic suppurative lung diseases.
• Statement 4. It may recede following lung transplantation in cystic fibrosis: Correct. Clubbing may regress after successful treatment of the underlying disease, including lung transplantation in patients with cystic fibrosis.
questions.learning: 1, 3 and 4 Clubbing is a bulbous enlargement of the distal phalanges caused by proliferation of connective tissue beneath the nail bed. It is commonly associated with chronic pulmonary, cardiac, gastrointestinal, and hepatobiliary diseases.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which part of the female body is considered the most reliable indicator among the given options?
questions.explanation: The rectouterine pouch, also known as the Pouch of Douglas, is the most dependent (reliant) part of the female peritoneal cavity in the upright position. It is located between the posterior wall of the uterus and the anterior wall of the rectum. Because it is the lowest point, clinical conditions such as hemoperitoneum, pelvic inflammatory disease exudates, or ruptured ectopic pregnancies result in fluid accumulation here. The posterior fornix (Option C) is the deepest part of the vagina and is anatomically related to this pouch, making it the site for culdocentesis. The ovarian fossa (Option B) is a depression in the lateral pelvic wall where the ovary sits but is not a dependent drainage area. The vesicouterine pouch (Option D) is located anteriorly between the bladder and uterus and is shallower and higher than the Pouch of Douglas. Therefore, in clinical diagnostics and imaging, the rectouterine pouch is the primary site checked for pathological fluid collection
questions.learning: The rectouterine pouch, also known as the Pouch of Douglas, is the most dependent (reliant) part of the female peritoneal cavity in the upright position.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A CSF sample of an elderly male presenting with meningitis is subjected to gram staining and revealed gram-positive bacilli. Which of the following is true regarding the motility of the causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Motile at 25°C, non motile at 37°C

The given scenario of an elderly male with meningitis and smear showing gram-positive bacillus is suggestive of Listeria infection. Listeria is motile at 25°C and non-motile at 37°C.

Listeria exhibits a characteristic slow tumbling end-over-end motility at 22–28°C but is non-motile at 37°C. This is because the peritrichous flagella are produced by the bacillus optimally between 20°C and 30°C. This is known as differential motility as the motility pattern changes with a change in temperature.

Listeria monocytogenes is a gram-positive bacillus. It can survive at refrigerator temperatures (4°C), under conditions of low pH and high salt. So it is able to overcome food preservation and safety barriers, making it an important foodborne pathogen. The virulence factor produced by Listeria is called listeriolysin O. This helps the bacteria to escape and causes septicemia. They are catalase-positive, will not produce H2S, and shows beta hemolysis. This helps to differentiate Listeria from other gram-positive bacilli.

L. monocytogenes enters the body after ingestion of contaminated foods such as refrigerated milk, cheese, fruit, or vegetables. Healthy persons exposed to L. monocytogenes in food may develop mild, self-limiting febrile gastroenteritis lasting 1–3 days. This develops after an incubation period of 6–48 hours. Symptoms include fever, chills, headache, myalgias, abdominal pain, and diarrhea.
questions.learning: Motile at 25°C, non motile at 37°C — The given scenario of an elderly male with meningitis and smear showing gram-positive bacillus is suggestive of Listeria infection.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Melanosis coli (brownish discoloration of colonic mucosa) can occur due to the long-term consumption of which one of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stimulant laxatives

Melanosis coli is a benign brown-black pigmentation of the colonic mucosa caused by accumulation of lipofuscin pigment within macrophages in the lamina propria. It is classically associated with long-term use of anthraquinone-containing stimulant laxatives, such as senna and cascara.

Why not the other options?

• B. NSAIDs: Can cause gastritis, peptic ulceration, and enteropathy, but are not a classic cause of melanosis coli.
• C. Proton pump inhibitors: Not associated with melanosis coli.
• D. 3rd-generation cephalosporins: May cause antibiotic-associated diarrhea/C. difficile infection but do not cause melanosis coli.
questions.learning: Stimulant laxatives Melanosis coli is a benign brown-black pigmentation of the colonic mucosa caused by accumulation of lipofuscin pigment within macrophages in the lamina propria.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which marked structure causes lateral rotation, flexion, and abduction at the hip joint, along with flexion at the knee joint?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2

Sartorius is involved in lateral rotation, flexion, and abduction at the hip joint, and flexion at the knee. The structure marked '2' is sartorius.

The sartorius muscle is known as the tailor muscle and is also the longest muscle in the body. The word "sartorius" is derived from the Latin word sartor, which translates to tailor, due to the way the individual will position one's leg while working.

Origin: Anterior superior iliac spine and the upper half of the notch below it.

Insertion: Into the superior aspect of the medial surface of the tibial shaft near the tibial tuberosity (joins aponeurosis of gracilis and semitendinosus to form pes anserinus).

Action: Flexion, abduction, and lateral rotation of the thigh; and flexion of the leg.

Innervation: By femoral nerve (L2 and L3)

Other options:

Option A: Rectus femoris is involved in flexion at the hip and extension at the knee.

Option C: Gracilis is involved in adduction at the hip and flexion and medial rotation at the knee.

Option D: Adductor longus is involved in adduction, flexion, and medial rotation at the hip.
questions.learning: 2 Sartorius is involved in lateral rotation, flexion, and abduction at the hip joint, and flexion at the knee. The structure marked '2' is sartorius.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 49-year-old woman from Nagaland presents with right-sided hearing loss and tinnitus. Examination reveals a dull tympanic membrane along with enlarged lymph nodes in the posterior triangle of the neck. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms—unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus with a dull tympanic membrane—indicate serous otitis media due to Eustachian tube obstruction. In a patient from Nagaland (an endemic area) with enlarged posterior triangle lymph nodes, this presentation is highly suspicious for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). Radiotherapy is the definitive management for NPC, as the tumor is highly radiosensitive. Regarding the distractors, grommet insertion and steroids (Options A, B, and C) might treat the symptoms of fluid in the ear but would fail to address the underlying malignancy causing the obstruction. A unilateral ear block in an adult, especially from Northeast India, must always be investigated for malignancy. Therefore, because NPC is the primary diagnosis suggested by the clinical cluster, radiotherapy is the standard treatment
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms—unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus with a dull tympanic membrane—indicate serous otitis media due to Eustachian tube obstruction.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is true for DOTS:
options: Every patient is given the same treatment
Streptomycin is given to all the patients
questions.explanation: DOTS stands for Directly Observed Treatment, Short-course, which is the internationally recommended strategy for tuberculosis control. The defining feature of DOTS is that a trained health worker or designated community member directly observes the patient swallowing their medication (Option A). This ensures strict compliance and reduces the risk of multi-drug resistant TB. Every patient is NOT given the same treatment (Option B); regimens are categorized based on whether the patient is new or previously treated. Streptomycin (Option C) is an injectable aminoglycoside reserved for specific cases and is not used for everyone. While the program has evolved to include a daily regimen (Option D) in many regions including India, the historical and most fundamental component that defines the "DOTS" acronym specifically is the supervised nature of the drug administration. Therefore, "Treatment under supervision" is the core principle and the correct true statement regarding DOTS

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Nitrogenous waste is excreted from the body in the form of __?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Urea

Nitrogenous wastes are excreted from the body in the form of urea.

Depending on their ecology and physiology, different animals excrete excess nitrogen as ammonia, uric acid, or urea.

In aqueous animals nitrogenous waste is excreted as ammonia. The constant excretion of water permits them to excrete the highly toxic ammonia, as it highly water soluble. Birds must both conserve water and maintain low weight and hence excreting nitrogen-rich uric acid. Many land animals, including humans, excrete nontoxic, highly water-soluble urea. High blood levels in renal disease are a consequence of impaired renal function.

Pearl PF0082: Urea Cycle and its disorders
questions.learning: Urea Nitrogenous wastes are excreted from the body in the form of urea. Depending on their ecology and physiology, different animals excrete excess nitrogen as ammonia, uric acid, or urea.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-year-old child has serial height and weight measurements consistently tracking parallel just above the 50th percentile on WHO growth charts. What is the most likely interpretation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Normal growth

A child whose height and weight consistently track along the same percentile (or growth channel) on the WHO growth chart is considered to have normal growth, even if the percentile is not exactly at the median. Growth velocity and maintenance of the growth curve are more important than the absolute percentile. The child:

• Has serial height and weight measurements
• Continues to grow parallel to the 50th percentile
• Shows no crossing of percentile lines

This indicates normal growth velocity and appropriate physical development.

Why not the other options?

• A. Familial short stature: Children have height below the expected percentile (usually <3rd percentile) but maintain a normal growth velocity; family members are also short.
• B. Constitutional delay of growth: Characterized by short stature with delayed bone age and delayed puberty, followed by a normal adult height.
• D. Idiopathic short stature: Height is < –2 SD (<3rd percentile) without an identifiable cause.
questions.learning: Normal growth — A child whose height and weight consistently track along the same percentile (or growth channel) on the WHO growth chart is considered to have normal growth, even if the percentile is not exactly at the median.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents to the outpatient department with left knee pain, which he notes is often worse at night. He has been using aspirin for pain relief. An X-ray of the knee is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical hallmark of Osteoid osteoma is bone pain that is worse at night and is dramatically relieved by Aspirin or other NSAIDs. This is due to the high concentration of prostaglandins within the tumor. The radiograph confirms the diagnosis by showing a radiolucent nidus (less than 2 cm) surrounded by an area of reactive sclerotic (dense) bone. Chondroblastoma (Option A) is an epiphyseal lesion with a different radiological appearance. Skeletal TB (Option C) causes "cold abscesses" and joint destruction rather than a discrete cortical nidus. Osteosarcoma (Option D) is a highly aggressive malignant tumor showing a "sunburst" periosteal reaction and large-scale bone destruction. Osteoid osteoma is a benign tumor, most common in the femur and tibia of young adults. While some may resolve spontaneously over several years, the preferred treatment is percutaneous radiofrequency ablation, which provides immediate and permanent pain relief. The specific response to Aspirin is the key diagnostic "trigger" in medical examinations
questions.learning: The clinical hallmark of Osteoid osteoma is bone pain that is worse at night and is dramatically relieved by Aspirin or other NSAIDs. This is due to the high concentration of prostaglandins within the tumor.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A young woman came to the clinic requesting a post-coital pill. Which of the following would you prescribe?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Levonorgestrel

Levonorgestrel can be prescribed to a young woman requesting a post-coital pill.

Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg single dose within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse, can be used for emergency contraception. Alternatively, it can also be administered in two doses of 0.75 mg. The first dose is taken within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse, and the 2nd dose is taken 12 hours apart. The tablets can be offered up to 120 hours but the efficacy decreases with the longer coital-drug interval.

Advantages of LNG tablets:

* It has no estrogen and its associated side effects.

* It can be offered to hypertensive, cardiac and diabetic women.

* It can be offered to a lactating woman.

* It can be given as late as 120 hours after unprotected intercourse (but efficacy decreases).

* Single-dose therapy is an advantage.

Combined oral pills consisting of both estrogen and progesterone act on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis to inhibit the release of GnRH (and thus subsequently LH and FSH) and thus inhibit ovulation.

Emergency contraception refers to backup methods for contraceptive emergencies that women can use within the first few days after unprotected intercourse to prevent an unwanted pregnancy. Administration of postcoital contraceptive agents that interfere with postovulatory events that can lead to pregnancy.

The various emergency contraceptive methods, along with their mechanism of action have been described below:

* Ethinyl estradiol 50 μg + norgestrel 0.25 mg is administered as two tablets within 72 hours of coitus, followed by the 2 tablets after 12 hours. The hormone may delay ovulation if taken soon after intercourse.

* Ulipristal is given as a 30 mg tablet and should be taken within 5 days. It is a synthetic progesterone hormone receptor modulator. The drug attaches to the progesterone receptor, delays ovulation, and suppresses endometrium, thereby preventing implantation.

* IUCD (intrauterine contraceptive device) prevents the implantation of a fertilized ovum. It does so by acting as a foreign body within the uterine cavity. This leads to increased contractility, tubal peristalsis, and leukocytic infiltration in the endometrium.

* Centchroman is administered as two tablets of 60 mg, taken twice over a duration of 24 hours and within 24 hours of intercourse. It acts by preventing the implantation of the blastocyst in the endometrium.

Pearl PF1657: Hormonal contraceptives

Oral pills:

* Combined oral contraceptive pills (COC)

* Mala D - Levonorgestrel 0.15 mg + Ethinyl estradiol  0.03 mg + Ferrous fumarate

* Mala N - Levonorgestrel 0.15 mg + Ethinyl estradiol  0.03 mg + Ferrous fumarate (Govt. supply, free of cost)

* Progesterone only pills (POP) - suitable for lactating women

* Norethisterone 350 μg

* Norgestrel 75 μg

* Levonorgestrel (LNG) 30 μg

* Once a month or long-acting pills - highly disappointing results

* Quinestrol (long-acting estrogen) + short-acting progesterone

* Gossypol - male pill : Cottonseed derivative and causes azoospermia and severe oligospermia

* Post-coital pills or interceptive

* Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg, 2 doses, 12 hours apart

* Mifepristone 10-600 mg

* Ulipristal 30 mg, within 5 days of intercourse

* Centchroman 60 mg, 2 tablets, within 24 hrs of intercourse

* GnRH agonists

* CuT IUCD, inserted within 5 days

Injectable contraceptives

* Progesterone only injectables

* DMPA 150 mg IM every 3 months

* NET-EN 200 mg IM every 2 months

* Combined injectables

* Cyclofem - DMPA 25 mg + Estradiol cypionate 5 mg

* Mesigyna - NET-EN 50 mg  + Estradiol valerate 5 mg

Subdermal implants

* Norplant I - Levonorgestrel 35 mg

* Norplant II or Jadelle - 2 rods with levonorgestrel 70 mg in each and released at a rate of 50 μg/day

Others

* Hormonal IUCD - Mirena which contains LNG 52 mg with release rate of 20 μg/day

* Orthoevra patch - Norelgestomin + Ethinyl estradiol weekly for 3 weeks, then patch free for 1 week

* Vaginal ring or Nuvaring - Etonogestrel + ethinyl estradiol daily release, use for 3 weeks with withdrawal for 1 week
questions.learning: Levonorgestrel Levonorgestrel can be prescribed to a young woman requesting a post-coital pill. Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg single dose within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse, can be used for emergency contraception.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During the autopsy of a 30-year-old man who died due to drowning, the pathologist observes several cut-like marks on the arms. In the context of drowning, these findings raise questions about their origin. What is the most likely explanation for these marks on the victim’s arms?
questions.explanation: The image shows multiple irregular cut-like wounds on the palm and fingers, which are characteristic of defense wounds. These injuries occur when a person actively tries to protect themselves from an assault, typically by raising their hands to block or grab a weapon. As a result, cuts are commonly seen on the palms, fingers, and forearms. In the context of drowning, the presence of such injuries suggests that the victim may have been attacked before or during entry into water, rather than accidental drowning alone. Defense wounds indicate struggle and possible homicidal involvement. Why Other Options Are Wrong (B) Self-inflicted injury: Usually more superficial, accessible, and patterned (C) Accidental cuts: Random and less localized to defensive areas (D) Washer-women hands: Refers to wrinkling of skin after prolonged immersion, not cuts

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with swelling under the left ear lobule and complains of pain. Which of the following structures is the likely cause of the pain?
options: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Greater auricular nerve

The cause of the pain in this patient complaining of pain in the parotid region is likely to be the greater auricular nerve.

The greater auricular nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin overlying the parotid gland and the ear lobule. Pain associated with swelling and inflammation in the parotid region could be transmitted through the greater auricular nerve. The parotid gland is covered by a parotid capsule that is derived from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia. Any acute inflammation of the gland such as acute sialadenitis results in pain in the preauricular region. The pain is mainly due to stretching of the capsule resulting in stimulation of the greater auricular nerve.

Other options:

Option A: The facial nerve is not the primary cause of pain in the parotid region due to swelling. The Hitzelberger sign(numbness in the posterosuperior meatal wall of the external auditory canal), associated with facial nerve involvement, is seen in acoustic neuroma and is not the cause of pain in this scenario.

Option D: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia is not the correct answer because the investing layer of deep cervical fascia itself does not transmit pain sensation. The investing layer of deep cervical fascia is a layer of connective tissue that envelops the neck and extends to cover the parotid gland, forming the parotid capsule. While inflammation or swelling in the parotid gland can stretch the capsule and cause pain, the actual transmission of pain sensation is mediated by sensory nerves, such as the greater auricular nerve, which innervates the skin over the parotid gland and the ear lobule.

The greater auricular nerve (Option B) is a more appropriate answer in this context, as it is responsible for carrying the pain sensation from the area of swelling and inflammation in the parotid region.

Option C: The auriculotemporal nerve can cause referred pain due to caries tooth, ulcerative lesions of the oral cavity, temporomandibular joint disorders, and sphenopalatine neuralgia. However, it is not the primary cause of pain in the parotid region due to swelling.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is considered a satisfactory dilation rate in a primigravida?
questions.explanation: In a primigravida, the minimum satisfactory rate of cervical dilatation during the active phase of labor is considered to be ≥ 0.5 cm per hour. This is the accepted lower limit used clinically to judge whether labor is progressing adequately. Although the average (mean) rate of dilatation in primigravida is around 1 cm/hour, any rate above 0.5 cm/hour is still considered satisfactory. If the rate falls below this, it suggests prolonged or abnormal labor, requiring further evaluation. Why Other Options Are Incorrect (B) 0.75 cm/hr: Possible but not the defined minimum standard (C) 1.2 cm/hr: More typical of multigravida (D) 1.5 cm/hr: Clearly seen in multigravida (faster labor)
questions.learning: In a primigravida, the minimum satisfactory rate of cervical dilatation during the active phase of labor is considered to be ≥ 0.5 cm per hour. This is the accepted lower limit used clinically to judge whether labor is progressing adequately.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A middle-aged female patient with RA for 5 years also has a family history of RA. She's on treatment with methotrexate with worsening symptoms. She was enrolled in a trial of a new epigenome-modifying drug. After 8 weeks, her symptoms improved. All of the following regarding this drug is true except:
options: It directly binds to cytokine receptors to block inflammatory signalling
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It directly binds to cytokine receptors to block inflammatory signalling

The stem gives:

• RA patient (chronic autoimmune arthritis)
• Methotrexate failure → escalation therapy
• “Epigenome-modifying drug” → think upstream gene regulation

Epigenetic drugs regulate gene expression upstream; they do NOT directly block cytokine receptors (that’s biologics like tocilizumab). Epigenetics = changing gene expression WITHOUT altering DNA sequence

Mechanisms include:

• Histone modification (acetylation/deacetylation)
• DNA methylation
• microRNA regulation

These affect inflammatory gene transcription.

| Feature | Epigenetic Drugs | Biologics

| ------- | ---------------- | ---------

| Level of action | Gene expression | Protein/cytokine

| Target | DNA/chromatin | Cytokines/receptors

| Example | HDAC inhibitors | Tocilizumab, Etanercept

| IL-6/TNF effect | ↓ production | Block action

| Specificity | Broad | Targeted

D) It directly binds to cytokine receptors to block inflammatory signalling

• This is the mechanism of biologics, not epigenetic drugs

| Drug | Target

| ---- | ------

| Tocilizumab | IL-6 receptor

| Etanercept | TNF-α

| Infliximab | TNF-α

These are receptor-level blockers, not gene modulators.

• RA synovium shows abnormal DNA methylation patterns
• Epigenetic therapy aims to “reset” this inflammatory memory

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive abdominal distention, shortness of breath, and swelling of the ankles over the past 3 months. Physical examination reveals a large pelvic mass, and pitting edema in the lower extremities. CT scan shows a solid right ovarian mass, significant ascites, and right-sided pleural effusion. After surgical removal of the mass, both the ascites and pleural effusion resolve completely, and the ankle swelling subsides. Histopathology confirms a benign ovarian fibroma. What is the mode of inheritance of this syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. No inheritance pattern (non-hereditary)

The clinical vignette describes Meig's syndrome, it is an acquired disorder without genetic association.

Meigs syndrome triad:

* Ovarian fibroma

* Pleural effusion

* Ascites that disappear after removal of the tumor

Meigs syndrome is mostly caused by ovarian fibroma. CA-125 levels may also be elevated. As it is a diagnosis of exclusion, a workup should be done to rule out malignancy. Exploratory laparotomy with surgical staging is the treatment of choice. Conservative surgery (salpingo-oophorectomy) is done. The clinical features resolve on resection of the fibroma.

Pseudo-Meigs syndrome presents with ascites and pleural effusion in association with benign ovarian tumors such as teratoma, struma ovarii, mucinous cystadenoma, etc.

Pearl PF0900: WHO Classification of Ovarian Tumors

I. Common epithelial tumors

* Serous tumors

* Mucinous tumors

* Endometrioid tumors

* Clear cell

* Brenner tumors (transitional cell tumors)

* Seromucinous

* Undifferentiated carcinoma

II. Sex cord-stromal tumors:

* Pure stromal cell tumors- Fibroma, Thecoma, Leydig cell tumor, Steroid cell tumor

* Pure sex cord tumors- Granulosa cell tumor (Adult/Juvenile), Sertoli cell tumor

* Mixed sex cord-stromal tumors- Sertoli–Leydig cell tumors

III. Germ cell tumors:

* Dysgerminoma

* Endodermal sinus tumor (Yolk sac tumor)

* Embryonal carcinoma

* Polyembryoma

* Non-gestational choriocarcinoma

* Teratoma (Mature/immature)

* Mixed forms

IV. Gonadoblastoma

* Pure

* Mixed with dysgerminoma or other germ cell tumors

V. Soft tissue tumors not specific to ovary
VI. Miscellaneous tumors
VII. Secondary (metastatic) tumors
VIII. Tumor-like conditions
