questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with severe pain below the knee, difficulty walking, and a history of prolonged bed rest due to severe back pain. Examination reveals discoloration of the right calf with increased calf circumference. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of unilateral calf pain, increased girth (swelling), and discoloration following a period of prolonged bed rest (immobilization) is highly characteristic of Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT). Immobilization is a major component of Virchow's triad, leading to venous stasis and thrombus formation. Cellulitis (Option A) typically presents with warmth, erythema, and fever, often with an identifiable skin break. Compartment syndrome (Option B) is a surgical emergency usually following trauma, characterized by pain out of proportion to findings and paresthesia, which is not suggested by a history of simple bed rest. Arterial claudication (Option C) involves pain triggered by exertion and relieved by rest, which is inconsistent with symptoms developing after immobilization. Management of DVT involves immediate anticoagulation to prevent the life-threatening complication of pulmonary embolism. Diagnosis should be confirmed using a D-dimer assay and lower limb venous Doppler ultrasonography to visualize the non-compressible venous segment
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of unilateral calf pain, increased girth (swelling), and discoloration following a period of prolonged bed rest (immobilization) is highly characteristic of Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An elderly woman presented with symptoms of confusion, thirst, and abdominal pain. On examination, she had pallor and thoracic spine tenderness. Her lab investigations showed the following findings. An X-ray of her skull is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis? * Hb - 6.9g/dL * WBC 4000/cm3 with normal differential count * Serum calcium 13mg/dL * Creatinine 2.3mg/dL * Total protein 9g/dL * Albumin 2.4g/dL * Urinalysis: positive for Bence-Jones proteins
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Multiple myeloma

The given clinical features along with hypercalcemia, elevated creatinine suggestive of renal failure, anemia, osteolytic bone lesions (CRAB features), hypoalbuminemia with elevated total proteins, and Bence Jones proteinuria make multiple myeloma the most likely diagnosis.

Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma cell dyscrasia with the proliferation of plasma cells derived from a single clone. It is associated with increased osteoclast activity with suppression of osteoblast activity, causing punched-out lytic lesions in the bone and hypercalcemia.

Signs and symptoms

* Bone pain is the most common symptom

* Pathologic fractures

* Recurrent bacterial infections

* Renal failure

* Normocytic normochromic anemia elevated ESR, Hypercalcemia, normal ALP (ALP is a marker of bone growth and hence is not increased in multiple myeloma)

* Radiography: Punched-out lytic lesions on X-ray

* Electrophoresis: Monoclonal elevation of one immunoglobulin

* Urinalysis: Free kappa and lambda light chains (Bence Jones proteins)

* Bone marrow biopsy: 10 to 20% plasma cells (normal is < 5%)

* Peripheral smear: Rouleaux formation (High level of M proteins in myeloma causes red cells in the peripheral blood smears to stick to one another in linear arrays, a finding referred to as rouleaux formation)

Revised International Myeloma Working Group criteria for the diagnosis of multiple myeloma:

Clonal bone marrow plasma cells ≥10% (or) Biopsy-proven bony or extramedullary plasmacytoma

Plus

Any one or more of the following myeloma-defining events:

* Evidence of end-organ damage attributable to the underlying plasma cell proliferative disorder, specifically:(CRAB features)

* HyperCalcemia: Serum calcium level >1 mg/dL higher than the upper limit of normal or >11 mg/dL

* Renal insufficiency: Creatinine clearance <40 mL/min or serum creatinine >2 mg/dL

* Anemia: Hemoglobin level of >20 g/L (2gm/dl) below the lowest limit of normal, or Hb <10 g/dL

* Bone lesions: One or more osteolytic lesions on skeletal radiography, computed tomography (CT), or positron emission tomography (PET)/CT.

* Any one or more of the following biomarkers of malignancy:

* Clonal bone marrow plasma cells ≥60%

* Serum involved/uninvolved free light-chain ratio of 100 or greater

* >1 focal lesion on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) that is at least 5 mm or greater in size.

Note:

* The presence of at least one of these markers is considered sufficient for a diagnosis of multiple myeloma, regardless of the presence or absence of symptoms or CRAB features.

* Each of these markers has been shown to be associated with an approximately 80% or higher risk of developing myeloma-related organ damage within two years.

Pearl PF0580: WHO Classification of Plasma Cell Neoplasms

Plasma cell neoplasms and variants

Plasma cell myeloma

• Non secretory: No secretion of Ig, No M component.

• Smoldering: M protein in serum ≥ 30 g/L and/or ≥10% clonal plasma cells in bone marrow, and no related organ or tissue impairment.

• Plasma-cell leukemia: >20% plasma cells in the peripheral blood or Absolute plasma cell count of >2 X 109/L.

Plasmacytoma

• Solitary plasmacytoma: Localized tumour of monoclonal plasma cells with no clinical features of plasma cell myeloma.

• Extramedullary(extraosseous) plasmacytoma: Localized plasma cell neoplasms that arise in tissues other than bone.

Monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition diseases

• Primary amyloidosis: Tumor secreting light chains that are deposited as beta-pleated sheet structure (amyloid light chain).

• Systemic light and heavy chain diseases: Secrete abnormal light or heavy chain or both, which do not form beta pleated sheet, stain Congo Red or contain amyloid P component.

Plasma cell neoplasms with associated paraneoplastic syndrome

POEMS syndrome- Polyneuropathy, organomegaly, Endocrinopathy, Monoclonal gammopathy, Skin changes.

TEMPI syndrome

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 46-year-old chronic alcoholic male presents to the OPD with fever, headache, shortness of breath, chest pain, and productive cough for the last two days. On examination, there was bronchial breathing on the right side, increased vocal fremitus, increased vocal resonance, and a dull note on percussion. The patient's plain radiograph is shown below. Which is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Klebsiella pneumoniae

The given clinical scenario is highly suggestive of lobar pneumonia. The above chest x-ray shows a bulging fissure sign. The likely causative organism is Klebsiella pneumoniae.

Klebsiella pneumonia is associated mostly with alcoholics and shows upper lobe involvement, cavitation, and pneumatocele (also seen in S. aureus). The patient presents with red currant-jelly sputum.

A bulging fissure sign is classically seen in Klebsiella pneumonia. It represents expansive lobar consolidation causing fissural bulging or displacement by copious amounts of inflammatory exudate within the affected parenchyma. Classically, it is associated with right upper lobe consolidation due to Klebsiella pneumonia.

Other diseases that manifest a bulging fissure include any space-occupying process in the lung, such as pulmonary hemorrhage, lung abscess, and tumor.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the type of hymen shown in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Septate hymen

The given image is suggestive of the septate hymen.

The hymen is the membranous vestige of the junction between the sinovaginal bulbs and the urogenital sinus, which perforates during fetal life to establish a connection between the vaginal lumen and the perineum. Defective perforation of this structure may result in the following variants of hymen

• Imperforate - without any opening
• Microperforate - tiny opening
• Annular - oval central opening
• Septate - two lateral openings partitioned by a bridge of hymenal tissue
• Naviculate - boatlike opening

Patients with septate hymen will typically complain of menstrual irregularities or difficulty with tampon placement or intercourse. Under topical anesthesia, a rapidly absorbable suture or free tie can be placed at the anterior and posterior aspects of the septal tissue, and the septum is resected between the two sutures.

Some of the variants of the hymen are:

Imperforate hymen results due to failure of canalization of the inferior end of the vaginal plate. Clinical features include primary amenorrhea, cyclical abdominal pain, and bluish bulging membranes at the vaginal opening. A simple cruciate incision in the membrane will restore normal reproductive function.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 48-year-old man with a long history of GERD presents with progressive dysphagia. Endoscopy shows salmon-colored mucosa extending above the gastroesophageal junction. Biopsy reveals intestinal-type epithelium with goblet cells. Which of the following classification is used to know the extent of the disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Prague criteria

Barrett esophagus is a complication of chronic GERD in which the normal stratified squamous epithelium of the distal esophagus is replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia). Endoscopically it appears as salmon-colored mucosa extending proximally above the gastroesophageal junction. To describe the extent of Barrett’s esophagus, the standard system used is the Prague C & M classification, which reports:

• C (Circumferential extent): length of continuous circumferential Barrett mucosa
• M (Maximal extent): maximum length of Barrett mucosa including tongues

This classification provides a reproducible way to document disease length, guide surveillance, and assess risk of progression to dysplasia and esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Other Options:

A. Milan criteria:

• Used in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
• Determines eligibility for liver transplantation (single tumor ≤5 cm or ≤3 tumors each ≤3 cm).
• Not related to esophageal disease.

B. Tokyo criteria:

• Used in acute cholangitis and cholecystitis.
• Helps in diagnosis and severity grading (Tokyo Guidelines).
• No role in Barrett esophagus or dysphagia evaluation.

C. Chicago criteria:

• Used in esophageal motility disorders based on high-resolution manometry.
• Classifies disorders like achalasia, distal esophageal spasm, EGJ outflow obstruction.
• Applies to motility disorders, not mucosal metaplasia like Barrett.
questions.learning: Prague criteria Barrett esophagus is a complication of chronic GERD in which the normal stratified squamous epithelium of the distal esophagus is replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with hearing loss and pulsatile tinnitus. Examination reveals conductive hearing loss with a negative Rinne test (bone conduction better than air conduction), and a reddish mass is seen behind the tympanic membrane. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of hearing loss, pulsatile tinnitus (hearing a heartbeat in the ear), and a reddish-blue mass visible behind an intact tympanic membrane is pathognomonic for a Glomus tumour (paraganglioma). Specifically, this could be a Glomus tympanicum or a Glomus jugulare. The reddish mass is often described as the "Rising Sun" sign. Acute otitis media (Option A) presents with severe pain and a bulging, opaque eardrum. Chronic otitis media (Option B) typically involves a perforation and discharge. Serous otitis media (Option D) involves fluid but appears amber or yellowish with bubbles, and lacks pulsatile tinnitus. Glomus tumors are highly vascular, benign growths arising from the chemoreceptor cells. Conductive hearing loss occurs because the mass restricts ossicular movement. Diagnosis is confirmed through imaging like CT (showing "moth-eaten" bone) and MRI. Management typically involves surgical excision or radiotherapy for large or inoperable cases. Recognizing pulsatile tinnitus and a vascular mass is the key to identifying this rare middle ear neoplasm
questions.learning: The clinical combination of hearing loss, pulsatile tinnitus (hearing a heartbeat in the ear), and a reddish-blue mass visible behind an intact tympanic membrane is pathognomonic for a Glomus tumour (paraganglioma).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During post-mortem examination of a person who died due to starvation, which finding is most likely to be observed?
questions.explanation: Starvation leads to a generalized atrophy of almost all internal organs as the body consumes its own tissues for energy. However, a characteristic and somewhat paradoxical finding in chronic starvation is a distended gallbladder. This occurs because there is no ingestion of food (especially fats) to trigger the release of cholecystokinin, which normally causes the gallbladder to contract and empty. Consequently, bile accumulates and thickens within the organ. Enlarged liver (Option B) is incorrect; the liver actually shrinks significantly, although it may appear fatty. Expanded lungs (Option C) and a hypertrophied heart (Option D) are not features of starvation; the heart, like other muscles, undergoes brown atrophy and decreases in size. Starvation victims also show a complete loss of subcutaneous fat (Omentum appears like a "lacy veil") and a sunken abdomen (scaphoid). The distended gallbladder is a classic forensic indicator used to support a diagnosis of death by starvation
questions.learning: Starvation leads to a generalized atrophy of almost all internal organs as the body consumes its own tissues for energy. However, a characteristic and somewhat paradoxical finding in chronic starvation is a distended gallbladder.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the earliest sign in Crohn's disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Aphthous ulcers

Aphthous ulcers, surrounded by a rim of erythematous mucosa, are the earliest lesions seen in a patient with Crohn's disease during endoscopy.

Crohn's colitis usually spares the rectum and is most severe in the ileocaecal region.

• In early Crohn's disease, small, punched-out aphthous ulcers are often seen (the result of submucosal lymphoid follicle expansion).
• In moderate disease, the aphthous ulcers coalesce into larger ulcers, which may take on the appearance of a star (stellate ulcers).
• As disease severity increases, submucosal edema and injury can result in cobblestoning of the mucosa (option A) and eventually the formation of serpiginous ulcers, which are typical findings in Crohn's disease.

Thorn-like extraluminal projections in barium studies are known as rose-thorn appearance, and are a typical sign of Crohn's disease. They represent deep penetrating linear ulcers or fissurings typically seen within stenosed terminal ileum with a thickened wall. (Options C and D)
questions.learning: Aphthous ulcers Aphthous ulcers, surrounded by a rim of erythematous mucosa, are the earliest lesions seen in a patient with Crohn's disease during endoscopy.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: While designing a banner on strategies to prevent the spread of non-communicable diseases, what major mistake did the intern make that prompted concern from the group of doctors?
questions.explanation: Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) like cardiovascular disease, cancer, and diabetes are largely driven by modifiable risk factors. Standard preventative measures include banning public smoking (Option A), restricting alcohol (Option B), and decreasing salt intake (Option D) to lower blood pressure. The intern's error was suggesting a shift from PUFA (Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids) with transfat. In reality, the medical recommendation is exactly the opposite: to eliminate transfats (which are highly harmful) and replace them with healthy PUFAs or MUFAs to improve the lipid profile. Transfats significantly increase LDL cholesterol and the risk of coronary heart disease. Promoting the intake of transfat would be a dangerous and erroneous medical instruction. This question emphasizes the need for accurate health communication in public health awareness campaigns to prevent providing misinformation that could worsen chronic disease outcomes

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Niacin is synthesized from?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tryptophan

The precursor for niacin is tryptophan and is coded by UGA in the mitochondria.

Tryptophan can be converted into niacin (vitamin B3). Approximately 60 mg of tryptophan is equivalent to 1 mg of dietary niacin (NADH & NAD+).

Tryptophan also produces serotonin and melatonin.

Clinical correlation: Deficiency of the enzyme kynureninase or Vit B6 results in niacin deficiency and pellagra-like symptoms and xanthurenic aciduria.
questions.learning: Tryptophan — The precursor for niacin is tryptophan and is coded by UGA in the mitochondria. Tryptophan can be converted into niacin (vitamin B3).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During minimally invasive inguinal hernia surgery, in order to obtain the “critical view of MPO (Myopectineal orifice)”, the space of Retzius must be dissected. At what distance must the dissection be carried out from the pubic tubercle and Cooper’s ligament?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2 cm

The “Critical View of the Myopectineal Orifice (MPO)” is an essential step during laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair (TEP/TAPP) to ensure complete mesh coverage of all potential hernia sites and minimize recurrence. Adequate dissection of the space of Retzius should extend at least 2 cm beyond the pubic tubercle and Cooper’s ligament.

• Dissection of the space of Retzius should be carried ≥2 cm medial to the pubic tubercle and Cooper’s ligament.
• This ensures:

• Complete exposure of the myopectineal orifice
• Adequate medial mesh overlap
• Reduced risk of mesh migration and hernia recurrence

Why not the other options?

• A. 0.5 cm: Inadequate medial dissection.
• B. 1 cm: Insufficient to achieve the critical view.
• D. 4 cm: More extensive than routinely required and not part of the standard definition of the critical view.
questions.learning: 2 cm The “Critical View of the Myopectineal Orifice (MPO)” is an essential step during laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair (TEP/TAPP) to ensure complete mesh coverage of all potential hernia sites and minimize recurrence.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: During evaluation of PUO, a patient's chest X-ray is as seen below. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Miliary tuberculosis

The given chest radiography image shows miliary tuberculosis.

It is the widespread dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, via hematogenous spread.

Classic miliary TB is defined as millet-like (mean, 2 mm; range, 1-5 mm) seeding of TB bacilli with uniform size and distribution in the lung, as seen on chest radiography. This particular sign is called the miliary shadow which is also seen in sarcoidosis and histoplasmosis.

Sputum-smear microscopy is negative in most cases.

Physical findings include hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy

Bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial biopsy are used to provide bacteriologic confirmation
questions.learning: Miliary tuberculosis — The given chest radiography image shows miliary tuberculosis. It is the widespread dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, via hematogenous spread.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: An epileptic patient presents with gum hypertrophy and dizziness. Which anti-epileptic drug is likely the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phenytoin

Gum hypertrophy and dizziness are commonly seen with phenytoin.

Gum hypertrophy (gingival hyperplasia) due to phenytoin therapy occurs due to tissue overgrowth secondary to altered collagen metabolism. The toothless portion of gums is not involved. It does not warrant discontinuation of the drug. It can be minimized by maintaining good oral hygiene.

The mechanism of action of phenytoin is the prolongation of Na+ ion channel inactivation. It slows down the rate of recovery of Na+ channels, thus limiting the propagation of the action potential.

Phenytoin also inhibits voltage-gated calcium channels, thereby decreasing calcium influx into the cell membrane. It also reduces the inward flow of potassium ions during repolarization. At higher or toxic doses, phenytoin enhances GABAergic activity and suppresses glutamate action.

Despite its narrow therapeutic index, phenytoin is used in the treatment of generalized tonic-clonic seizures, complex partial seizures, status epilepticus, trigeminal neuralgia, and behavioural disorders.

It is contraindicated in pregnancy as it can lead to fetal hydantoin syndrome. This syndrome is characterised by craniofacial anomalies like hypertelorism and epicanthal folds, short nose and deep nasal bridge, malformed and low set ears, short neck, hypoplastic distal phalanges and underdevelopment of nails of fingers and toes, growth retardation, cognitive deficits and motor developmental delay.

Other side effects of phenytoin include behavioural changes, increased frequency of seizures, gingival hyperplasia, megaloblastic anaemia, osteomalacia, hirsutism and hypersensitivity reactions.

Drugs causing gum hypertrophy - Mnemonic "CAP N":

* Cyclosporine

* Amlodipine

* Phenytoin

* Nifedipine

* Hirsutism

* Hypersensitivity reactions: rashes, lymphadenopathy

* Hyperglycemia

* Hypocalcemia and osteomalacia

* Hallucinations and behavioural abnormalities

* Hepatotoxicity

* Fetal Hydantoin Syndrome

* Cerebellar and vestibular symptoms: ataxia, nystagmus

* Hypotension and arrhythmias on IV use

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a recent history of throat infection presents with a characteristic water hammer pulse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A "water hammer" (collapsing) pulse, also known as Corrigan's pulse, is pathognomonic for aortic regurgitation. The history of a throat infection points to a prior streptococcal infection triggering rheumatic fever, which is a major cause of valvular damage, particularly affecting the aortic valve. Infective endocarditis (Option B) can cause aortic regurgitation but usually presents with acute fever and embolic signs like splinter hemorrhages. Mitral stenosis (Option C) classically presents with a small, low-volume pulse rather than a collapsing one. Aortic stenosis (Option D) features a "pulsus parvus et tardus," which is slow-rising and low-amplitude. The water hammer pulse results from the rapid ejection of a large stroke volume into the aorta followed by immediate backflow into the left ventricle during diastole

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In the image provided, which refractive error is observed in the depicted condition?
questions.explanation: The image depicts "Keratoconus," characterized by progressive thinning and cone-shaped protrusion of the cornea. Because the cornea becomes both steeper (more powerful) and irregular in shape, it induces two specific refractive errors: Myopia and Astigmatism. The steepening causes light to focus in front of the retina (high axial myopia), while the irregular cone shape causes light to focus at multiple different points (irregular astigmatism). Option B, C, and D are incorrect because hypermetropia is caused by a flat cornea or short eyeball, which is the opposite of this pathology. Patients with keratoconus often present with a history of frequent prescription changes and "ghosting" of images. Advanced signs include Munson’s sign (V-shape of the lower lid on downgaze) and Vogt’s striae. Treatment ranges from rigid gas permeable (RGP) contact lenses to corneal cross-linking (CXL) or penetrating keratoplasty in severe cases
questions.learning: The image depicts "Keratoconus," characterized by progressive thinning and cone-shaped protrusion of the cornea. Because the cornea becomes both steeper (more powerful) and irregular in shape, it induces two specific refractive errors: Myopia and Astigmatism.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman arrives at the emergency department about 6 hours after consuming a large overdose of paracetamol tablets. What is the most likely clinical course or progression of paracetamol poisoning in this situation?
options: Increase in liver enzymes within 24 hours
Paracetamol achieves peak concentration within 4 hours
questions.explanation: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) toxicity occurs when the normal metabolic pathways are overwhelmed, leading to the production of the toxic metabolite NAPQI via CYP2E1. In Stage I (0–24 hours post-ingestion), patients are often asymptomatic or have minor symptoms like nausea. However, subclinical hepatotoxicity begins, and a measurable increase in liver enzymes (AST, ALT) can occur within this first 24-hour window as damage starts. Clinical liver failure (Option B) typically develops in Stage III, which is 72–96 hours post-ingestion, not within the first day. While paracetamol reaches peak plasma levels within 2 hours, toxicity is not defined by this peak (Option C). Recovery (Option D) or progression to organ failure happens after 5 days, whereas 72 hours marks the peak of hepatic damage. Therefore, monitoring for early enzyme elevation is the most likely first sign of progression
questions.learning: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) toxicity occurs when the normal metabolic pathways are overwhelmed, leading to the production of the toxic metabolite NAPQI via CYP2E1.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following fertility-related statistics most appropriately gives the approximate magnitude of “completed family size”?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Total Fertility Rate (TFR)

• Total Fertility Rate (TFR) is the average number of children a woman would bear during her reproductive lifetime if she experienced the current age-specific fertility rates throughout her reproductive years.
• Therefore, TFR provides the best approximate measure of a population’s completed family size.

Why not the others?

• (a) Total Fertility Rate TFR — Correct: Approximates the average completed family size under prevailing fertility rates.
• (b) Total Marital Fertility Rate TMFR: Measures fertility among married women only; it is not the standard overall measure of completed family size.
• (c) Net Reproduction Rate NRR: Measures the average number of daughters a newborn girl will bear during her lifetime; it reflects replacement rather than family size.
• (d) Age-Specific Fertility Rate ASFR: Gives the fertility rate for a specific age group, not the total reproductive performance.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A resident doctor gets pricked with a needle while attending an HIV positive patient. The regimen to be given is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Zidovudine + Lamivudine + Indinavir

Amongst the given options, a three-drug combination of Zidovudine+Lamivudine+Indinavir is preferred.

Three drug combination is preferred as per the US Public health service guidelines, WHO guidelines, and MOHFW 2020 guidelines.

A PEP regimen for HIV should have Lamivudine + Tenofovir + Lopinavir/ritonavir to be taken for 4 weeks after exposure. It should ideally be started within 2 hours and definitely within 72 hours. Here as the Lopinavir/ritonavir is not part of the options, one can choose, the indinavir-based combination as the best of the available options.

Nevirapine is not preferred for use in PEP. Previous NACO 2018 guidelines mentioned the use of 2 drug combinations but it is no longer preferred.

Exposures that may warrant occupational PEP include:

• Parenteral or mucous membrane exposure (splashes to the eye, nose, or oral cavity)
• The following bodily fluids may pose a risk of HIV infection: blood, blood-stained saliva, breast-milk, genital secretions, and cerebrospinal, amniotic, rectal, peritoneal, synovial, pericardial, or pleural fluids.

Exposures that do not require PEP include:

• When the exposed individual is already HIV-positive
• When the source is established to be HIV-negative
• Exposure to bodily fluids that do not pose a significant risk: tears, non-blood-stained saliva, urine, and sweat.

To ensure no transmission has occurred, follow-up with HIV antibody testing should be done for at least 6 months post-exposure (e.g. at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months).

Note: This is an AIIMS 2020 recall question. It may not reflect the latest guidelines. Kindly refer to the attached pearl for the same.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24 year old primigravida presents with painless vaginal bleeding in the first trimester. On examination the cervical os is closed and uterine size is normal. Gestational sac is visible on ultrasound. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Threatened abortion

The given clinical features are suggestive of a threatened abortion.

The patient presents with a bloody vaginal discharge or bleeding through a closed cervical os. On ultrasound, gestational sac can be visible. In about two thirds of the cases pregnancy continues beyond 28 weeks. If the pregnancy continues, there is an increased risk of preterm labor, placenta previa, intrauterine growth restriction and fetal anomalies.

Treatment:

* Bed rest

* Analgesics if there is pain

* Progesterone

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An intern finds a patient unresponsive, and an emergency ECG reveals a cardiac arrhythmia. A DC shock is administered, but the arrhythmia persists and the patient remains unresponsive. What should be the next most appropriate step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation: The ECG waveform exhibits chaotic, irregular electrical activity without identifiable P waves or QRS complexes, which is diagnostic of Ventricular Fibrillation (VF). According to Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support (ACLS) guidelines, when an initial DC shock (defibrillation) fails to restore a rhythm and the patient remains unresponsive, the immediate next step is to resume high-quality Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR). CPR should be continued for two minutes before another rhythm check or shock is delivered. Synchronized cardioversion (Option A) is used for stable tachyarrhythmias with a pulse, not for pulseless VF. Delivering another immediate shock (Option C) is incorrect as it interrupts vital chest compressions. Epinephrine (Option D) is typically administered after the second unsuccessful shock. High-quality CPR is essential to maintain coronary and cerebral perfusion until a shock can successfully reset the heart
questions.learning: The ECG waveform exhibits chaotic, irregular electrical activity without identifiable P waves or QRS complexes, which is diagnostic of Ventricular Fibrillation (VF).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy presents with recurrent bacterial infections and Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia. The flow cytometry analysis of the boy (Boxes 3& 4) is shown below (Boxes 1 & 2 are normal). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hyper IgM syndrome

The deficiency of the CD40 and its absence in B cells interferes with class switching and the production of memory cells. The B-cell response to antigens, is unaffected, accounting for the presence of increased IgM antibodies. Hence, the condition is known as Hyper IgM syndrome.

The given clinical scenario and the flow cytometry is suggestive of Hyper IgM syndrome. The flow cytometry shows the following findings:

• In comparison of image 3 to 1, where side scatter is plotted against CD 19: B-cell gating is present.
Gating of B cells means selecting a cell during a flow cytometry experiment for further analysis or data presentation.CD 19 is widely expressed on B cells. Hence the graph shows B cell gating. Side scatter measurement provides information about the granularity of a cell.
• In comparison of image 4 to 2, where CD 40 is plotted against CD 19: B cells are present only in quadrant 4, which means that there is CD 40 deficiency.

The deficiency of the CD40 and its absence in B cells interferes with class switching and the production of memory cells. The B-cell response to antigens is unaffected, accounting for the presence of increased IgM antibodies. Hence, the condition is known as Hyper IgM syndrome.

Given below is the explanation of how to interpret flow cytometry results:

Interpretation of results:

Quadrant 1- Cells marked in green: -VE for A antigen, +VE for B antigen

Quadrant 2- Cells marked in purple: -VE for both the antigens.

Quadrant 3- Cells marked in yellow: +VE for both the antigens

Quadrant 4- Cells marked in red: +VE for A antigen, -VE for B antigen

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 57-year-old man was brought to the hospital with complaints of dizziness and breathlessness. During his physical examination, you notice the following discolouration over his face. He is presently being treated with amiodarone, metoprolol, verapamil, lisinopril, and amlodipine. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Amiodarone

The image shows grey-blue discoloration over this patient's face and the drug responsible for this is amiodarone.

Long-term treatment with amiodarone is responsible for skin pigmentation. Elderly men are at an increased risk of developing this.

Ultraviolet light reacts with amiodarone and its metabolites to cause local vasodilatation. This increases the diffusion of amiodarone and its metabolites, resulting in their deposition in the tissues, causing pigmentation. Therefore, it is usually seen in sun-exposed areas.

Cessation of amiodarone, avoiding exposure to sunlight using sunscreen cream is recommended.

Amiodarone is an iodine-containing compound that is structurally related to thyroid hormone. It is a class III antiarrhythmic drug, which increases the duration of an action potential by blocking potassium channels. It thereby increases the time taken for repolarization. It also prolongs the refractory period and suppresses abnormal automaticity. It also has weak calcium channel blocking, sodium channel blocking, and adrenergic blocking actions.

It is used to maintain normal sinus rhythm during atrial fibrillation and prevent recurrent ventricular tachycardia.

Adverse effects of amiodarone:

• Prolonged usage of amiodarone causes interstitial lung disease.
• Heart blocks, bradycardia and QT prolongation
• Hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism
• Corneal micro-deposits and vortex keratopathy, optic neuropathy

Drug interactions of amiodarone

• Causes digoxin toxicity by decreasing its renal clearance.
• Increases concentration of quinidine and procainamide
• Potentiates the anticoagulant effect of warfarin when given simultaneously
questions.learning: Amiodarone — The image shows grey-blue discoloration over this patient's face and the drug responsible for this is amiodarone. Long-term treatment with amiodarone is responsible for skin pigmentation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 35-year-old female came to the clinic with headache and visual field loss. A pituitary adenoma was found compressing the optic chiasma. What visual field defect will be seen in the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bitemporal hemianopia

The pituitary tumour compressing the optic chiasma results in bitemporal hemianopia.

Pituitary macroadenoma can compress the optic chiasm, causing bitemporal hemianopia, which leads to the loss of vision in the temporal halves of the visual fields in both eyes. This occurs when damage to the middle part of the optic chiasm affects the crossing fibres from the nasal retina of each eye while the uncrossed fibres from the temporal retinas remain intact. As a result, individuals retain central vision but lose peripheral vision on the sides.

The most common cause of bitemporal hemianopia is a pituitary adenoma. Other common causes include:

* suprasellar aneurysms

* chronic arachnoiditis

* suprasellar tumours like craniopharyngioma and suprasellar meningioma

Other options:

Option B: Loss of the same half of the visual field in both eyes (e.g., right half of both eyes causes right homonymous hemianopia), but here it's the temporal fields of both eyes.

Option C: Homonymous anopia, sometimes used loosely, but strictly means loss of the same entire visual field ('an-' = absence) in both eyes.

Option D: Inferior quadrantanopia is seen in the lesion of parietal lobe optic radiation → “pie on the floor” defect.

Pearl PF2187: Lesions in the optic pathway

Transection of the pathways at the locations indicated by the letters causes the visual field defects shown in the diagram above.

* The fibers from the nasal half of each retina decussate in the optic chiasm, so that the fibers in the optic tracts are those from the temporal half of one retina and the nasal half of the other.

* A lesion that interrupts the optic nerve causes blindness in that eye.

* Lesions affecting the optic chiasma destroy fibers from both nasal hemiretinas and produce a heteronymous (opposite sides of the visual fields) hemianopia.

* A lesion in one optic tract causes blindness in half of the visual field and is called homonymous (same side of both visual fields) hemianopia (half-blindness).

* Occipital lesions may spare the fibers from the macula because of the separation in the brain of these fibers from the other subserving vision.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the type of abuse as shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bagging

The above image shows bagging, a type of volatile substance abuse. It refers to inhaling and exhaling into a bag that has been filled with a small amount of a volatile substance.

Sniffing/snorting is done by inhaling directly from the neck of a container, such as jerry cans and petro-fillers.

Huffing is the act of inhaling chemical vapours from a cloth soaked with a volatile substance, which is then held close to the nose and mouth to achieve an intoxicating effect.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 56-year-old multiparous woman presented with grade II/III uterine prolapse with cystocele. She complains of passing urine on coughing and sneezing. What is the type of urinary incontinence seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stress incontinence

The type of urinary incontinence present in a patient with prolapse and cystocele experiencing urination on coughing and sneezing is stress incontinence.

Stress incontinence refers to the involuntary leakage of urine when there is increased intraabdominal pressure (eg, coughing, sneezing, laughing, Valsalva maneuver). There is an absence of detrusor muscle contraction, seen in urodynamic studies.

Causes:

* Age and menopause - due to estrogen deficiency

* Multiparity - due to loss of pelvic muscle tone

* Obesity

* Smoking

* Constipation, chronic cough

* Pelvic organ prolapse

* Pregnancy - due to the effect of progesterone and pressure of the gravid uterus on the bladder neck.

* Puerperium - due to descent of the bladder neck, loss of urethro-vesical angle, and reduced pelvic muscle tone

* Surgical repair of vesicovaginal fistula

Grading of genuine stress incontinence (GSI) :

* Grade I: Incontinence with only severe stress, such as coughing, sneezing, and jogging.

* Grade II: Incontinence with moderate stress, such as fast walking, and going up and down the stairs.

* Grade III: Incontinence with mild stress such as standing.

Investigations are only done prior to surgery to confirm the diagnosis. They include the stress test, cotton swab or Q tip test, Marshall and Bonney’s test, urethroscopy, and urodynamic studies. These are not required prior to conservative management.

Conservative management includes Kegel's pelvic exercises, electric nerve stimulation, devices like pessaries, vaginal cones, and artificial sphincters. Medical treatment with estrogen creams, anti-adrenergic, venlafaxine, and imipramine may be useful.

Other options:

Option A: Overflow incontinence is an old term that refers to the inability to empty the bladder, with involuntary, continuous urinary dribbling. Currently, it refers to another presentation of urge incontinence.

Option B: Urge incontinence is the involuntary escape of urine when there is an imminent need to urinate. It occurs due to detrusor muscle overactivity or detrusor instability. It is seen more commonly in old women with decreased bladder capacity, decreased sensation, and central nervous system (CNS) inhibition.

Option D: Neurogenic bladder occurs in patients with neurogenic dysfunction leading to detrusor hyperreflexia. Conditions such as multiple sclerosis, stroke, Parkinson's disease, and spinal injury give rise to this. They present with urgency or urge incontinence.
questions.learning: Stress incontinence — The type of urinary incontinence present in a patient with prolapse and cystocele experiencing urination on coughing and sneezing is stress incontinence.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presents with an anesthetic patch in the areas on the face as shown in the image below. Which of the following nerves is the most commonly involved in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Facial nerve

The clinical scenario points to a case of leprosy and the most commonly involved cranial nerve is the facial nerve.

Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It affects the skin, cutaneous and peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes. The most commonly affected peripheral nerves are the posterior tibial nerve followed by ulnar, median, and lateral popliteal nerves. The most commonly involved cranial nerve is the facial nerve.

Leprosy has a long incubation period, usually ranging from 2 to 12 years. It commonly presents as an area of numbness on the skin or a visible skin lesion which could be a hypopigmented or erythematous macule. Lesions usually involve the face, extensor aspect of the limbs, trunks, and buttocks. The lesions have impaired nerve function and poor hair growth. The patients may also present with burns or ulcers of the anesthetic limb.

Classification systems of leprosy include:

• Ridley Jopling classification:

• Tuberculoid (TT)
• Borderline tubercular (BT)
• Borderline (BB)
• Borderline lepromatous (BL)
• Lepromatous (LL)

• WHO classification:

• Paucibacillary
• Multibacillary

The cardinal signs for the diagnosis of leprosy include:

• Characteristic skin lesions- hypopigmented or erythematous lesions with definite impairment of sensation.
• Peripheral nerve involvement- thickening of the nerve with sensory impairment. Nerve tenderness can also be seen.
• Detection of acid-fast bacilli in slit-skin smear, skin biopsy, or positive biopsy PCR.

The presence of two of the three signs can establish the diagnosis of leprosy. Other tests done for diagnosis of leprosy include nerve biopsy in pure neural leprosy and PGL-1 antibody in cases in low bacterial load.
questions.learning: Facial nerve — The clinical scenario points to a case of leprosy and the most commonly involved cranial nerve is the facial nerve. Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 60-year-old patient with an acute ischemic stroke is planned for thrombolytic therapy using alteplase. The patient weighs 80 kg. What is the appropriate immediate (stat) dose of alteplase for this patient?
questions.explanation: The standard protocol for intravenous thrombolysis in acute ischemic stroke using Alteplase (rt-PA) is a total dose of of body weight, with a maximum dose of . For a patient weighing 80 kg, the total dose would be . The protocol dictates that 10% of this total dose must be administered as an immediate (stat) intravenous bolus over 1 minute. Therefore, the bolus dose is . Among the provided options, 8 (Option A) is the closest standard dose increment. The remaining 90% (64.8 mg) is then infused over the next 60 minutes. Options B (10), C (12), and D (15) exceed the required 10% bolus dose for this patient. Accurate dosing is critical to achieve effective clot dissolution while minimizing the severe risk of intracerebral hemorrhage. Thrombolysis must be initiated as early as possible, typically within a 4.5-hour "golden hour" window from the onset of stroke symptoms, provided that a non-contrast CT head has ruled out intracranial hemorrhage

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
The latent period, contraction period, and relaxation period of a skeletal muscle are 10 ms, 40 ms, and 50 ms respectively. Calculate the tetanizing frequency.

ms- millisecond
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 25 per second

The tetanizing frequency of the given skeletal muscle is 25 per second.

In the question, it is given that the contraction period is 40 msec (40 msec is 0.04 seconds)

Tetanizing frequency = 1/contraction period

Therefore, tetanizing frequency = 1/40 millisecond = 1/0.04 per second = 1000/40 per second = 25 per second.

When there is a repeated stimulus to a muscle fiber before relaxation, it produces an additional contraction of the muscle. The second contraction adds to the first contraction and the total strength of contraction increases. This phenomenon is known as a summation of contractions.

With repeated stimulation, contraction occurs repeatedly before any relaxation has occurred. This causes the individual responses to fuse into one continuous contraction. Such a response is called tetanus (tetanic contraction).

Tetanizing frequency is the minimum frequency required for producing tetanus.

Tetanus is of two types.

• Complete tetanus- when no relaxation occurs between stimuli
• Incomplete tetanus- when periods of incomplete relaxation occur between the summated stimuli.

questions.text: Breast cancer of size 6 x 8 cm with dimpling with invasion of Pectoralis Major and ipsilateral matted axillary nodes belongs to what TNM stage?

Correct answer: A. T3N2M0

Tumor size = 6 × 8 cm

Largest dimension = 8 cm

So tumor is:

• 5 cm → T3

Dimpling of skin

Skin dimpling/tethering alone does not make it T4.

T4 requires:

• Ulceration
• Satellite skin nodules
• Peau d’orange
• Chest wall invasion

Invasion of Pectoralis Major

Invasion of pectoralis major muscle alone is NOT chest wall invasion.

Chest wall invasion (T4a) means invasion of:

• Ribs
• Intercostal muscles
• Serratus anterior

NOT pectoralis muscle.

Hence still T3, not T4.

Ipsilateral matted axillary lymph nodes

Matted/fixed ipsilateral axillary nodes = N2

No distant metastasis mentioned

→ M0

Final TNM Stage

| --------- | -----

| Tumor >5 cm | T3

| Matted axillary nodes | N2

| No metastasis | M0

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is an inhibitor of the intestinal mucosal transporter NPC1L1, responsible for the absorption of dietary and biliary cholesterol?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ezetimibe

Ezetimibe is a cholesterol absorption inhibitor that selectively blocks the Niemann–Pick C1-Like 1 (NPC1L1) transporter on the brush border of enterocytes in the small intestine. This reduces the absorption of dietary and biliary cholesterol, leading to decreased hepatic cholesterol stores and increased LDL receptor expression, thereby lowering LDL cholesterol.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Atorvastatin: An HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (statin) that decreases hepatic cholesterol synthesis, not intestinal absorption.
• B. Fenofibrate: A PPAR-α agonist that primarily lowers triglycerides by increasing lipoprotein lipase activity.
• C. Metformin: An oral antidiabetic drug that reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis and improves insulin sensitivity; it has no effect on NPC1L1.
questions.learning: Ezetimibe Ezetimibe is a cholesterol absorption inhibitor that selectively blocks the Niemann–Pick C1-Like 1 (NPC1L1) transporter on the brush border of enterocytes in the small intestine.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of these vaccines does not follow the open vial policy?
questions.explanation: The "Open Vial Policy" allows certain multi-dose vaccine vials to be used for multiple sessions (up to 28 days) if they are stored correctly and the vaccine vial monitor (VVM) is intact. However, this policy specifically "does not apply" to reconstituted vaccines, which must be discarded within 4 to 6 hours. The "Measles" vaccine (Option D) is a lyophilized (freeze-dried) vaccine that must be reconstituted before use; therefore, it does not follow the open vial policy. Other vaccines that do not follow the policy include BCG and JE vaccines. OPV (Option A), DPT (Option B), TT (Option C), and Hepatitis B are all liquid-form vaccines that do follow the open vial policy, provided all safety criteria are met. This policy is critical in cold chain management to reduce vaccine wastage while ensuring potency and safety. Clinicians and health workers must strictly observe the 4-hour discard rule for measles to prevent serious adverse events like toxic shock syndrome
questions.learning: The "Open Vial Policy" allows certain multi-dose vaccine vials to be used for multiple sessions (up to 28 days) if they are stored correctly and the vaccine vial monitor (VVM) is intact.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Vitamin K in its coenzyme form is regenerated by the enzyme ____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Epoxide reductase

The coenzyme form of Vitamin K is regenerated by the enzyme epoxide reductase.

Epoxide reductase reduces Vitamin K epoxide to its coenzyme form hydroquinone.

Note: In addition to vitamin K reductase, epoxide reductase can also catalyse the reduction of quinone to hydroquinone. Thus, it can regenerate hydroquinone by itself.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following foods possesses the highest biological value?
questions.explanation: Biological value (BV) is a measure of the proportion of absorbed protein from a food that becomes incorporated into the proteins of the organism's body. It reflects how efficiently the body can utilize the dietary protein. Among all whole food sources, the Egg (Option D) has the highest biological value, typically rated at 100 (or close to 94 depending on the scale). This is because egg protein contains all the essential amino acids in the ideal proportions for human health, making it the "reference protein" for comparing others. Milk (Option C) also has a very high BV, approximately 85-91. Soyabean (Option B) has a BV of about 74, and Pulses (Option A) generally have lower biological values, around 50-60, because they are often deficient in certain essential amino acids like methionine. Therefore, eggs are recognized as the superior dietary source in terms of protein utilization efficiency
questions.learning: Biological value (BV) is a measure of the proportion of absorbed protein from a food that becomes incorporated into the proteins of the organism's body.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The hormone acting on post ovulatory endometrium is :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Progesterone

The hormone acting on the post-ovulatory endometrium is progesterone.

Endometrium undergoes changes (endometrial cycle) during the menstrual cycle due to the action of various hormones. The basal zone (lower 1/3rd of the endometrium in contact with the myometrium) is uninfluenced by hormones and shows no change during the cycle. The rest (functional zone) shows the following changes:

1. Regenerative phase (first 2 to 3 days)- the regeneration of glands and the stromal cells from the basal zone. Endometrial thickness is about 2mm.
2. Proliferative phase (5 or 6th day to 14th day) - estrogen (option D) causes the glands to become more tubular and perpendicular to the surface and increases the thickness to 10-12mm on the 14th day (at the time of ovulation)
3. Secretory phase(15th day till menstrual bleeding) - post ovulation, estrogen-primed endometrium is acted by progesterone (from corpus lutetium) and causes increased blood flow (spiraling of arteries) and increases tortuosity of glands (saw-toothed/cork-screwed glands). The thickness of the endometrium is maximum (12mm) in this phase.
4. Menstruation (last 4 or 5 days) - estrogen and progesterone are withdrawn due to the regression of corpus luteum (lack of fertilization). This results in the shedding of the functional zone (menstrual bleeding).

Other options:

Option A: The luteinizing hormone (LH) is secreted by the anterior pituitary and is crucial for ovulation to occur on the 14th day of the menstrual cycle.

Option B: Follicular stimulating hormone (FSH) is secreted by the anterior pituitary. The ovarian follicle with the most sensitivity to FSH becomes the dominant follicle for the current cycle and the rest undergo autolysis.
questions.learning: Progesterone — The hormone acting on the post-ovulatory endometrium is progesterone. Endometrium undergoes changes (endometrial cycle) during the menstrual cycle due to the action of various hormones.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: While examining a patient’s jugular venous pulse, a physician observes a prominent V wave in the waveform. Which clinical condition is most commonly associated with this finding?
questions.explanation: The 'v' wave in the jugular venous pulse (JVP) waveform corresponds to atrial filling while the tricuspid valve is closed during ventricular systole. A prominent (large) 'v' wave is a classic physical sign of tricuspid regurgitation. In this condition, blood leaks backward from the right ventricle into the right atrium during systole, significantly increasing the pressure and volume in the atrium and producing an exaggerated 'v' wave. Aortic regurgitation (Option B) affects the left side of the heart and does not directly produce JVP changes. Tricuspid stenosis (Option C) would result in a prominent 'a' wave due to forceful atrial contraction against a narrowed valve. Atrial fibrillation (Option D) is characterized by the absence of the 'a' wave. Bedside assessment of the JVP waveform is a vital diagnostic skill in cardiology, allowing the clinician to differentiate between various right-sided heart pathologies. Thus, a giant 'v' wave is pathognomonic for severe tricuspid regurgitation
questions.learning: The 'v' wave in the jugular venous pulse (JVP) waveform corresponds to atrial filling while the tricuspid valve is closed during ventricular systole. A prominent (large) 'v' wave is a classic physical sign of tricuspid regurgitation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old male patient with past history of tuberculosis was brought to the emergency department with complaints of breathing difficulty. On examination, there is shortness of breath, and prominent neck veins. While recording the patient's blood pressure, a significant drop in systolic pressure during inspiration was noted from 80mmHg to 60mmHg. The X-ray is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cardiac tamponade

The given clinical scenario of breathing difficulty, prominent neck veins, pulsus paradoxus (significant drop in blood pressure >10 mm Hg), and X-ray image showing cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio more than 0.5) in a patient with a past history of tuberculosis is suggestive of cardiac tamponade.

Cardiac tamponade is characterized by the accumulation of fluid in the pericardial space leading to impairment of diastolic relaxation of the cardiac chambers. This leads to a decline in cardiac output. The characteristic signs of cardiac tamponade are:

* Tachycardia and hypotension

* Pericardial rub

* Pulsus paradoxus - paradoxical reduction in the systemic blood pressure (>10 mm Hg) on inspiration.

* Beck's triad - hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and elevated jugular venous pressure with prominent x descent and absent y descent. The sensitivity of jugular venous distention in detecting tamponade is 100%.

ECG shows reduced voltage and electrical alternans; an Echocardiogram shows a swinging heart sign.

Other options:

Option A: While constrictive pericarditis can also lead to elevated jugular venous pressure, it typically does not cause the classic physical findings associated with cardiac tamponade, such as pulsus paradoxus (significant drop in systolic blood pressure during inspiration) and the absence of heart sounds. Patients with constrictive pericarditis demonstrate a prominent y descent.

Option C: Pleural effusion refers to the pathological accumulation of fluid in the pleural space. It may present with dyspnea, pleuritic pain, dry cough, and associated symptoms like fever, weight loss, edema, and ascites depending on the etiology. On examination, there may be tachypnea, dullness on percussion and decreased/absent breath sounds at the base(s). X-ray shows a classical meniscus sign.

Option D: Acute pericarditis is an inflammation of the pericardium characterized by retrosternal chest pain that is aggravated by deep inspiration and a supine position and relieved by sitting and leaning forward. .On auscultation, 85% of patients have a pericardial friction rub. This appears as a rough scratching sound at end of expiration when the patient is sitting and leaning forward. On ECG There is widespread elevation of ST segments; depression of PR segment below the TP segment

Pearl PF1591: Causes of Pulsus Paradoxus

Physiological causes

Obesity

Pregnancy

Cardiovascular causes

Cardiac tamponade – most common cause

Constrictive pericarditis ( in 1/3rd cases )

Massive pulmonary embolism

Severe CCF

Hypovolemic shock

Respiratory causes

Severe obstructive lung disease

Acute severe asthma

Severe emphysema

Tension pneumothorax

Pearl PF0262: JVP waveform and the abnormalities

1) The a-wave corresponds to atrial contraction.

Abnormality
Conditions

Prominent a-waves
Pulmonary hypertension, right atrial thrombus/ mass, and tricuspid stenosis

Cannon a-waves

Complete AV block, ventricular tachycardia, and premature atrial/ junctional/ ventricular beats

Absent a-waves
Atrial fibrillation

2) The c-wave corresponds to the bulging of tricuspid valve into right atrium during ventricular contraction.

3) The x-descent corresponds to atrial relaxation during atrial diastole.

Abnormality
Conditions

Absent x-descent
Severe tricuspid regurgitation

Rapid x-descent
Cardiac tamponade

4) The v-wave corresponds to the venous filling of right atrium.

Abnormality
Conditions

Dominant v-waves
Tricuspid regurgitation

5) The y-descent corresponds to the passive emptying of the right atrium into right ventricle.

Abnormality
Conditions

Prolonged y-descent
Tricuspid stenosis

Rapid y-descent

Constrictive pericarditis and isolated severe tricuspid regurgitation

Absent y-descent
Cardiac tamponade

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with the complaint of inability to close the eye, drooling of saliva, and deviation of the angle of the mouth. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Facial nerve

Facial nerve (CN VII) palsy causes ipsilateral lower motor neuron facial paralysis, leading to:

• Inability to close eye → orbicularis oculi paralysis
• Drooling of saliva → loss of buccinator tone
• Deviation of angle of mouth to opposite side → unopposed normal side
• Loss of forehead wrinkling (LMN lesion)

Functions of facial nerve:

• Motor: Muscles of facial expression
• Parasympathetic: Lacrimal, submandibular, sublingual glands
• Sensory: Taste from anterior 2/3 of tongue

Why not others:

• Trigeminal nerve (CN V): Mastication, facial sensation (not facial expression)
• Oculomotor nerve (CN III): Eye movements, ptosis
• Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX): Taste posterior 1/3, swallowing

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the typical Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) in a healthy adult?
questions.explanation: The Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is a measure of how much filtrate the kidneys produce each minute. In a healthy adult, the typical GFR is approximately 125 ml/min. This equates to roughly 180 liters per day. However, about 99% of this filtrate is reabsorbed, resulting in a normal urine output of 1-2 liters per day. Values like 200 ml/min (Option B) are abnormally high (hyperfiltration), while 100 ml/min (Option C) or 150 ml/min (Option D) are outside the standard "normal" range. GFR is the gold standard for assessing kidney function. It is often estimated (eGFR) in clinical practice using the patient's serum creatinine level, age, sex, and race. A persistent decline in GFR below 60 ml/min for more than three months is diagnostic of Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD). Maintaining a steady GFR is essential for regulating the body's fluid balance, electrolyte levels, and the excretion of nitrogenous waste products like urea and creatinine
questions.learning: The Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is a measure of how much filtrate the kidneys produce each minute. In a healthy adult, the typical GFR is approximately 125 ml/min.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: While calculating the infant mortality rate, what population is represented in the denominator?
questions.explanation: The Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) is a critical indicator of a nation's overall health status and socio-economic development. It is defined as the number of deaths of infants under one year of age per 1,000 live births in a given year. Therefore, the numerical denominator used to express this rate is 1,000. Rates expressed per 100 (Option A) are simple percentages. A denominator of 100,000 (Option D) is used for the Maternal Mortality Ratio, reflecting the much rarer occurrence of maternal deaths. Option C (10,000) is not a standard multiplier for vital health statistics. IMR is influenced by various factors including maternal health, nutrition, and access to neonatal care. Reducing IMR is a primary goal of global health initiatives like the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG 3). Accurate reporting using the standard per-thousand denominator allows for the comparison of health performance across different regions and time periods, guiding policy decisions and resource allocation for pediatric care
questions.learning: The Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) is a critical indicator of a nation's overall health status and socio-economic development. It is defined as the number of deaths of infants under one year of age per 1,000 live births in a given year.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency room with central chest pain and has a known history of heart disease. An ECG is provided. Based on the ECG findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The provided ECG demonstrates significant ST-segment elevation in the anterior leads (V2-V4) and lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6). Crucially, there is reciprocal ST-segment depression in the inferior leads (III and aVF), which is a hallmark finding that differentiates a myocardial infarction (MI) from other conditions like pericarditis. This pattern indicates an acute injury involving the anterior wall (supplied by the LAD) and the lateral wall (supplied by the LCX or diagonal branches). Inferolateral MI (Option B) is incorrect because it would require ST elevation in inferior leads, whereas they show depression here. Acute pericarditis (Option C) typically presents with diffuse ST elevation across most leads and lacks localized reciprocal changes. Constrictive pericarditis (Option D) is a chronic condition characterized by low voltage QRS or nonspecific changes rather than acute ST elevation. Thus, the localized elevations and reciprocal depressions confirm an Anterolateral MI

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, which did not subside even after 3 weeks of birth, was observed in a neonate. On investigating, liver enzymes, PT/INR and albumin levels were normal. No hemolysis was seen on a peripheral blood smear. A drop in bilirubin level was observed within a week after treating with phenobarbital. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Crigler Najjar type 2

Jaundice persisiting 3 weeks after birth is suggestive of pathological jaundice. Among the given options, Crigler Najjar type 2 presents with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia which responds to phenobarbital therapy.

Dubin Johnson (option C) and Rotor (option A) syndromes lead to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

Crigler Najjar type 2 is an autosomal recessive disease with non-hemolytic, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia caused by homozygous missense mutations in the enzyme UDP UGT1A1 resulting in reduced (partial) enzymatic activity.

The differences between Crigler-Najjar type 1 and type 2 are described in the table below:

Crigler Najjar Type 1

Crigler Najjar Type 2

Autosomal recessive

Autosomal recessive

UDPGT is absent

UDPGT is reduced

Severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia

Less severe

Pale stools

Normal-coloured stools

May proceed to kernicterus and does not respond to phenobarbitone

Does not proceed to kernicterus and is responsive to phenobarbitone
questions.learning: Crigler Najjar type 2 Jaundice persisiting 3 weeks after birth is suggestive of pathological jaundice. Among the given options, Crigler Najjar type 2 presents with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia which responds to phenobarbital therapy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The mechanism of action of tissue plasminogen activator is _____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Enhance fibrin degradation

The mechanism of action of the tissue plasminogen activator is to enhance fibrin degradation.

Tissue plasminogen activators activate plasminogen bound to fibrin, and catalyze the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin, resulting in increased formation of plasmin. This results in fibrinolysis of formed thrombus (thrombolysis).

It is indicated in pulmonary embolism with hemodynamic instability, acute ischemic stroke, and acute myocardial infarction. Recombinant variants of t-PA like reteplase and tenecteplase have a longer half-life.

All thrombolytics can cause bleeding, which may be counteracted by the administration of antifibrinolytics, such as aminocaproic acid and tranexamic acid.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A teenage girl presents to the outpatient department with delayed puberty, short stature, and widely spaced nipples. What is the most likely karyotype?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of delayed puberty, short stature, and a "shield chest" with widely spaced nipples is pathognomonic for Turner Syndrome. As discussed in Q.148, this is a chromosomal disorder where one X chromosome is partially or completely missing. The most common and probable karyotype is 45, XO. 46, XO (Option A) is a non-standard notation for Turner's. 47, XXX (Option C), or Triple X syndrome, usually involves tall stature and mild learning disabilities, but not primary amenorrhea or short stature. 46, XY (Option D) is the normal male karyotype; in a phenotypic female, it would suggest Swyer syndrome (pure gonadal dysgenesis), which presents with delayed puberty but normal height. Turner patients also frequently have webbed necks and cardiovascular anomalies. Management focuses on growth hormone therapy during childhood and estrogen replacement to induce secondary sexual characteristics at puberty. This specific physical triad is a classic board exam "spotter" for the 45, XO genotype

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the role of inhibin?
questions.explanation: Inhibin is a peptide hormone produced by the granulosa cells of the ovary in females and the Sertoli cells of the testis in males. Its primary physiological role is to provide negative feedback to the anterior pituitary gland to selectively inhibit the secretion of Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH). This inhibition is critical for the selection of the dominant follicle during the menstrual cycle and for regulating spermatogenesis. Option A is incorrect as activin, another peptide hormone, stimulates FSH release. Inhibin does not have a direct role in the inhibition (Option C) or stimulation (Option D) of prolactin (PRL). Clinically, inhibin B levels are used as a marker of ovarian reserve, while elevated inhibin levels can serve as a tumor marker for granulosa cell tumors of the ovary. Understanding these hormonal feedback loops is essential for diagnosing and managing infertility and neuroendocrine disorders

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which media is most suitable for the optimal growth of E.coli?
questions.explanation: Escherichia coli is a gram-negative rod and a member of the Enterobacteriaceae family. The most suitable and standard media for its optimal growth and identification is MacConkey agar (Option D). MacConkey agar is both selective (inhibiting gram-positives) and differential. E. coli is a strong lactose fermenter, so it produces bright pink-colored colonies on this medium. Chocolate agar (Option A) is an enriched medium for fastidious organisms like H. influenzae. Thayer-Martin (Option B) is a specialized medium for Neisseria species. SDA (Sabouraud Dextrose Agar, Option C) is used for the cultivation of fungi. Because MacConkey agar allows for the rapid differentiation of E. coli from non-lactose fermenting gut pathogens, it is the definitive choice for standard enteric bacteriology
questions.learning: Escherichia coli is a gram-negative rod and a member of the Enterobacteriaceae family. The most suitable and standard media for its optimal growth and identification is MacConkey agar (Option D).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following groups is not included in the high-risk core population for HIV transmission?
options: Men who have sex with men
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Long-distance truck drivers

Long-distance truck drivers are not included in the high-risk core population for HIV transmission. They are part of the bridge population.

Target interventions for the control of AIDS transmission are done for high-risk core populations like:

• sex workers
• Men who have sex with men
• Transgender
• Injecting drug users

Bridge populations like migrants and long-distance truckers also receive targeted interventions for the control of AIDS transmission.

The services offered through targeted interventions include detection and treatment for sexually transmitted diseases and condom distribution.
questions.learning: Long-distance truck drivers Long-distance truck drivers are not included in the high-risk core population for HIV transmission. They are part of the bridge population.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to Sustainable Development Goals, which of the following statement is false ?
options: End the epidemics of AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria and combat hepatitis
Reduce the global maternal mortality ratio to less than 70 (per 100,000 live births)
Reduce the neonatal mortality rate to as low as 25 (per 1,000 live births)
Reduce under-5 mortality to as low as 25 (per 1,000 live births)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Reduce the neonatal mortality rate to as low as 25 (per 1,000 live births)

The statement "Reduce the neonatal mortality rate to as low as 25 (per 1,000 live births)" is false, and the true statement is "Reduce the neonatal mortality rate to as low as 12 (per 1,000 live births)".

SDG (Sustainable Development Goals) comprises 17 goals and 170 targets for Agenda 2030.

* The MDGs came to an end in December 2015 and were replaced by the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

* 17 SDGs take their place and as of 1st January 2016, the SDGs of the 2030 agenda for sustainable development officially came into force.

* The five P's of the new agenda are People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, and Partnership.

Health is positioned in one comprehensive goal SDG 3.

* Target 3.1: To reduce the global maternal mortality ratio to less than 70 (per 100,000 live births)

* Target 3.2: To reduce neonatal mortality and under-5 mortality by as low as 12 and 25 (per 1,000 live births) respectively.

* Target 3.3: To end the epidemics of AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, and neglected tropical diseases and combat hepatitis, water-borne diseases, and other communicable diseases.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Neurovascular bundle is absent in which compartment of the leg?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior superficial compartment

Posterior superficial compartment of the leg does not contain any neurovascular bundle.

The posterior compartment of the leg is divided into the deep and superficial parts by the transverse intermuscular septum.

The contents of the posterior superficial compartment are gastrocnemius, plantaris, and soleus muscle.

Neurovascular components in various compartments of leg are as follows:

• Anterior compartment: Anterior tibial artery and Deep fibular/peroneal nerve
• Posterior deep compartment: Tibial nerve and posterior tibial vessels in the deep plane.
• Lateral Compartment: Superficial peroneal/fibular nerve and peroneal/fibular vessel. Peroneal artery is a branch of posterior tibial artery.

Note: MRI is the best imaging modality for evaluating the soft tissues of the leg.
questions.learning: Posterior superficial compartment Posterior superficial compartment of the leg does not contain any neurovascular bundle. The posterior compartment of the leg is divided into the deep and superficial parts by the transverse intermuscular septum.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 36-year-old girl presented with tremors and weight loss. Her ophthalmic examination shows the following findings. Identify the true statement regarding the following condition.
options: Medial rectus is the first muscle to be involved.
The muscles and connective tissue around the eye shares similar antigen with diseased organ
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The muscles and connective tissue around the eye shares similar antigen with diseased organ

The clinical scenario of tremors, weight loss, and the image showing exophthalmos are suggestive of Graves ophthalmopathy. The muscles and connective tissue around the eye share similar antigens with diseased organ i.e. Thyroid.

Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) receptors have been found in the orbit's connective tissues and fibroblasts. TSH stimulates the production of inflammatory cytokines. Thyroid eye disease is considered an autoimmune disease where orbital fibroblasts are the primary target and extraocular muscles are secondarily involved. Thyroid follicular cells and orbital fibroblasts likely share a common antigen.

TAO is also linked to increased glycosaminoglycan synthesis, which results in restrictive myopathy. Fat accumulation is caused by orbital fibroblast proliferation and differentiation into adipocytes.

Graves ophthalmopathy, also known as dysthyroid eye illness or thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy (TAO), is one of the most serious ocular manifestations of Graves disease. Between the ages of 25 and 50, it's the leading cause of unilateral and bilateral proptosis in adults. It is seen in 10% of cases without hyperthyroidism.

Proptosis, eyelid retraction, lid retraction, lid lag on downgaze, restricted myopathy, and perhaps compressive optic neuropathy are clinical manifestations that could potentially be used for diagnosis.

American Thyroid Association (ATA) has classified Graves’ ophthalmopathy, irrespective of the hormonal status into the following classes. This classification is also known as Werner classification which reflects the severity of the ophthalmopathy and is well known by the acronym NO SPECS.

Other options

Option A: Thyroid eye disease is associated with HLA-DR3 and HLA-B8.

Option B: The most common ocular motility defect is unilateral elevator palsy due to involvement of the inferior rectus followed by limitation of abduction due to medial rectus palsy.

Option D: Thyroid eye disease is 4-6 times more common in females.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 26-year-old female presents with recurrent epigastric pain. On CECT, a cystic mass is found in the lesser sac, corresponding to the head and neck of the pancreas. Laboratory findings show high CEA and high mucin. Amylase levels were normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mucinous cystic neoplasm

Mucinous Cystic Neoplasm (MCN)

MCN typically occurs in young or middle-aged women.

• Cystic mass in the lesser sac
• Located around head and neck of pancreas

Pancreatic cystic tumors commonly project into the lesser sac.

High CEA/ mucin

• Suggests mucin-producing tumor
• Amylase is normal-This helps rule out pseudocyst.

Lesion | Key Demographic | Location | Fluid Markers | Duct Communication | Clinchers

| ------ | --------------- | -------- | ------------- | ------------------ | ---------

| Serous Cystadenoma | Elderly females | Body/tail | Low CEA, low mucin | No | Honeycomb, central scar, benign

| Mucinous Cystic Neoplasm (MCN) | Middle-aged women | Body/tail (not head) | High CEA, high mucin, amylase low | No | Ovarian stroma, premalignant

| IPMN | Elderly males | Head predominant | High amylase, ± high CEA | Yes | Dilated duct, fish-mouth ampulla with mucin

| Pseudocyst | Post-pancreatitis | Anywhere | High amylase, low CEA | No | No epithelial lining, resolves/conservative first
