questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which one of the following is increased in hypothalamic hamartoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. GnRH

Hypothalamic hamartoma is caused by increased release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH).

Hypothalamic hamartoma, a neuronal migration defect, is the most common cause of organic central precocious puberty. The onset of breast development before the age of 8 years in females and the onset of testicular development (>4 mL) before the age of 9 years in males are suggestive of central precocious puberty.

It is a congenital malformation that consists of ectopically located neural tissue characterized by

* Early-onset of puberty

* Seizures associated with unnatural crying or laughing episodes are known as gelastic seizures.

Tuberculous meningitis, tuberous sclerosis, and astrocytomas can also cause central precocious puberty.

Hypothalamic hamartomas are congenital non-progressive lesions in the hypothalamus that occur during foetal development. Two anatomical subtypes are recognised depending on the location of the mass-like lesion. The first type is the intrahypothalamic lesion that connects with the posterior hypothalamus and third ventricle; they appear near the mammillary bodies and are usually associated with gelastic seizures. The second type is the parahypothalamic or pedunculated lesion located near the anterior hypothalamus, tuber cinereum, or pituitary stalk and attaches only to the floor of the third ventricle. It is usually associated with signs of precocious puberty caused by increasing the release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH). These lesions typically develop a disabling course presenting with multiple seizure types, cognitive decline, and psychiatric symptoms
questions.learning: GnRH Hypothalamic hamartoma is caused by increased release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH). Hypothalamic hamartoma, a neuronal migration defect, is the most common cause of organic central precocious puberty.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Reflex responsible for tachycardia during right atrial distension is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bainbridge reflex

Reflex responsible for tachycardia during right atrial distension is Bainbridge Reflex.

The stretch receptors of the atria that elicit the Bainbridge reflex transmit their afferent signals through the vagus nerves to the medulla of the brain. Then efferent signals are transmitted back through vagal and sympathetic nerves to increase heart rate and strength of heart contraction. Thus, this reflex helps prevent damming of blood in the veins, atria, and pulmonary circulation.

Other options:

Option A: Bezold–Jarisch Reflex: Activation of chemosensitive vagal C fibers in the cardiopulmonary region causes profound bradycardia, hypotension and a brief period of apnoea followed by rapid shallow breathing.

Option C: Cushing Reflex: When intracranial pressure is increased, the blood supply to Rostral Ventro-Lateral Medulla (RVLM) neurons is compromised. The local hypoxia and hypercapnia cause an increase in discharge from the neurons, producing hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration.

Option D: J Reflex: The stimulation of the J-receptors (C receptors/juxta-pulmonary capillary receptors) causes apnea followed by rapid breathing, bradycardia, and hypotension.
questions.learning: Bainbridge reflex Reflex responsible for tachycardia during right atrial distension is Bainbridge Reflex. The stretch receptors of the atria that elicit the Bainbridge reflex transmit their afferent signals through the vagus nerves to the medulla of the brain.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Identify the fracture?
questions.explanation: The X-ray shows a fracture fragment located at the lateral epicondyle of the distal humerus, with fixation in place. The supracondylar region appears intact, which rules out a supracondylar fracture. The fracture is localized laterally, confirming involvement of the lateral epicondyle, a site of muscle attachment. Such fractures are often associated with a fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH injury) and are among the common pediatric elbow injuries. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Medial epicondyle fracture: The medial epicondyle is intact in the image, with no avulsion fragment seen on the medial side. (C) Supracondylar fracture: There is no fracture line above the condyles; the supracondylar area is preserved. Typical signs like displacement or angulation are absent. (D) Infra-condylar fracture: This is not a standard classification for humeral fractures (more relevant to femur), so it is not applicable here
questions.learning: The X-ray shows a fracture fragment located at the lateral epicondyle of the distal humerus, with fixation in place. The supracondylar region appears intact, which rules out a supracondylar fracture.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with a history of chest trauma with breathlessness on examination is found to have systolic BP of 90 mm of Hg, SpO₂ of 85%, GCS 8/15 and absent breath sounds. What is the next step?
options: Secure airway, needle thoracotomy and IV fluids
Blood transfusion and send for CT
Take history, administer IV Dextrose, and send for eFAST
CT scan of the head and secure the airway
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Secure airway, needle thoracotomy and IV fluids

According to the ATLS trauma management principle (ABCDE approach).

A – Airway

• GCS ≤ 8 → airway must be secured (intubation).

B – Breathing

• Absent breath sounds + chest trauma → suspect tension pneumothorax
• Immediate needle thoracotomy (needle decompression).

C – Circulation

• Hypotension (90 mmHg) indicates shock
• Start IV fluids for resuscitation.

Blood transfusion and CT❌

• CT is done only after patient stabilization.
• Patient is hemodynamically unstable, so immediate life-saving treatment is needed.

Take history, give IV dextrose, eFAST ❌

• Primary survey and life-saving interventions come first.
• History is secondary survey.

CT head and secure airway ❌

• Breathing problem (tension pneumothorax) must be treated immediately before CT→ because CT scan takes time and tension pneumothorax is life threatening.
• Tension pneumothorax → Air in pleural space → lung collapse→ This causes Mediastinal shift → ↓ venous return → hypotension
• Indicates respiratory compromise + obstructive shock, hence needs to be treated immediately with needle decompression.
questions.learning: Secure airway, needle thoracotomy and IV fluids According to the ATLS trauma management principle (ABCDE approach). A – Airway • GCS ≤ 8 → airway must be secured (intubation).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An adult male presents with a history of intermittent purulent discharge, occasionally tinged with blood, from an external opening in the perianal region. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presence of an external opening in the perianal region that produces intermittent purulent discharge and blood is the hallmark of a Fistula in ano. This is a chronic abnormal track communicating between the anal canal and the perianal skin, most commonly resulting from a previous perianal abscess. Hemorrhoids (Option A) cause painless bright red bleeding during defecation but not a discharging skin opening. A pilonidal sinus (Option B) is located in the sacrococcygeal (tailbone) region, further from the anus. A perianal abscess (Option C) is the acute, painful inflammatory stage before a fistula forms. Goodsall's rule is used to predict the internal path of the fistula based on the location of the external opening. Diagnosis is clinical but may be aided by MRI to map complex tracks. Management is surgical, involving fistulotomy for simple tracks or specialized procedures like the Seton technique or LIFT for complex fistulas to preserve anal sphincter function and prevent incontinence
questions.learning: The clinical presence of an external opening in the perianal region that produces intermittent purulent discharge and blood is the hallmark of a Fistula in ano.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: While performing an endoscopy, a constriction is felt at the oesophageal junction, 25 cm from the upper incisors. Which of the following structures is responsible for this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arch of aorta

The constriction is felt due to the arch of aorta and left bronchus crossing the esophagus at 25 cm from the upper incisor teeth.

Normally, the esophagus shows 3 constrictions at the following levels measured from upper incisors:

* Junction of the esophagus with cricopharynx (15 cm from the incisor teeth)

* Crossed by arch of aorta and left bronchus (25 cm from the incisor teeth)

* It pierces the diaphragm (40 cm from the incisor teeth)

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which statement correctly characterizes a single-exposure point-source epidemic?
options: Has more than one incubation period
questions.explanation: A single exposure point source epidemic occurs when a large group of susceptible individuals is exposed to a single common source (like contaminated food at a party) at a specific point in time. The characteristic feature of this type of epidemic is that it is explosive in nature, meaning there is a rapid rise in the number of cases followed by a relatively quick decline. All cases typically occur within a single incubation period (making Option A incorrect). The resulting epidemic curve characteristically has a single peak (Option B is incorrect). A slow rise and fall (Option D) is characteristic of a propagated epidemic, where the disease spreads slowly from person to person. Identifying an epidemic as "point source" is vital for outbreak investigations, as it directs health officials to search for a localized, time-limited source of contamination. The explosive nature of such outbreaks often overwhelms local healthcare facilities rapidly, requiring an immediate and intensive public health response
questions.learning: A single exposure point source epidemic occurs when a large group of susceptible individuals is exposed to a single common source (like contaminated food at a party) at a specific point in time.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 70-year-old man presents with chronic hip pain. Imaging reveals lytic lesions on hip X-ray, laboratory tests show hypercalcemia, and bone marrow examination demonstrates 42% plasma cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical constellation of persistent bone pain, lytic lesions on X-ray, and hypercalcemia in an elderly patient is highly suggestive of Multiple Myeloma. The definitive diagnostic clue provided is the bone marrow biopsy revealing 42% plasma cells; the standard diagnostic threshold is clonal plasma cells. Multiple Myeloma is a malignant proliferation of plasma cells that secrete cytokines (like IL-6) which activate osteoclasts, leading to "punched-out" bone destruction and the release of calcium into the blood. CLL (Option B) involves a proliferation of mature small lymphocytes and presents with lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. ALL (Option C) involves immature lymphoblasts and is primarily a disease of childhood. CML (Option D) is characterized by a massive increase in mature and immature granulocytes and is associated with the Philadelphia chromosome. Multiple Myeloma is often remembered by the "CRAB" mnemonic: Calcium elevation, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, and Bone lesions. This case perfectly illustrates the pathological and biochemical hallmarks of this common hematological malignancy
questions.learning: The clinical constellation of persistent bone pain, lytic lesions on X-ray, and hypercalcemia in an elderly patient is highly suggestive of Multiple Myeloma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Graham Steell murmur is heard in _____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pulmonary regurgitation

Graham Steell murmur is the early to mid-diastolic murmur heard in pulmonary regurgitation.

Graham Steell murmur is a high-pitched murmur heard best at the left second intercostal space and is often louder with inspiration. This murmur occurs due to pulmonary regurgitation, which in this case, is secondary to pulmonary hypertension. It can also be seen in patients with COPD due to the development of cor pulmonale leading to pulmonic hypertension.

Other options:

Option A: Pulmonary stenosis is a narrowing of the pulmonary valve or artery, obstructing blood flow from the right ventricle to the lungs. It is associated with a harsh systolic ejection murmur heard best at the left upper sternal border, often with a systolic thrill.

Option C: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a condition where the heart muscle thickens, often affecting the interventricular septum. It is associated with a systolic ejection murmur that increases with the Valsalva manoeuvre and decreases with squatting.

Option D: A ventricular septal defect (VSD) is a congenital heart defect where there is an abnormal opening in the septum between the left and right ventricles. It is typically associated with a holosystolic murmur heard at the left lower sternal border.
questions.learning: Pulmonary regurgitation Graham Steell murmur is the early to mid-diastolic murmur heard in pulmonary regurgitation. Graham Steell murmur is a high-pitched murmur heard best at the left second intercostal space and is often louder with inspiration.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: During spermatogenesis, the process in which sperm cells develop from spermatogonia in the testes, the secretion of FSH (Follicle-Stimulating Hormone) in a male is inhibited by which factor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inhibin

The secretion of FSH in a male is inhibited by negative feedback effect of Inhibin secreted by sertoli cells.

* GnRH stimulates the anterior pituitary gland to secrete follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH).

* FSH stimulates inhibin production by the Sertoli cells. This inhibin inhibits FSH production by directly acting on the anterior pituitary.

* LH stimulates Leydig cells to secrete testosterone, which in turn inhibits LH. Testosterone inhibits LH secretion by acting directly on the anterior pituitary and by inhibiting the secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) from the hypothalamus.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
Which of the following instruments are used in the caesarean section?

1. Bard-Parker blade
2. Doyen's retractor
3. Cusco's speculum
4. Allis forceps
5. Shirodkar's uterine clamp
6. Green Armytage forceps
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 4, 6

Of the given list/combination of instruments 1, 2, 4, 6 are commonly used in the cesarean section.

Cesarean section is an operative procedure in which the fetuses are delivered through an incision on the abdominal and uterine walls.

The given image summarizes the various instruments used in the lower segment cesarean section.

Bard-Parker blade (scalpel with blade) has a handle with a notch to fit the blade. It is usually held by pencil grip. Commonly for abdominal incisions, we use blade no: 22. Other uses include incision of skin and sub-cutaneous tissues, cutting the clamped pedicles, and performing sharp dissections.

The given image shows various Bard-Parker blades.

Doyen's retractor is used to retract the abdominal wall as well as the bladder to facilitate better exposure of the lower uterine segment during cesarian operation. It is also used to pull back the soft tissues to widen the surgical field during laparotomy.

The image below shows Doyen's retractor.

Alli's forceps: It is identified by the distal blades and a tip that has teeth that do not oppose each other. There is also a lock in the proximal part.

Uses:

• To catch hold of the margins and angles of the uterine flaps in LSCS after the delivery of the baby in settings where the Green-Armytage hemostatic clamp is not available.
• To catch hold the anterior lip of the cervix
• To hold the apex of the episiotomy wound during the repair.
• To catch hold of the margins of the peritoneum, rectus sheath, vaginal mucosa during the repair.
• To catch hold of the torn ends of the sphincter ani externus prior to suture in the repair of complete perineal tear.

The given image shows Alli's forceps.

Green armytage forceps have a broad tip as shown in the image and hence are used to compress a wide area. It is used as a hemostat in caesarian sections. In LSCS (Lower segment Caesarean section), the cut uterine edges can bleed and Green Armytage forceps are applied to the edge of the incision for hemostasis.

Cusco's speculum is a self-retaining bivalve speculum used for visualization of the cervix, vaginal fornices, and for performing pap smears.

The instrument shown in the image is Cusco’s speculum.

Shirodkar's uterine holding clamp has blades with curved transverse bars with gaps between them when it is locked. This gap makes it atraumatic and is used to lift, hold and steady the uterus during sling surgeries and tubal procedures.

The image below shows Shirodkar's uterine clamp.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 4, 6 Of the given list/combination of instruments 1, 2, 4, 6 are commonly used in the cesarean section. Cesarean section is an operative procedure in which the fetuses are delivered through an incision on the abdominal and uterine walls.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which amino acid will not be synthesized due to B12 deficiency in a patient with history of ileectomy with elevated homocysteine levels, increased methylmalonyl CoA and peripheral neuropathy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Methionine

Vitamin B12 deficiency (e.g., after ileectomy, where B12 is absorbed) leads to impairment of two key reactions:

1.      Homocysteine → Methionine (via methionine synthase, B12-dependent)

2.      Methylmalonyl-CoA → Succinyl-CoA (via methylmalonyl-CoA mutase)

Biochemical consequences:

• ↑ Homocysteine (cannot convert to methionine)
• ↓ Methionine synthesis
• ↑ Methylmalonyl-CoA → contributes to neurological damage

Clinical relevance:

• Peripheral neuropathy (due to myelin damage)
• Megaloblastic anemia
• Seen in ileal resection (ileectomy) due to impaired B12 absorption

Why other options are incorrect:

• Cysteine: Formed from homocysteine (via B6-dependent pathway), not directly dependent on B12
• Glutathione: Synthesized from glutamate, cysteine, glycine
• Tryptophan: Essential amino acid (not synthesized in body)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman, having lost her newborn, is producing breast milk, which risks developing into a breast abscess due to milk stasis and incomplete emptying. Which drug can prevent this complication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cabergoline

Dopamine (from hypothalamus) tonically inhibits prolactin secretion from anterior pituitary.

So: ↑ Dopamine → ↓ Prolactin → ↓ Milk production

Why Cabergoline Works

Cabergoline = D2 receptor agonist → mimics dopamine → suppresses prolactin → stops lactation → prevents milk stasis → prevents breast abscess

Why the Others Fail

| Drug | Class | Effect on Prolactin

| ---- | ----- | -------------------

| Mifepristone | Progesterone/glucocorticoid antagonist | No effect on prolactin

| Cabergoline ✓ | D2 agonist | ↓ Prolactin → suppresses lactation

| Chlorpromazine | D2 antagonist (antipsychotic) | ↑ Prolactin → causes galactorrhea

| Metoclopramide | D2 antagonist (antiemetic) | ↑ Prolactin → causes galactorrhea

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A blood spill in the operation theatre must be cleaned with _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chlorine compound

Sodium hypochlorite, a compound of chlorine, is the best disinfectant for surface blood spills. It is used with a concentration of 0.5-5%.

If the spill contains large amounts of blood or body fluids, clean the visible matter with disposable absorbent material and discard the contaminated materials in appropriate, labelled containment.

A 1:10–1:100 dilution of 5.25%–6.15% sodium hypochlorite (i.e., household bleach) or an EPA-registered tuberculocidal disinfectant has been recommended for decontaminating blood spills.
questions.learning: Chlorine compound Sodium hypochlorite, a compound of chlorine, is the best disinfectant for surface blood spills. It is used with a concentration of 0.5-5%.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following courts has the authority to commute a death sentence?
questions.explanation: Under the Indian legal system, while a Session Court (Option A) or an Additional Session Court (Option B) can pass a death sentence, the sentence cannot be executed until it is confirmed by the High Court. The High Court has the specific authority to confirm, commute, or set aside the death sentence during this mandatory review process. Further appeals can be made to the Supreme Court. Additionally, the President of India and the Governors of States have the constitutional power to grant pardons and commute death sentences. Options A, B, and D in the original list might be incomplete, but the High Court's role in the "confirmation" and potential commutation of capital punishment is a fundamental principle of criminal procedure. This mandatory oversight is a legal safeguard to ensure that the death penalty is reserved for only the "rarest of rare" cases, as mandated by judicial precedent

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is macrocytic anaemia seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Liver disease

Liver disease features non-megaloblastic macrocytic normochromic anaemia.

MCV >100 fl indicates macrocytic anaemia. The causes for the same, divided by morphology, are:

*

Megaloblastic:

Vitamin B12 deficiency

Folate deficiency

Thiamine deficiency

Drugs - Methotrexate, Zidovudine, Hydroxyurea

Orotic aciduria

*

Non-megaloblastic:

Alcohol use

Liver disease

Hypothyroidism

Hemolysis*

*Note: Hemolysis can be associated with macrocytosis because of compensatory reticulocytosis. However, MCV can be normal depending on the degree of hemolysis.
questions.learning: Liver disease Liver disease features non-megaloblastic macrocytic normochromic anaemia. MCV >100 fl indicates macrocytic anaemia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Banana sign on USG is associated with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Spina bifida

The banana sign on USG is seen in spina bifida.

Banana sign is an abnormal anterior curvature of the cerebellum along with effacement of the cisterna magna that produces this appearance. It is seen in spina bifida and is also associated with Arnold-Chiari malformation.

Spina bifida is a congenital anomaly occurring due to incomplete development of the neural tube. The most commonly cited signs present in spina bifida are the banana sign and the lemon sign.

The lemon sign occurs due to the overlapping of the frontal bones due to the posterior shift of intracranial contents as shown below.

Other options:

Option B: Omphalocele is a congenital midline anterior abdominal wall defect through which the solid abdominal viscera or bowel herniates. The herniated abdominal contents are covered by a membranous sac as shown below.

The image below shows an ultrasound image of the fetus suggestive of an omphalocele (asterisk).

Option C: Nuchal translucency (NT) is used to antenatally screen Downs syndrome (Trisomy 21) during the first trimester. NT is the maximum thickness of the translucent area between the skin and soft tissue over the fetal spine at the back of the neck. When the NT measurement is increased, it is a marker for fetal aneuploidy and structural anomalies. The ultrasound image below shows increased NT thickness and absent nasal bone of a fetus with Trisomy 21 at 11 weeks gestation.
questions.learning: Spina bifida — The banana sign on USG is seen in spina bifida. Banana sign is an abnormal anterior curvature of the cerebellum along with effacement of the cisterna magna that produces this appearance.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Thyroid hormone acts via which among the following receptor?
options: Transmembrane receptor linked to tyrosine kinase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nuclear receptor

The thyroid hormone receptors belong to nuclear receptors.

The nuclear receptor is a broad term that includes receptors located in both the nucleus and cytoplasm. This is because even for the receptors that are located in the cytoplasm, the end effect is seen via the nucleus.

Pearl PF0103: Classification of Hormones by Mechanism of Action

A) Hormones that bind to intracellular receptors

* Cytoplasmic receptors

* Steroids such as glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids and androgens

* Nuclear receptors

* Thyroid hormones

* Vitamins A and D

B) Hormones that bind to cell surface receptors

* GPCR - G protein-coupled receptors

* Gs - stimulation of the 2nd messenger cAMP

* Examples: ACTH, CRH, TSH, LH, FSH hCG, Catecholamines (β receptors), Vasopressin (V2 receptors), Secretin, Somatostatin, and Glucagon.

* Gi - inhibition of the 2nd messenger cAMP

* Examples: Catecholamines (ɑ2 receptors), Acetylcholine (M2, M4), Somatostatin

* Gq - The 2nd messenger is Phospholipase C (IP3 DAG Ca2+)

* Examples: Parathyroid hormone, GnRH - Gonadotropin-releasing hormone, GHRH - Growth hormone releasing hormone, TRH, Catecholamines (ɑ1 receptors), Vasopressin (V1 receptor), Gastrin, Cholecystokinin and Oxytocin.

* cGMP as the 2nd messenger

* Examples: Atrial natriuretic factor, Nitric oxide

* Tyrosine kinase receptors such as those that employ Janus kinase (JAK-STAT pathway) or MAP kinase pathway

* Growth hormone, Growth factors (GFs) - eg: IGF, VEGF, FGF, PDGF etc, Erythropoietin, Insulin and Prolactin.

Note: Even though the cytoplasmic receptors are present in the cytoplasm, once the hormone-receptor complex is formed it moves to the nucleus for its actions.
questions.learning: Nuclear receptor — The thyroid hormone receptors belong to nuclear receptors. The nuclear receptor is a broad term that includes receptors located in both the nucleus and cytoplasm.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
Arrange the following causes of neonatal mortality from maximum to the least (according to the verbal autopsy report 2010-2013 data).

1. Prematurity and low birth weight
2. Birth injuries and birth asphyxia
3. Congenital anomalies
4. Sepsis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1>2>4>3

According to verbal autopsy report 2010-2013 data, the correct sequence of causes of neonatal mortality from maximum to least is prematurity and low birth weight> birth injuries and birth asphyxia> sepsis> congenital anomalies. (1>2>4>3)

Neonatal deaths are deaths that occur during the neonatal period, that is between birth and 28 completed days after birth. It is calculated by using the following formula:

Neonatal mortality rate = Number of deaths of children under 28 days of age in a year x 1000/Total live births in the same year

Important causes of neonatal mortality include ( from maximum to least)

• Prematurity & low birth weight
• Birth asphyxia & birth trauma
• Neonatal pneumonia
• Other non-communicable diseases
• Sepsis
• Congenital anomalies
• Diarrhoeal diseases
• Injuries
• Tetanus

Note: Recent 2020 SRS (Sample Registration System) report shows the following:

• Neonatal mortality rate to be 20.
• Infant mortality rate to be 28.
• Under 5 mortality rate to be 32.
questions.learning: 1>2>4>3 According to verbal autopsy report 2010-2013 data, the correct sequence of causes of neonatal mortality from maximum to least is prematurity and low birth weight> birth injuries and birth asphyxia> sepsis> congenital anomalies.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not an indicator of fetal lung maturity?
options: Nile blue test showing >50% of blue cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Nile blue test showing >50% of blue cells

Nile blue test showing >50% orange cells is a sign of fetal lung maturity, not blue cells.

Tests for the assessment of fetal lung maturity include:

The Nile blue test involves staining desquamated fetal cells from amniotic fluid with 0.1% Nile blue sulfate. The presence of orange cells > 50% suggests lung maturity. Lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio at 31 to 32 weeks is 1, and at 35 weeks ratio is 2. The ratio ≥2 indicates lung maturity (option A).

The shake test or bubble test (Clement's test) (option B) involves mixing amniotic fluid with 95% ethanol, shaking it for 15 seconds, and observing it for 15 minutes. A complete ring of bubbles at the meniscus is a positive test and indicates lung maturity. This is a useful bedside test.

The presence of phosphatidylglycerol, (option C) saturated phosphatidylcholine and lamellar body count (>50,000/mcL) indicates lung maturity.

Glucocorticoids accelerate lung maturation and lower the incidence of respiratory distress and neonatal mortality in preterms if the birth was delayed for at least 24 hours after initiation of betamethasone. A single course of corticosteroids is recommended for women between 24 and 36 weeks who are at risk of delivery within 7 days. Intramuscular injections of either 2 doses of 12 mg betamethasone are given 24 hourly or 4 doses of 6 mg dexamethasone are given 12 hourly.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is responsible for maintaining data about births and deaths in India?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sample registration system

The Sample Registration System is responsible for maintaining data about births and deaths in India.

SRS was initiated in the mid-1960s to provide reliable estimates of birth and death rates at the National and State levels. It is a dual-record system where there is continuous registration of births and deaths and a 6-month independent survey by an investigator-supervisor. It provides reliable health information, age-specific fertility and mortality rates, infant mortality,under-five and adult mortality.

Other options:

Lay reporting is defined as the collection of information, its use, and its transmission to other levels of the health system by non-professional health workers.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida at 38 weeks pregnancy was put on oxytocin drip in view of slow labour at the rate of 30 mIU/min by the newly appointed registrar. She complains of confusion and starts throwing fits. What electrolyte imbalance is expected to have happened in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hyponatremia

Oxytocin, especially when administered in high doses or with large volumes of electrolyte-free intravenous fluids, has an antidiuretic (vasopressin-like) effect. High-dose oxytocin infusion causes:

• Increased water reabsorption due to its ADH-like action
• Dilutional hyponatremia
• Cerebral edema leading to:

• Headache
• Confusion
• Nausea/vomiting
• Seizures (fits)
• Coma in severe cases

Why not the other options?

• A. Hypokalemia: Not a characteristic complication of oxytocin infusion.
• C. Hypocalcemia: Does not occur as a direct effect of oxytocin.
• D. Hypernatremia: Oxytocin causes water retention, leading to hyponatremia, not hypernatremia.
questions.learning: Hyponatremia Oxytocin, especially when administered in high doses or with large volumes of electrolyte-free intravenous fluids, has an antidiuretic (vasopressin-like) effect.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which benign ovarian tumor is most commonly encountered, tends to involve both ovaries, and typically affects women of reproductive age?
questions.explanation: The most common benign ovarian tumor in women of reproductive age is the benign teratoma, also known as a mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst). It arises from germ cells and contains tissues from all three germ layers such as hair, teeth, and sebaceous material. Benign teratomas are: 1. The most common ovarian tumor in young women 2. Often bilateral (≈10–20% cases) 3. Typically seen during the reproductive years They are usually slow-growing and asymptomatic but may present with abdominal pain or complications like torsion. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Epithelial cell tumor → More common overall but seen in older women, not typically bilateral benign tumors in young females (B) Follicular cysts → Functional cysts, not true tumors and usually unilateral (C) Sex cord stromal tumor → Less common and not typically bilateral

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient with 6 weeks amenorrhea and a positive pregnancy test came with complaints of lower abdominal pain, moderate bleeding PV. She was hemodynamically stable. On USG, there was no gestational sac in the uterus. Ovaries were normal and no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. What is the next line of management?
options: Declare as complete abortion and follow-up in 15 days
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Follow-up with beta-HCG

The patient presents with a history of 6 weeks of amenorrhea, a positive urine pregnancy test, abdominal pain and moderate vaginal bleeding. However, the ultrasound examination does not reveal a gestational sac in the uterus, which could indicate either an ectopic pregnancy or an abortion. In such cases, the next line of management is to follow up with beta-HCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) levels.

Beta-HCG levels above 1500 mIU/mL are considered the discriminatory value, beyond which a gestational sac should be visible on transvaginal ultrasound.

If the gestational sac is not visible on ultrasound and the beta-HCG levels are above 1500 mIU/mL, it suggests an ectopic pregnancy. On the other hand, if the beta-HCG levels are below 1500 mIU/mL, they can be repeated after 48 hours and interpreted as follows:

• Decreasing HCG levels between day 1 and day 3 suggest a possible abortion.
• If the HCG levels rise during this period but does not double, it indicates a likely ectopic pregnancy.

Note: While some institutions set the discriminatory threshold for HCG levels at ≥ 1500 mIU/mL, others use ≥ 2000 mIU/mL.
questions.learning: Follow-up with beta-HCG — The patient presents with a history of 6 weeks of amenorrhea, a positive urine pregnancy test, abdominal pain and moderate vaginal bleeding.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient underwent surgery for breast carcinoma. She now presents with painless swelling involving the arm as shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lymphedema

The generalized swelling of the left arm of the patient post-surgery for breast carcinoma is suggestive of post-mastectomy lymphedema.

Lymphoedema occurs when interstitial fluid accumulates due to defective lymphatic drainage. It is a common complication of breast cancer treatment, involving axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy. Sentinel lymph node dissection (SLND) reduces the risk of lymphedema significantly.

Clinical signs and symptoms are observed in the ipsilateral arm. A significant increase in limb size due to swelling is seen. Other symptoms are heaviness, tightness, numbness, tingling, limb fatigue, and reduced limb mobility.

Diagnosis is predominantly based on the clinical swelling of the arm. The girth of the affected arm >2 centimetres than the normal limb, a 200-mL or more increase in limb volume, or a 5% or greater limb volume change are other diagnostic criteria.

Management:

1. Limb elevation, elastic arm stockings, and pneumatic compression devices to reduce swelling.
2. Using a low-pH water-based moisturizer to prevent dry skin caused by excess fluid accumulation.
3. Manual lymphatic drainage (MLD) by a therapist followed by simple lymphatic drainage (SLD) by the patient daily aids interstitial fluid evacuation.
4. Surgical options include lymphaticovenular anastomosis, liposuction, and debulking.

Other options:

Option B:   Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to lymphangiosarcoma seen in chronic long-standing lymphedema following mastectomy (more than 10 years). They present as single/multiple bluish-red skin and subcutaneous nodules. They can ulcerate and hemorrhage.

Option C: Axillary venous thrombosis or Paget-Schrotter disease is seen in patients doing rigorous exercise and in weightlifters. The compression of the subclavian vein at the thoracic outlet causes painful swelling of the arm.

Option D: Cellulitis (lymphangitis) is a bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue. It is characterized by a painful area of erythematous and edematous tissue.
questions.learning: Lymphedema — The generalized swelling of the left arm of the patient post-surgery for breast carcinoma is suggestive of post-mastectomy lymphedema. Lymphoedema occurs when interstitial fluid accumulates due to defective lymphatic drainage.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman is diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis. What associated complication is shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Scleromalacia perforans

Scleromalacia perforans is the associated complication of rheumatoid arthritis that is shown in the image.

Scleromalacia perforans is a specific type of necrotizing scleritis without inflammation, characterized by progressive scleral thinning. The uveal tissue appears to shine through it. Spontaneous perforation is a rare complication of the condition. It is typically seen in elderly women with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis. A yellowish patch of melting sclera can be seen. This is due to the obliteration of blood supply.

Clinical features include pain, photophobia, and lacrimation. The affected eye appears red. Medical management includes steroids and immunosuppressants. In severe cases, surgical treatment by scleral patch graft may be done.

Other options:

Option B - Ciliary staphyloma is used to describe the bulge of an area of weak sclera lined by the ciliary body. Common causes include scleritis, developmental glaucoma, and end-stage primary or secondary glaucoma. Thinning of the sclera, secondary to perforating injury, can also result in the condition.

Option C - Coloboma is a congenital anomaly, that develops due to a defect in the closure of the embryonic cleft. It is characterized by poorly developed uveal tissue. In some cases, it might be deficient. The lens, choroid, and retina may also be involved.

The image below shows coloboma of the right eyelid.

Option D - Malignant melanoma of the conjunctiva appears as a mass near the limbus. It can be pigmented or non-pigmented. It is usually seen in elderly patients. The choroid, iris, ciliary body, and eyelids can also develop the tumor.

The image below shows malignant melanoma of the choroid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents to the physician with a 3-month history of pain in her right shoulder. She is physically active and regularly plays tennis. The pain is reproduced when the shoulder is externally rotated against resistance. Injury of which of the following tendons is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Infraspinatus

The infraspinatus muscle is one of the rotator cuff muscles responsible for external rotation of the shoulder. Pain reproduced with external rotation against resistance indicates injury to the infraspinatus tendon, commonly seen in overhead athletes such as tennis players.

Thus, isolated pain with resisted external rotation localizes the pathology to the infraspinatus tendon.

Why not other options:

B. Pectoralis major: Causes adduction & internal rotation, not external rotation.

C. Subscapularis: Main internal rotator of shoulder.

D. Supraspinatus: Responsible for abduction initiation (0–15°).
questions.learning: Infraspinatus — The infraspinatus muscle is one of the rotator cuff muscles responsible for external rotation of the shoulder. Pain reproduced with external rotation against resistance indicates injury to the infraspinatus tendon, commonly seen in overhead…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young patient presents with a severe headache. He has never experienced a headache of this severity before. He has hypertension and nuchal rigidity on examination. Which of the following could be the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Subarachnoid hemorrhage

The clinical manifestations of neck stiffness and severe headache (like never before) suggests a diagnosis of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is the bleeding into the subarachnoid space, which is the area between the arachnoid membrane and the pia mater surrounding the brain. The diagnosis is suspected when a hyperattenuating material is seen filling the subarachnoid space. Most commonly this is apparent around the circle of Willis, on account of the majority of berry aneurysms occurring in this region, or in the Sylvian fissure.

Young males with a history of spontaneous sudden onset severe headaches with seizures should raise suspicion for subarachnoid hemorrhage (aneurysmal). The most common cause of SAH is head trauma and the second common cause is the rupture of a saccular aneurysm.

Symptoms include:

* Severe headache (thunderclap headache)

* Rapid onset vomiting

* Confusion or a lowered level of consciousness

* Seizures

* Neck stiffness or neck pain

Other options:

Cluster headache is a rare form of primary headache. It is characterized by deep excruciating pain that is usually retroorbital, and unilateral. It usually lasts for short duration of 8-10 weeks a year followed by a pain-free interval. It is associated with lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, and ptosis. In acute cases, oxygen therapy is useful. Subcutaneous and nasal sumatriptan can be used.

The classic clinical triad of fever, headache, and neck rigidity is suggestive of meningitis. Other common complaints are nausea, vomiting, and photophobia. Nuchal rigidity (“stiff neck”) is the pathognomonic sign of meningitis. Hip and knee flexion on passive flexion of the neck is called Brudzinsky's sign.

Encephalitis presents similar to meningitis with fever, altered mental status, and focal or diffuse neurological symptoms.

Pearl PF1866: Intracranial haemorrhage
questions.learning: Subarachnoid hemorrhage — The clinical manifestations of neck stiffness and severe headache (like never before) suggests a diagnosis of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old male working in a stone industry presents with breathlessness and cough. CT Chest shows calcified mediastinal lymph nodes and pulmonary nodules. He is diagnosed with silicosis. Which of the following statements are correct? 1. Silicosis typically involves lower lobes of the lung. 2. The patient is at a higher risk of developing pulmonary tuberculosis. 3. Pulmonary fibrosis after occupational exposure to silica is dose-dependent. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2 and 3 only

• 1. Silicosis typically involves lower lobes: Incorrect

• Silicosis classically produces small rounded opacities predominantly in the upper lobes.
• Hilar and mediastinal lymph-node calcification may produce the characteristic “eggshell” calcification.

• 2. Increased risk of pulmonary tuberculosis: Correct

• Silicosis significantly increases susceptibility to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
• The combination is called silicotuberculosis.

• 3. Pulmonary fibrosis is dose-dependent: Correct

• The risk and severity of silicosis correlate with the cumulative dose and duration of silica exposure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman presents with repeated episodes of fever, vomiting, and right upper abdominal pain radiating toward the neck. On clinical examination, Murphy’s sign is positive. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The constellation of right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain, fever, and vomiting in a middle-aged female is highly indicative of biliary disease. The pathognomonic clinical finding provided is a positive Murphy’s sign, where the patient experiences a sudden cessation of inspiration due to pain when the gallbladder is palpated during a deep breath. This sign is highly sensitive for acute cholecystitis. Gallbladder carcinoma (Option B) typically presents with chronic pain, jaundice, or a palpable mass rather than acute inflammation. Peptic ulcer disease (Option C) usually causes epigastric pain related to meals and does not present with a Murphy's sign. While acute appendicitis (Option D) can sometimes present with RUQ pain in cases of a retrocaecal or subhepatic appendix, Murphy's sign specifically targets gallbladder inflammation. The radiation of pain to the neck or shoulder is due to phrenic nerve irritation. Consequently, the clinical evidence points decisively toward acute cholecystitis as the primary diagnosis requiring further ultrasound verification and management

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the most common location of Nasopharyngeal carcinoma:
questions.explanation: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) most commonly arises from the Fossa of Rosenmüller (recessus pharyngeus). In endoscopic or anatomical diagrams of the nasopharynx, this is a deep, slit-like space located posterior to the torus tubarius (the opening of the Eustachian tube). In the provided image, label 2 corresponds to this characteristic anatomical site. NPC has a strong association with the Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) and is highly prevalent in certain regions like Southern China. Early symptoms are often subtle and include unilateral middle ear effusion (glue ear) due to Eustachian tube blockage or painless neck lymphadenopathy (Trottier’s triad). Other locations in the nasopharynx (Options A, C, and D) such as the roof or the posterior wall are less common primary sites. Because the tumor is often hidden in this recess, NPC is frequently diagnosed at a locally advanced stage, requiring a high index of clinical suspicion

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department with a persistent dry cough, without fever or other associated symptoms. The patient recently started antihypertensive medication. What is the most likely cause of the cough?
questions.explanation: The development of a persistent dry cough after starting a new medication for high blood pressure is a classic side effect of ACE inhibitors (like Enalapril or Lisinopril). ACE inhibitors work by blocking the Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE). This enzyme is also responsible for the breakdown of bradykinin in the lungs. When ACE is inhibited, levels of bradykinin accumulate, irritating the pulmonary sensory nerves and triggering the cough. Option A and B are incorrect because bradykinin is the sole mediator responsible for this specific side effect; changes in renin or Angiotensin II do not directly cause cough. Histamine (Option D) mediates allergic coughs but is not linked to ACE inhibitor use. Clinically, this cough is non-productive and usually resolves within weeks of discontinuing the drug. The standard management is to switch the patient to an Angiotensin Receptor Blocker (ARB), which does not affect bradykinin metabolism. Therefore, Option C is the definitive pharmacological cause
questions.learning: The development of a persistent dry cough after starting a new medication for high blood pressure is a classic side effect of ACE inhibitors (like Enalapril or Lisinopril).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During intrauterine development, the talus, a tarsal bone of the foot, begins ossification at a specific gestational age. At what time during fetal life does ossification of the talus occur?
questions.explanation: The ossification of the tarsal bones follows a specific chronological sequence during intrauterine development. The talus typically begins to ossify at 7 months of intrauterine life. It is the second tarsal bone to ossify, following the calcaneus, which begins ossification at approximately 5 to 6 months of gestation. The cuboid bone is usually the third, ossifying shortly before birth, often at 9 months. Options A (3 months), C (9 months), and D (2 months) are incorrect for the talus. While the primary centers for long bones appear much earlier (around the 8th week or 2nd month), the tarsal bones are mostly cartilaginous at birth, except for the calcaneus, talus, and sometimes the cuboid. Identifying the presence of these ossification centers on fetal radiographs or ultrasounds can be a useful clinical indicator for assessing gestational age and skeletal maturity in a developing fetus
questions.learning: The ossification of the tarsal bones follows a specific chronological sequence during intrauterine development. The talus typically begins to ossify at 7 months of intrauterine life.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with coronary artery disease presents to you with chest pain and palpitations. The ECG is shown below. Which of the following can be used in the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intravenous amiodarone

The clinical scenario along with the ECG points to a diagnosis of ventricular tachycardia. Intravenous amiodarone (class III antiarrhythmic) can be used in the management of this condition.

The patient here complaining of chest pain, and palpitations and has ECG changes showing wide QRS complex tachycardia with absent p waves is likely to have acute ventricular tachycardia. Since the patient is stable and has an underlying coronary artery disease the drug of choice is intravenous amiodarone.

Ventricular tachycardias can be defined as three or more pre-ventricular contractions at a rate >100/minute.

ECG changes include wide QRS complexes, absence of P waves, and ventriculoatrial dissociation. It can be broadly classified as sustained VT or non-sustained VT. Nonsustained VT has QRS complexes lasting <30 seconds while sustained VT lasts for >30 seconds. In monomorphic VT, all QRS complexes look the same. Polymorphic VT has QRS complexes varying in shape or direction in the same lead.

Most monomorphic VT have an underlying cardiac disease. Symptoms of ventricular tachycardia include palpitations, syncope, and shortness of breath.

In a hemodynamically stable patient, amiodarone, procainamide, and lidocaine can be used to treat the condition. In the presence of heart disease, intravenous amiodarone is the drug of choice. In hemodynamically unstable patients, electrical cardioversion is done. Further management depends on the underlying heart condition and frequency of VT. Frequent episodes warrant the use of antiarrhythmics or catheter ablation.

Torsades de Pointes is a type of polymorphic VT occurring with QT prolongation. It can progress to ventricular fibrillation which is treated with defibrillation. Recurrent episodes can be managed with intravenous magnesium sulfate.

Other causes of wide QRS complexes include supraventricular tachycardias with bundle branch block and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

Other options:

Options A and D: Metoprolol is a selective β1-antagonist and a class II antiarrhythmic. It can be used in hypertension, angina, and heart failure. The intravenous form can be used for initial management in acute myocardial infarction.

Option B: Oral amiodarone can be used in the chronic treatment of atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, and ventricular fibrillation. It has shown a modest beneficial effect on mortality after acute myocardial infarction.
questions.learning: Intravenous amiodarone — The clinical scenario along with the ECG points to a diagnosis of ventricular tachycardia. Intravenous amiodarone (class III antiarrhythmic) can be used in the management of this condition.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 24-year-old presents with a scrotal swelling as shown in the image. The swelling is brilliantly transilluminant and the testes cannot be palpated separately. A CT scan was done which showed fluid collection in tunica vaginalis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hydrocele

In the above clinical scenario, there is a unilateral scrotal swelling where the testes cannot be palpated separately, and is transilluminant points towards a diagnosis of hydrocele.

Hydrocoele is an accumulation of fluid within the tunica vaginalis. Hydrocele can be congenital or acquired. Congenital hydrocele is seen in children due to patent processes vaginalis. Acquired hydrocele can be secondary to inflammation or infection of the epididymis or testes. It is translucent on transillumination test and testes will not be separately palpable due to tense fluid collection. As it arises in the scrotum, it is possible to get above the swelling. Cough impulse is absent.

USG will show anechoic (due to fluid) reflection.

CT scan shows fluid collection within the scrotal sac.

Treatment involves Jaboulay's operation, in which the eversion of the sac upon itself is done to prevent refilling of the hydrocoele sac. The other method of treating the hydrocele is plicating the redundant tunica which can be done when the sac wall is thin. This is known as the Lord's operation.

Other options:
Option A:  Hernia is a reducible swelling in which the examiner cannot get above the swelling and testes are palpable.

Option B: Varicocele is a dilatation of the pampiniform plexus which feels like a dragging sensation to the patient. A scrotal swelling is not a usual presentation.

Option C: Seminoma is the most common germ cell tumour of the testes. They are hard on palpation. The CT scan will show homogenous hyperdensity and not fluid collection.
questions.learning: Hydrocele — In the above clinical scenario, there is a unilateral scrotal swelling where the testes cannot be palpated separately, and is transilluminant points towards a diagnosis of hydrocele.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a radiological finding in a patient with left heart failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Focal oligemia

Focal oligemia is not a radiological feature of left heart failure. It is seen in pulmonary embolism and is also called Westermark’s sign.

It is defined by a hyperlucent area with decreased vascularity due to oligemia of the involved part of the lung. It is caused by a cutoff of circulation due to an embolus, leading to the loss of visibility of a patch of pulmonary vasculature on an X- ray.

Radiological signs of left heart failure include :

• Cardiomegaly - enlargement of the cardiac silhouette (increased cardiothoracic ratio)
• Upper lobe pulmonary venous congestion (cephalisation of vessels)
• Interstitial edema.
• Kerley B lines - horizontal lines in the periphery of the lower posterior lung fields as shown below.

Other radiological signs of Pulmonary embolism :

• Hampton’s hump - a peripheral wedged-shaped density usually located at the pleural base
• Palla’s sign - an enlarged right descending pulmonary artery
questions.learning: Focal oligemia Focal oligemia is not a radiological feature of left heart failure. It is seen in pulmonary embolism and is also called Westermark’s sign.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with a history of bronchospasm is found to have a tumor in the ileum along with elevated urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5- HIAA) levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Carcinoid syndrome is a paraneoplastic condition caused by neuroendocrine tumors (carcinoid tumors), most commonly found in the ileum. These tumors secrete excessive serotonin into the systemic circulation, bypassing liver metabolism when they metastasize. The elevated serotonin levels lead to clinical manifestations such as bronchospasms (wheezing), diarrhea, and cutaneous flushing. Serotonin is subsequently metabolized and excreted in the urine as 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), making elevated 5-HIAA the hallmark diagnostic marker for this syndrome. Neuroblastoma (Option B) is a pediatric tumor that secretes catecholamines. Chromaffinoma (Option C), or pheochromocytoma, also secretes catecholamines and presents with hypertension. Leiomyoma (Option D) is a benign smooth muscle tumor that does not have neuroendocrine activity. Therefore, the combination of an ileal tumor, respiratory symptoms, and excessive urinary 5-HIAA confirms the diagnosis of carcinoid syndrome
questions.learning: Carcinoid syndrome is a paraneoplastic condition caused by neuroendocrine tumors (carcinoid tumors), most commonly found in the ileum. These tumors secrete excessive serotonin into the systemic circulation, bypassing liver metabolism when they metastasize.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Long-standing pelvic inflammation may lead to which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pyometra

Long-standing pelvic inflammation may lead to pyometra. This refers to the collection of pus in the uterine cavity.

The initial infection involves the cervix uteri and urethra which may extend to Bartholin glands, skene glands, endometrium, and fallopian tubes. Unilateral pain and swelling over the labia may be caused by the inflammation of the Bartholin glands.

Depending on the extent of tissue involved, PID can be classified into five stages

• Stage I - Acute salpingitis without peritonitis - No adhesions
• Stage II - Acute salpingitis with peritonitis - purulent discharge
• Stage III - Acute salpingitis with superimposed tubal occlusion or tubo ovarian complex
• Stage IV - Ruptured tubo-ovarian abscess
• Stage V - Tubercular salpingitis

Long-standing pelvic inflammation may also lead to:

• Dyspareunia
• Infertility
• Ectopic pregnancy
• Formation of adhesions like hydrosalpinx, pyosalpinx, tubo-ovarian abscess
• Chronic pelvic pain

Note: Chronic pelvic inflammation leads to dense adhesions between the uterus and the appendages. Thus, it becomes difficult to define the uterus from the pelvic masses. They form a hard mass which is called the frozen pelvis.

The most common cause of the spread of PID: Ascending infection along with sperms
The only PID that does not spread with the sexual route is genital TB. It has a hematogenous spread.
The most common PID in virgin females is genital TB.
Investigation of choice in PID: Abdominal USG
The surest sign of salpingitis is pus extruding from the fimbrial end of the tube.
questions.learning: Pyometra Long-standing pelvic inflammation may lead to pyometra. This refers to the collection of pus in the uterine cavity.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient presented with complaints of hematuria and recurrent urinary tract infection. You notice the following finding in his CECT. What is the likely condition indicated by the arrow in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Horse shoe kidney

The given image shows a horseshoe kidney. It is prone to obstruction, reflux, and stone formation.

Horseshoe kidney is the most common congenital anomaly of the kidneys. Horseshoe kidneys are a type of renal fusion anomaly. They are formed when the lower poles of the two kidneys fuse during organogenesis to form an isthmus. They are typically low-lying as the inferior mesenteric artery interferes with its ascent due to its size and the presence of an isthmus.

It presents as a fixed, nonmobile, firm mass in the midline at the level of the 4th lumbar vertebra and is resonant on percussion. It is associated with an increased risk of infection, stone formation, hydronephrosis, and tuberculosis.

It has a 2:1 male preponderance. Individuals with horseshoe kidneys are prone to reflux, obstruction, and stone formation.

Other options:

Option A: The image of polycystic kidney disease on CT abdomen is shown below: Multiple bilateral cysts are seen.

Option C: Hydronephrosis is aseptic dilatation of the pelvicalyceal system due to partial or intermittent obstruction to urinary outflow.

Option D: Pancake kidney (also known as discoid kidney, disc kidney, lump kidney, fused pelvic kidney, or cake kidney) is a rare renal fusion anomaly where both the upper and lower poles of the kidney are fused giving it an appearance of a pancake. questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with difficulty initiating urination and urinary retention. Ultrasound shows a post-void residual volume of 130 mL. Which medication is commonly used to manage this condition?
questions.explanation: This 60-year-old male presents with classic Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms (LUTS) and a high post-void residual urine volume, which are diagnostic of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH). 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, such as finasteride and dutasteride, are commonly used for long-term management of BPH. These drugs inhibit the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), the androgen primarily responsible for prostatic growth. Reduction in DHT levels leads to gradual shrinkage of the prostate, thereby decreasing mechanical obstruction and improving urinary flow over time. Alpha-1 blockers (e.g., tamsulosin) are also frequently used, especially for rapid symptomatic relief, as they relax smooth muscle in the prostate and bladder neck but do not reduce prostate size. Calcium channel blockers (Option A), ACE inhibitors (Option C), and aldosterone antagonists (Option D) are antihypertensive agents and have no therapeutic role in BPH. Patients with a significantly increased post-void residual volume (>100 mL) are at risk of recurrent urinary tract infections, bladder stones, and renal impairment. Appropriate pharmacologic therapy can delay or prevent surgical interventions such as TURP. Counseling regarding adverse effects, including sexual dysfunction, is essential during treatment
questions.learning: This 60-year-old male presents with classic Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms (LUTS) and a high post-void residual urine volume, which are diagnostic of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic presents with agitation, global confusion, disorientation, hallucinations, fever, hypertension, diaphoresis, and autonomic hyperactivity after 48 hours of alcohol cessation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient's clinical presentation of agitation, global confusion, and autonomic hyperactivity (fever, hypertension, diaphoresis) starting 48 hours after the cessation of alcohol is the hallmark of Delirium Tremens (DT). DT is the most severe manifestation of alcohol withdrawal and is a medical emergency. Wernicke Encephalopathy (Option B) presents with the triad of confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia due to thiamine deficiency. Korsakoff Psychosis (Option C) is a chronic memory disorder following Wernicke's, characterized by confabulation. Magnan Phenomena (Option D), or formication, is a sensory hallucination of crawling insects that can occur within the context of DT but is not the diagnosis itself. DT requires aggressive treatment with benzodiazepines and intravenous fluids to prevent cardiovascular collapse and death. Its high mortality rate necessitates immediate hospitalization in an intensive care setting for close monitoring of vital signs and neurological status
questions.learning: The patient's clinical presentation of agitation, global confusion, and autonomic hyperactivity (fever, hypertension, diaphoresis) starting 48 hours after the cessation of alcohol is the hallmark of Delirium Tremens (DT).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A microbiology resident is revising heterophile antibody-based agglutination tests used in infectious diseases. Which of the following tests is NOT based on the detection of heterophile antibodies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rose–Waaler test

Heterophile agglutination tests detect cross-reacting antibodies produced against one antigen that agglutinate unrelated antigens because of shared epitopes.

The Rose–Waaler test is not a heterophile test. It is an autoantibody test used for the detection of Rheumatoid Factor (RF).

In this test:

• Sheep RBCs are coated with rabbit anti-sheep erythrocyte antibodies.
• Rheumatoid factor (IgM against the Fc portion of IgG) causes agglutination.

Thus, it detects an autoantibody, not a heterophile antibody.

Why the other options are heterophile tests?

• A. Paul–Bunnell test ✅: Detects heterophile antibodies produced in infectious mononucleosis (EBV) that agglutinate sheep or horse erythrocytes.
• B. Weil–Felix test ✅: Detects antibodies in rickettsial infections that cross-react with Proteus OX strains (OX2, OX19, OXK).
• D. Cold agglutination test ✅: Detects cold-reacting IgM antibodies produced in Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection that agglutinate human red blood cells at low temperatures.
questions.learning: Rose–Waaler test Heterophile agglutination tests detect cross-reacting antibodies produced against one antigen that agglutinate unrelated antigens because of shared epitopes.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Calculate the respiratory quotient (RQ) in a patient with 50kg body weight, if the CO2 exhaled is 200ml/min and O2 consumed is 250 ml/min.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 0.8

The respiratory quotient is 0.8.

The respiratory quotient is the ratio of carbon dioxide production to oxygen utilization.

In the given question, the CO2 production is 200mL/min, while the O2 consumption is 250mL/min.

Therefore,

Respiratory quotient = 200/250 = 0.8

The respiratory quotient (RQ) is used for determining the metabolic utilization of various foods.

• When carbohydrates are metabolized with one molecule of oxygen, one carbon dioxide molecule is released. Therefore, the RQ of carbohydrates = 1.
• When fats are oxidized, for every 100 molecules of oxygen consumed, 70 molecules of CO2 are released. Therefore, the RQ of fats is 0.70.
• Similarly, the respiratory quotient for proteins is 0.80.
questions.learning: 0.8 The respiratory quotient is 0.8. The respiratory quotient is the ratio of carbon dioxide production to oxygen utilization.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 35-year-old man wakes up after sleeping with his arm hanging over a chair and complains of pain and sensory symptoms. In this condition, which sequence correctly represents the order of susceptibility of different nerve fiber types to compression?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario describes "Saturday night palsy," a compression injury of the radial nerve. Nerve fibers have different sensitivities to external stressors based on their size and myelination. When subjected to pressure or mechanical compression, large myelinated fibers are the most susceptible, following the order: A > B > C. Fiber type A (specifically Alpha) is the most sensitive to pressure, while Type C is the least. In contrast, if the stressor were local anesthesia, the order would be C > B > A, as small unmyelinated fibers are blocked most easily. If the stressor were hypoxia, Type B fibers would be the most susceptible. Because this patient experienced mechanical compression by draping his arm over a chair, the largest and most metabolically demanding fibers (Type A) are affected first, making Option B the correct hierarchy
questions.learning: The clinical scenario describes "Saturday night palsy," a compression injury of the radial nerve. Nerve fibers have different sensitivities to external stressors based on their size and myelination.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-year-old unimmunized child presents to the emergency room with fever, cough, and difficulty breathing. Examination reveals a tonsillar pseudomembrane that bleeds when removed and a swollen neck giving a “bull-neck” appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a "bull-neck" appearance (due to massive cervical lymphadenopathy) and an adherent, grayish pseudomembrane on the tonsils that bleeds upon removal is pathognomonic for Diphtheria . The risk is significantly higher in an unimmunized child. Diphtheria is caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, which produces a powerful exotoxin. Infectious mononucleosis (Option A) and common tonsillitis (Option B) can cause membranes, but they are typically exudative and wipe off easily without bleeding. Oral candidiasis (Option D) presents with white, curd-like patches but not severe neck swelling and systemic toxicity. Therefore, the combination of specific physical signs and lack of immunization makes Diphtheria the definitive diagnosis. Management requires immediate administration of diphtheria antitoxin and antibiotics (erythromycin or penicillin) to prevent lethal complications like airway obstruction, myocarditis, and polyneuropathy. Public health reporting and contact tracing are also mandatory
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a "bull-neck" appearance (due to massive cervical lymphadenopathy) and an adherent, grayish pseudomembrane on the tonsils that bleeds upon removal is pathognomonic for Diphtheria .

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: High fat intake according to FDA is?
options: Diet should contain 400 kcal from carbohydrates
Diet should contain 800 kcal from fat
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diet should contain total 1000 kcal

High fat intake according to FDA is a diet that should contain a total of 1000 kcal.

High fat diets have low carbohydrates, <50 grams/day. This equates to <250 kcal/day in the form of carbohydrates, not 400 kcal (option A). The percentage of calories from fat is >50% (option D), which would equate to about 500-600 kcal from fats (option C). The diet should contain a total of 800 - 1000 kcal.

Ketogenic diets mainly incorporate low carbohydrates (<50 grams/day), low protein, and high fats. Gluconeogenesis from the glucogenic amino acids in the diet and fat oxidation are utilized to meet the metabolic demands of the body. Ketogenic diets are especially useful for the treatment of intractable epilepsy.
questions.learning: Diet should contain total 1000 kcal High fat intake according to FDA is a diet that should contain a total of 1000 kcal. High fat diets have low carbohydrates, 50% (option D), which would equate to about 500-600 kcal from fats (option C).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The POCSO Act is related to which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Child sexual abuse

The POCSO (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences) Act is related to child sexual abuse.

POCSO Act defines a child as any person below eighteen years of age. It defines different forms of sexual abuse, including penetrative and non-penetrative assault, as well as sexual harassment and pornography.

The Act deems a sexual assault to be "aggravated" under certain circumstances, such as when the abused child is mentally ill or when the abuse is committed by a person in a position of trust or authority vis-à-vis the child, like a family member, police officer, teacher, or doctor.

People who traffic children for sexual purposes are also punishable under the provisions relating to abetment in the Act. The Act prescribes stringent punishment graded as per the gravity of the offence, with a maximum term of rigorous imprisonment for life and a fine.
questions.learning: Child sexual abuse — The POCSO (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences) Act is related to child sexual abuse. POCSO Act defines a child as any person below eighteen years of age.
