questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 39-year-old G6P2L1A3 presents with a history of previous 2 LSCS with PAS. What will you NOT counsel her about?
options: Risk of bladder injury in case of PAS
Risk of bowel injury in case of PAS
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Risk of bowel injury in case of PAS

Placenta accreta spectrum is mainly associated with massive hemorrhage, bladder invasion, and need for peripartum hysterectomy. Bowel injury is not a typical or expected complication.

Placenta accreta spectrum includes abnormal adherence of placenta to the uterine wall due to defective decidua basalis. Types of PAS

| Type | Depth of invasion

| ---- | -----------------

| Placenta accreta | Attached to myometrium

| Placenta increta | Invades myometrium

| Placenta percreta | Penetrates through uterus

In severe cases, placenta may invade adjacent organs, most commonly the bladder.

| Complication | Reason

| ------------ | ------

| Massive hemorrhage | Placenta cannot separate

| Blood transfusion requirement | Severe bleeding

| Bladder injury | Placental invasion into bladder

| Peripartum hysterectomy | Life-saving procedure

Thus A, B, and D are valid counseling points.
questions.learning: Risk of bowel injury in case of PAS Placenta accreta spectrum is mainly associated with massive hemorrhage, bladder invasion, and need for peripartum hysterectomy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Kussmaul’s sign is a clinical feature of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Constrictive pericarditis

Kussmaul’s sign is a paradoxical rise (or failure to fall) in jugular venous pressure (JVP) during inspiration due to impaired right ventricular filling. It is a classic finding in constrictive pericarditis, where the rigid pericardium restricts ventricular expansion.

Why not the other options?

• B. Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy: Characterized by a systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva; Kussmaul’s sign is not a feature.
• C. Anteroseptal myocardial infarction: May cause LV failure or arrhythmias but does not typically produce Kussmaul’s sign.
• D. Dilated cardiomyopathy: Causes elevated JVP in heart failure, but Kussmaul’s sign is not characteristic.
questions.learning: Constrictive pericarditis Kussmaul’s sign is a paradoxical rise (or failure to fall) in jugular venous pressure (JVP) during inspiration due to impaired right ventricular filling.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the following line shown in the below picture:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ohngren line

The given image shows Ohngren's line. It is an imaginary line passing through the medial canthus of the eye and the angle of the mandible. It is used for the classification of maxillary carcinoma.

Growth situated above the plane (supra structure) tends to be more aggressive and poorly differentiated and has a poor prognosis. Growth situated below the plane (infrastructure) is more amenable to treatment and has a better prognosis.

Other options:

Option A: Proper alignment of the face is determined by the Frankfort plane, a horizontal line bisecting the inferior border of the infraorbital rim and the superior border of the external auditory canal.

Option B: Donaldson's line passes through the horizontal semicircular canal and bisects the posterior canal. It is the landmark for the endolymphatic sac which lies anterior and inferior to it.

ELS: Endolymphatic sac, HSCC: Horizontal semicircular canal, PSCC: Posterior semicircular canal, PF dura: Posterior fossa dura

Option C: Ledermann’s classification uses two horizontal lines of Sebileau, one passes through the floor of the orbit and another passes through the floor of the maxillary antra dividing the face into supra structure (ethmoid, sphenoid, frontal sinuses, and the olfactory area of nose), mesostructure (maxillary sinus and respiratory part of nose) and infrastructure (alveolar process). It is used to classify maxillary carcinoma.
questions.learning: Ohngren line — The given image shows Ohngren's line. It is an imaginary line passing through the medial canthus of the eye and the angle of the mandible.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In an elderly patient who has undergone complete surgical excision of a glioblastoma, what should be the next step in management?
questions.explanation: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is a highly aggressive brain tumor, and postoperative management depends on patient factors such as age and performance status. In elderly patients, especially those who may not tolerate aggressive therapy, the preferred next step after surgical excision is often radiotherapy alone. This is because combined chemoradiation (Stupp protocol) can be associated with increased toxicity and may not be well tolerated in older individuals. Radiotherapy helps to: 1. Control residual microscopic disease 2. Delay tumor progression 3. Improve symptoms and survival Thus, in elderly patients or those with poor functional status, radiotherapy alone is considered appropriate and safer. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Bevacizumab → Used in recurrent GBM (B) No further treatment → Incorrect; GBM always requires adjuvant therapy (C) Chemoradiation → Standard in younger/fit patients, not always elderly
questions.learning: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is a highly aggressive brain tumor, and postoperative management depends on patient factors such as age and performance status.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 72-year-old former pilot presents with rapidly progressive dementia accompanied by myoclonus, ataxia, and visual disturbances. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The MRI shows bilateral hyperintensities in the pulvinar/thalamic region — the classic "Pulvinar sign" or "Hockey stick sign" pathognomonic of Variant CJD (vCJD). Combined with rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, ataxia, and visual disturbances in a former pilot with possible prion exposure, this confirms vCJD. Key Features: 1. Pulvinar sign on DWI/FLAIR — bilateral thalamic hyperintensities 2. Rapidly progressive dementia 3. Myoclonus, ataxia, visual disturbances 4. Age 72 with occupational exposure history Why other options are wrong: (A) Alzheimer's disease is incorrect because Alzheimer's shows slow progressive dementia over years with hippocampal/cortical atrophy on MRI — no pulvinar hyperintensities or myoclonus. (B) Vascular dementia is incorrect because vascular dementia shows multiple cortical/subcortical infarcts on MRI with stepwise progression — not the bilateral symmetric thalamic hyperintensities seen here. (C) Sporadic CJD is incorrect because sporadic CJD shows cortical ribboning and basal ganglia hyperintensities on DWI — pulvinar sign is specifically associated with variant CJD, not sporadic CJD
questions.learning: The MRI shows bilateral hyperintensities in the pulvinar/thalamic region — the classic "Pulvinar sign" or "Hockey stick sign" pathognomonic of Variant CJD (vCJD).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the name of the online portal used for delivering mental healthcare services via telephone and other digital platforms for mental disorders such as schizophrenia, under the National Mental Health Programme?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tele-manas

Tele-MANAS is the national digital mental health platform launched under the National Mental Health Programme to provide telephonic and online mental health services.

It offers 24×7 toll-free counseling, referral, and follow-up care for conditions including schizophrenia, depression, anxiety, and substance use disorders.

| Feature | Details

| ------- | -------

| Services | Telephonic counselling and psychiatric support

| Coverage | Available across India

| Target conditions | Depression, anxiety, schizophrenia, substance abuse

| Access | Toll-free helpline

Other portals like NIKSHAY (TB), U-WIN (immunization), and Quinitin are unrelated to mental health services.

| Option | Program

| ------ | -------

| A. NIKSHAY | Portal for tuberculosis patient management

| B. Tele-MANAS | ✔ Tele mental health services

| C. Quinitin | Not a recognized national health portal

| D. U-WIN | Digital platform for immunization tracking
questions.learning: Tele-manas Tele-MANAS is the national digital mental health platform launched under the National Mental Health Programme to provide telephonic and online mental health services.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 7-year-old child from a low socioeconomic background presents with cerebrospinal fluid findings of lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose (30 mg%), and markedly elevated protein levels (300 mg%). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings of high protein, low glucose, and a predominant lymphocytic pleocytosis are classically seen in Tubercular Meningitis (TBM). This CSF profile reflects the chronic inflammatory response caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis in the meninges. Differential diagnosis reasoning: 1. Viral meningitis usually shows normal or mildly reduced glucose levels with only a modest rise in protein. 2. Acute bacterial meningitis characteristically presents with neutrophilic predominance and markedly reduced glucose levels. 3. Partially treated bacterial meningitis may show lymphocytic predominance, but the subacute to chronic course over two months strongly supports TBM rather than bacterial infection. Additionally, the patient’s low socioeconomic background increases the epidemiological likelihood of tuberculosis, especially in endemic regions
questions.learning: The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings of high protein, low glucose, and a predominant lymphocytic pleocytosis are classically seen in Tubercular Meningitis (TBM).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following developmental milestones is attained first in infants?
questions.explanation: Fine motor development in infants follows a predictable sequence, generally moving from the ulnar (pinky) side of the hand to the radial (thumb) side. The ulnar palmar grasp, where the infant uses the pinky and ring fingers to press an object against the palm, is the earliest grasp attained, typically around 4–5 months of age. This is followed by the radial palmar grasp (Option C) at approximately 6–7 months, where the thumb and radial fingers are used. The immature pincer grasp (Option A), which involves the pads of the thumb and forefinger, develops around 9 months. Finally, the mature pincer grasp (Option B), using the tips of the thumb and index finger, is attained at about 10–12 months. Understanding these milestones is essential for developmental screening; a delay in this progression may indicate neurological or musculoskeletal issues. Thus, the ulnar palmar grasp represents the foundational step in the refinement of hand dexterity and object manipulation
questions.learning: Fine motor development in infants follows a predictable sequence, generally moving from the ulnar (pinky) side of the hand to the radial (thumb) side.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 24-year old male patient presents with anemia. His father and paternal aunt had a similar illness that was treated successfully by splenectomy. His peripheral blood smear is similar to that shown in the illustration below. Which of the following additional abnormalities is expected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Howell-Jolly bodies

The above image showing spherocytes present on the peripheral blood smear and, along with the history, strongly suggest a diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis (HS). The presence of Howell-Jolly bodies is an additional abnormality which can be expected here.

It is an autosomal dominant inheritance disorder. It is due to defective ankyrin, band 3, spectrin, or band 4.2 proteins causing a defect in the red cell membrane. This causes red cells to shed membrane vesicles and transform into spherocytes. The non-deformable spherocytes get trapped in the splenic cords and are phagocytosed by macrophages.

* Most common mode of inheritance of HS: Autosomal dominant

* Most common gene mutation in autosomal dominant HS: Ankyrin > Band 3

Clinical presentation:

The patients usually present with anemia, gall stones, splenomegaly, and jaundice but the age of presentation varies with the severity of the disease. They might also have a family history.

Aplastic crisis might occur where red cell production comes to a halt due to parvovirus infection. This lasts for 1 to 2 weeks which is usually the time required for the immune system to clear the virus. Blood transfusions may be needed during this period.

Morphology :

* The most common finding is spherocytosis, which presents as small, dark-staining (hyperchromic) red cells without the central zone of pallor but this is not specific to HS.

* Features seen in HS are :

* Reticulocytosis- increased reticulocyte count

* Howell-Jolly bodies- dense basophilic nuclear remnants in the RBCs.

* Marrow erythroid hyperplasia

* Hemosiderosis

* Splenomegaly as a result of congested Billroth cords and increased phagocytes.

Diagnosis:

Based on family history, peripheral smear findings, and laboratory investigations an adequate diagnosis is made. Increased osmotic fragility is seen in majority of the cases. They also show an increased MCHC (mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration) due to cellular dehydration.

Note- Heinz bodies: Undeterred oxidation of hemoglobin in the RBCs leads to the formation of denatured precipitates known as Heinz bodies. These bodies damage the RBC membrane. When these RBCs pass through the splenic cords, macrophages pluck out these precipitates, giving them the characteristic appearance of bite cells. They are seen in cases of chemical poisoning, drug toxicity, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, or the presence of unstable hemoglobin (e.g. hemoglobin Köln)

Below image shows Heinz bodies and bite cells.
questions.learning: Howell-Jolly bodies — The above image showing spherocytes present on the peripheral blood smear and, along with the history, strongly suggest a diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis (HS).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following hormone-action combinations are correct? a. Epinephrine → Glycolysis b. Thyroxine → Decrease blood glucose c. Glucagon → Gluconeogenesis d. Insulin → Increased protein synthesis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. a, c and d

Hormones regulate metabolism by coordinating glucose homeostasis, protein metabolism, and energy production.

Correct hormone–action pairs:

• a. Epinephrine → Glycolysis ✓ (stimulates glycogenolysis and glycolysis in skeletal muscle to provide rapid energy)
• c. Glucagon → Gluconeogenesis ✓ (stimulates hepatic gluconeogenesis during fasting)
• d. Insulin → Increased protein synthesis ✓ (promotes amino acid uptake and protein synthesis while inhibiting proteolysis)

Why not b?

• Thyroxine → Decrease blood glucose ✗

• Thyroxine does not lower blood glucose.
• It increases the basal metabolic rate and enhances intestinal glucose absorption, hepatic gluconeogenesis, and glycogenolysis, often causing a mild increase in blood glucose and insulin requirement.
questions.learning: a, c and d Hormones regulate metabolism by coordinating glucose homeostasis, protein metabolism, and energy production. Epinephrine → Glycolysis ✓ (stimulates glycogenolysis and glycolysis in skeletal muscle to provide rapid energy) • c.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The image shows methylene blue dye being injected in the peritumoral region. What is this procedure useful for?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sentinel lymph node biopsy

The utility of injection of methylene blue in the region around the tumor is done for sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLN) in patients without clinically positive lymph nodes.

SLN biopsy rationale:

• Afferent lymphatics from a primary tumor first drain into the sentinel node before draining into the other nodes. So, if a sentinel lymph node is positive for metastsis, it is possible that the other axillary nodes are also involved. Hence, axillary dissection would be necessary.
• If the sentinel node is tumor-free, then regional nodal metastasis is unlikely.

The nodes can be identified using fluorescein dye, methylene blue, or radioactive sulfur colloid-labeled albumin. The dye can be injected into the peritumoral tissue, subareolar, periareolar, or intradermal plane.

Contraindicated in patients with inflammatory breast cancer, stage T4 disease, a history of previous breast cancer or chest wall surgery, breast scarring, and radiotherapy.
questions.learning: Sentinel lymph node biopsy — The utility of injection of methylene blue in the region around the tumor is done for sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLN) in patients without clinically positive lymph nodes.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with a crush injury following a road traffic accident develops crepitus, and the amputation site shows a reddish-brown wound within three days. What is the most likely condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a crush injury following a road traffic accident (RTA), characterized by the presence of crepitus (air in tissues) and a reddish-brown discharge within a short three-day window, is pathognomonic for Gas gangrene. This life-threatening infection is primarily caused by Clostridium perfringens, an anaerobic, spore-forming bacterium that thrives in devitalized, ischemic tissue. Impetigo (Option B) is a superficial skin infection. Tetanus (Option C) presents with neuromuscular symptoms like lockjaw rather than tissue necrosis and crepitus. Cellulitis (Option D) involves spreading inflammation of the dermis but lacks the rapid gas production and severe toxemia associated with clostridial myonecrosis. Management is a surgical emergency requiring aggressive debridement, high-dose intravenous antibiotics (penicillin and clindamycin), and sometimes hyperbaric oxygen therapy. Failure to recognize the early signs of gas gangrene, such as a "mousy" odor and rapid skin discoloration, can result in high mortality or the need for extensive limb amputation to control the spread of the infection
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a crush injury following a road traffic accident (RTA), characterized by the presence of crepitus (air in tissues) and a reddish-brown discharge within a short three-day window, is pathognomonic for Gas gangrene.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient presented with severe abdominal pain. On examination, the patient's BP is 80/40 mm hg, and the following finding is noted. CT abdomen is normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute Pancreatitis

The image is that of a patient with flank ecchymosis, this is known as the Grey Turner sign and is seen in patients with acute pancreatitis.

Acute pancreatitis is a rapidly progressing inflammatory condition of the pancreas associated with significant mortality and morbidity.

The major risk factors for developing this condition are the presence of gallstones and alcohol abuse.

Patients present with moderate to severe epigastric pain associated with vomiting and loss of appetite. On examination, there is guarding and abdominal tenderness. Rarely, patients may present with Grey Turner and Cullen signs. Grey Turner sign is characterized by flank ecchymosis whereas in Cullen sign patients present with periumbilical ecchymosis.
questions.learning: Acute Pancreatitis — The image is that of a patient with flank ecchymosis, this is known as the Grey Turner sign and is seen in patients with acute pancreatitis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 6-year-old child is brought to the paediatric clinic by his parents, with complaints of difficulty breathing through the nose, frequent mouth breathing, and speech difficulties. The child has visible crowding of the upper front teeth and frequently complains of ear discomfort. On examination, the child has nasal obstruction and enlarged adenoids, as seen on nasopharyngoscopy. Otoscopic examination reveals bilateral dull tympanic membranes, as well as mild conductive hearing loss. Which type of tympanogram is most likely to appear in this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type B Tympanogram

The given clinical scenario of a child with mouth breathing, malocclusion of teeth, nasal obstruction and enlarged adenoids, along with bilateral dull tympanic membranes, points towards the diagnosis of serous otitis media secondary to adenoid hypertrophy, which is characterised by a type B curve on a tympanogram.

Adenoid hypertrophy causes typical facies characterised by an elongated face with a dull expression, an open mouth, a hitched-up upper lip, prominent upper teeth causing crowding (malocclusion of teeth), a high arched hard palate (due to loss of the tongue's molding action on the palate), and a pinched-in nose due to disuse atrophy of the alae nasi.

Enlarged adenoids in children can present as nasal obstruction, recurrent acute otitis media, and serous otitis media. Chronic nasal obstruction resulting in mouth breathing leads to this characteristic facial appearance in children. Patients can also present with a speech disorder, most probably rhinolalia clausa (hyponasality) due to adenoid hypertrophy.

Serous otitis media, also known as secretory otitis media, mucoid otitis media, or glue ear, is characterised by the accumulation of nonpurulent, serous effusion in the middle ear cleft. Glue ear can occur either due to eustachian tube dysfunction (adenoid hyperplasia, chronic sinusitis, tonsillitis or rhinitis, cleft palate, or tumours of nasopharynx) or due to increased secretory activity of the middle ear mucosa (allergy, unresolved otitis media, or viral infections).

Glue ear is commonly seen in children aged 5-8 years and is associated with insidious onset of hearing loss (not exceeding 40 dB), mild earaches, and a history of upper respiratory tract infections. Delayed or defective speech may also result from hearing loss.

Otoscopy shows:

* Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex

* A thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus

* Fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen when the tympanic membrane is transparent.

The otoscopy image of serous otitis media is shown below:

A B-type tympanogram is expected in a case of serous otitis media. Here, compliance decreases. The fluid accumulation causes decreased mobility of the tympanic membrane, leading to a flat or dome-shaped curve. This results in a B-type tympanogram, as shown below:

Enlarged adenoids in children can present as nasal obstruction, rhinolalia clausa, recurrent acute otitis media, and serous otitis media. Adenoid facies, characterised by an elongated face, open mouth, teeth crowding, high-arched hard palate, and pinched-in nose, may also be present.

The tuning fork test reveals a conductive type of hearing loss, and audiometry reveals hearing loss in the range of 20–40 dB. The fluid accumulation in glue ear causes decreased mobility (compliance) of the tympanic membrane, leading to a flat or dome-shaped curve or type B curve on a tympanogram.

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

* Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, and antibiotics.

* Surgical management is done if the condition cannot be controlled with medications. It includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid with grommet insertion. Adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy may be required and are usually done at the time of myringotomy.

Other options:

Option A: Type A indicates a normal tympanogram.

Option C: Tympanometry displays an Ad type tympanogram, indicating high compliance near ambient pressure. It can be seen in ossicular discontinuity or a thin and lax tympanic membrane.

Option D: Tympanometry shows an As type of tympanogram in which there is reduced compliance at or near the ambient air pressure.

Pearl PF1978: Pure tone audiometry (PTA)

A pure tone is the sound of a single frequency. An audiometer is a device that generates pure tones and its frequency can be increased or decreased by 5Hz.

The threshold for air conduction (AC) of sound frequencies from 125-8000 Hz and the threshold for bone conduction (BC) of sound frequencies from 250-4000 Hz is measured and the result is plotted on an audiogram.

Normal thresholds:

* For AC: 15 dB

* For BC: 25 dB

Symbols used in pure tone audiometry:

Disease
Findings in PTA audiogram

Conductive hearing loss
AC abnormal, BC normal, air-bone gap present

Sensorineural hearing loss
Both AC and BC are abnormal and no air-Bone gap

Mixed hearing loss
Both AC and BC abnormal and air-bone gap present

Presbycusis, ototoxicity, noise-induced hearing loss (higher frequencies affected first)
Downsloping or descending audiogram

Early stages of Meniere's disease (lower frequencies affected first)
Upsloping or ascending audiogram

Congenital hearing loss and cochlear otosclerosis (mid-frequency hearing loss)
U-shaped or trough-shaped or cookie bite shaped audiogram

Early cases of noise-induced hearing loss

Acoustic dip - characteristic dip in both AC and BC at 4000 Hz

Otosclerosis
Carhart's notch- dip at 2000 Hz in BC curve

Pearl PF1696: Types of curves in tympanogram

Pearl PF2005: Myringotomy

Indications:

* Acute suppurative otitis media:

* Severe earache with the bulging tympanic membrane.

* Incomplete resolution with opaque drum and persistent conductive deafness.

* Complications of acute otitis media,e.g.facialparalysis, labyrinthitis or meningitis with the bulging tympanic membrane.

* Serous otitis media.

* Aero-otitis media (to drain fluid and “unlock” the eustachian tube).

* Atelectatic ear (grommet is often inserted for long-term aeration).

Contraindication: Suspected intratympanic glomus tumor.

Incisions:

* In acute suppurative otitis media, a circumferential incision is made in the posteroinferior quadrant of the tympanic membrane, midway between the handle of malleus and tympanic annulus, avoiding injury to the incudostapedial joint.

* In serous otitis media, a small radial incision is given in the anteroinferior quadrant and all the effusion is sucked out.

Complications:

* Injury to incudostapedial joint or stapes.

* Injury to jugular bulb with profuse bleeding, if jugular bulb is high and floor of the middle ear dehiscent.

* Middle ear infection.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text:
Match the following drugs with the targets of their actions.

A. Trastuzumab
1. BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase

B. Infliximab
2. mTOR

C. Sirolimus
3. TNF α

D. Imatinib
4. HER2/neu
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A-4, B-3 , C-2 , D-1

The correct pairs are as follows:

A. Trastuzumab
4. HER2/neu

B. Infliximab
3.  TNF α

C. Sirolimus
2. mTOR

D. Imatinib
1. BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase

Trastuzumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody against the external domain of HER2/neu. It is indicated as an adjuvant in the management of metastatic HER-2-positive breast cancer.

Infliximab binds with high affinity to TNF-α and prevents the cytokine from binding to its receptors. Infliximab is used for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis; it is used in combination with methotrexate in patients who do not respond to methotrexate alone. Infliximab is also used for the treatment of the symptoms of moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease.

Sirolimus is an antimetabolic and antiproliferative drug. It acts by forming a complex with an immunophilin called FKBP-12, which in turn inhibits the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR). mTOR is a protein kinase that blocks cell cycle progression at the G1 phase to S phase transition. It is used in the prophylaxis of organ transplant rejection.

Imatinib is a first-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitor. Imatinib attacks BCR-ABL translocation and is used in chronic myelocytic leukemia. It also inhibits c-kit and produces extended control of GI stromal tumors.
questions.learning: A-4, B-3 , C-2 , D-1 — The correct pairs are as follows: A. BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase Trastuzumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody against the external domain of HER2/neu.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: You are working as an internal medicine consultant at a private clinic. A patient with chronic renal disease requiring hemodialysis is admitted under you. You advise diet and fluid control and keep him under observation. However, the patient progresses to take ayurvedic supplements and sometimes skips your instructions without disclosing it. His conditions worsen and he develops difficulty in breathing. His attendant files a complaint in court alleging the negligence of the doctor. Which of the following acts as a defence for the doctor in court?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Contributory negligence

In the given case, since the patient did not adhere to the proper instructions of the doctor, it was partly or wholly his fault. This is termed contributory negligence. Proper documentation as to how ordinary care was not exercised on part of the patient can be useful in a court of law.

Contributory negligence occurs when a patient or his personal attendant shows unreasonable conduct or absence of ordinary care, which when combined with the negligence of the doctor, has contributed to the injury. In this case, the patient’s or attendant’s negligence should be the direct, proximate cause and without which the injury would not have occurred

Other options:

Option A: Vicarious liability is not a defence against professional negligence. Vicarious liability (liability for the actions of another): An employer is responsible not only for his own negligence but also for the negligence of his employees.

Option B: Res ipsa loquitur means 'the thing speaks for itself'. It is used as supportive evidence of negligence on part of the doctor eg: leaving behind a scalpel or scissor whilst operating leading to sepsis/peritonitis speaks for itself.

Option C: Therapeutic misadventure may serve as a defence against negligence. It basically refers to an adverse outcome that could not have been anticipated despite reasonable care. eg: a rare side effect of a drug or blood loss due to an anomalous artery despite exercising caution.

Pearl PF1453: Contributory negligence

Contributory negligence occurs when a patient or his personal attendant shows unreasonable conduct or absence of ordinary care, which when combined with the negligence of the doctor, has contributed to the injury. In this case, the patient’s or attendant’s negligence should be the direct, proximate cause and without which the injury would not have occurred.

So, contributory negligence occurs when both the doctor and patient are negligent. The direct or proximate cause of the injury should be the patient’s negligence, which means that if the patient was not negligent, the injury could have been prevented.

Contributory negligence usually occurs when the doctor is negligent and the patient:

* Fails to give an accurate medical history, and as a result, the doctor may misdiagnose or mistreat the patient.

* Fails to follow the doctor’s instructions

* Refuses to take the treatment

* Leaves the hospital against doctor’s advice

* Does not inform the doctor or seek further medical assistance if the symptoms persist or worsens.

Contributory negligence is a defence for doctor’s negligence in civil cases. However, from case to case, the liability of a doctor may vary from complete non-liability to substantial liability for the damages. Under the doctrine of comparative negligence, the court has the right to hold both parties liable for their negligent actions.

Limitations / Exceptions to contributory negligence:

A. The doctor will be held guilty in the following conditions:

1. The doctor failed to provide proper instructions to the patient

* Ex: Doctor applies a tight plaster cast (doctor is negligent) to the patient’s leg and did not tell the patient to inform if he develops any numbness (no proper instruction). The patient develops numbness and has not informed the doctor (patient is negligent). After few days patient developed a permanent injury.

2. Last clear chance doctrine: It is applicable when the doctor fails to take necessary action to prevent damage due to a negligent act of the patient, even after getting a clear chance to take such action.

* Ex: Doctor applies a tight plaster cast (doctor is negligent) to the patient’s leg and told the patient to inform if he develops any numbness (gave proper instruction). The patient developed numbness and has not informed the doctor (patient is negligent). Next day patient informed the doctor, but the doctor did not remove the cast and said he was busy (There was a clear last chance, but the doctor neglected again). After few days patient developed a permanent injury.

B. The doctor/person will not be held guilty in the following conditions:

1. Avoidable consequences rule: It occurs when an injury is caused due to doctor’s negligence, and the patient has done a negligent act, which further aggravated the injury caused by the doctor, and the patient could have avoided the consequence by not doing such act. In such cases, the doctor need not pay anything, and the patient will be held guilty.

* Ex: A patient had a lacerated wound. The doctor examined the patient and had not done any dressing or provided any antibiotics (the doctor is negligent). However, the doctor instructed the patient to avoid contamination and asked him to visit the clinic next week. When the patient went home, he applied cow dung on his wound every day thinking that the wound would heal faster and didn't visit the doctor after one week. The wound got infected and developed pus and aggravated the injury.

* Here, despite the doctor being negligent in the first instance, the patient is responsible for his injury as he performed an unnecessary, avoidable act, which aggravated the injury. The doctor need not pay anything.

2. Good Samaritan doctrine: A person who assists another person who is in serious danger cannot be charged with contributory negligence. unless such assistance is reckless or rash.

* Ex: A person was travelling on a road and saw a car accident, where the victim was unconscious and was stuck inside the car. He called the ambulance. The paramedical staff instructed him not to mobilize the victim until they arrived. Meanwhile, the car was caught in fire (serious danger), and the person tried to remove the victim carefully out of the car (assisted the victim and was not reckless). However, the victim already had a cervical bone fracture due to the accident, which got mobilized while he was being removed out of the car and as a result, suffered an injury to the spine that led to paralysis (victim’s injury was aggravated). In such a case, the good samaritan doctrine would apply and the person who tried to help, will not be charged under contributory negligence.
questions.learning: Contributory negligence — In the given case, since the patient did not adhere to the proper instructions of the doctor, it was partly or wholly his fault.

The routine auscultation of the heart is:

* Auscultate at the apex with the diaphragm.

* Turn the patient on to the left side and auscultate for any murmurs of MR(using diaphragm) or MS(using bell)

* Turn the patient to the supine position, recline at 45 degrees and auscultate at the tricuspid area for murmurs of TR, TS, VSD

* Auscultate at the pulmonic area (PS,PR, PDA)

* Auscultate at the aortic area (AS, HOCM)

* Sit the patient forward and auscultate again at the tricuspid area in held expiration(AR)

* Auscultate over the carotid arteries for any bruits or radiation of any murmurs.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The oocyte phase in post-ovulation is:
options: Primary oocyte arrested in prophase – I
Secondary oocyte completed in prophase – II
Primary oocyte arrested in prophase – II
Secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase – II
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase – II

After ovulation, the oocyte is a secondary oocyte that has completed meiosis I and entered meiosis II.

It remains arrested in metaphase II until fertilization occurs.

Primary oocyte arrest in prophase I occurs prenatally, not post-ovulation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In which of the following reflexes, gastric emptying is delayed when acidic content enters the duodenum?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Enterogastric

In the enterogastric reflex, gastric emptying is delayed when acidic content enters the duodenum.

When the food enters the duodenum, multiple reflexes are initiated from the duodenal wall which passes back to the stomach. These reflexes slow or stop the stomach emptying if the volume of the chyme in the duodenum becomes too much. These reflexes are called enterogastric reflexes.

This reflex can be triggered due to the following reasons:

• Presence of irritants and acids in duodenal chyme (most sensitive factor)
• Distension of duodenum due to the presence of an excessive volume of chyme
• Rapid entry of hypertonic or hypotonic fluids into the duodenum
• Presence of breakdown products of protein digestion and sometimes fat
questions.learning: Enterogastric — In the enterogastric reflex, gastric emptying is delayed when acidic content enters the duodenum. When the food enters the duodenum, multiple reflexes are initiated from the duodenal wall which passes back to the stomach.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the primary purpose of using gamma radiation in sterilization?
questions.explanation: Gamma radiation is a form of ionizing radiation (usually from a Cobalt-60 source) used for "cold sterilization". Its primary clinical purpose is the industrial sterilization of "pre-packed, disposable, heat-sensitive" medical items like plastic syringes, needles, catheters, and surgical sutures. It is highly effective because gamma rays have deep penetrative power and can kill microorganisms without raising the temperature of the items. Contaminated clothes and carcasses (Option B) are usually disposed of via incineration. Gloves and aprons (Option C) can be sterilized with radiation, but they are more commonly treated with ethylene oxide gas or autoclaving depending on the material. Bacterial vaccines and IV solutions (Option D) are sterilized by filtration or careful heat processing, as radiation could damage the biological/chemical integrity of the product. Gamma radiation ensures that single-use medical devices are completely sterile before they reach the hospital setting

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with untreated hyperthyroidism is scheduled for a total thyroidectomy. Pre-anesthetic check-up (PAC) was not done adequately. Which of the following complications is most likely to occur during surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Arrhythmia

A patient with untreated hyperthyroidism undergoing surgery(thyroidectomy) is at significant risk for a thyroid storm (also known as a thyrotoxic crisis), which usually presents with hypotension, cardiac arrhythmias, hyperpyrexia and other symptoms.

Thyroid storm is a rare but severe life-threatening complication of hyperthyroidism induced by the release of excessive thyroid hormones.

Causes:

* Abrupt cessation of antithyroid medications

* Infection

* When a thyrotoxic patient has been inadequately prepared for thyroidectomy.

* Thyroid or non-thyroid surgery

* Trauma in patients with untreated thyrotoxicosis

* Amiodarone administration

* Exposure to iodinated contrast agents

* Following RAI (radioactive iodine) therapy

Features:

* They present 12–24 hours after surgery with hyperpyrexia and severe dehydration

* Cardiovascular: Circulatory collapse, hypotension, palpitations, tachycardia, cardiac arrhythmias, cardiac failure

* GI symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice.

* Neurological symptoms: restlessness, irritability, delirium, tremor, convulsions, and coma

Treatment:

* Supportive measures – rehydration by proper fluid therapy, tepid sponging, cooling blankets

* Thionamides like Propylthiouracil (PTU), methimazole or carbimazole are used as they inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis. Propylthiouracil blocks the peripheral conversion of thyroxine (T4) into the more active triiodothyronine (T3) and serves as the preferred drug in thyroid storm. However, the risk for severe liver injury and acute liver failure associated with PTU therapy makes either carbimazole or methimazole the first choice thionamides in patients with deranged liver function tests.

* Lugol’s iodide is given one hour after intake of thionamides. They inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis by Wolff- Chaikoff effect. Large doses of iodide inhibit the organic binding of the iodide and hence decrease thyroid hormone synthesis.

* Propranolol is used to reduce tachycardia and other adrenergic manifestations. It also reduces the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.

* Glucocorticoids – reduce the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 and controls the shock.

* Digoxin, cardiac monitoring is crucial.

Pearl PF1414: Thyroid storm / Thyrotoxic crisis:

It is an emergency caused by an acute exacerbation of hyperthyroidism.

Precipitating factors:

* Abrupt cessation of antithyroid medications

* Infection

* When a thyrotoxic patient has been inadequately prepared for thyroidectomy.

* Thyroid or non-thyroid surgery

* Trauma in patients with untreated thyrotoxicosis

* Amiodarone administration or exposure to iodinated contrast agents

* Following RAI therapy.

Clinical features:

* Fever

* Central nervous system agitation or depression

* Cardiovascular and GI dysfunction, including hepatic failure

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rupture of biceps tendon

The image shows Popeye sign and it is seen in rupture of proximal tendon of biceps.  Proximal tendon of biceps refers to both long head and short head of biceps.

Popeye sign: On flexing the elbow there is an extremely prominent bulge of the muscle belly as its unrestrained fibers contract.

The proximal biceps tendon makes up 90-97% of all biceps tendon ruptures. In isolation, it has little effect on the upper limb function

The 4 most common areas of tendon rupture include:

* Quadriceps

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the histological slide shown below of the structure
questions.explanation: The given histological slide shows closely packed acinar cells with dark-stained nuclei and granular cytoplasm, characteristic of the exocrine pancreas. In addition, there are lighter-staining regions scattered within the tissue, one of which is indicated by the arrow. These pale areas represent the Islets of Langerhans, the endocrine component of the pancreas. This combination of dark exocrine acini and light endocrine islets is a hallmark feature of pancreatic tissue. The acini are responsible for secreting digestive enzymes, while the islets produce hormones such as insulin and glucagon. Why Other Options Are Wrong (A) Lymph node: Shows lymphoid follicles and germinal centers, not acini or islets. (B) Glomerulus: Found in the kidney, characterized by a tuft of capillaries within Bowman’s capsule. (C) Spleen: Shows red pulp and white pulp, not glandular acinar arrangement

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with a six-month history of recurrent, large-volume, watery diarrhea. She reports experiencing multiple episodes per day, often waking her at night. She has also noted significant weight loss and episodes of muscle weakness. Laboratory findings reveal hypokalemia. Imaging studies of the abdomen show a mass in the tail of the pancreas. Which pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. VIPoma

This patient with recurrent, large-volume, watery diarrhea with laboratory evidence of hypokalemia and a mass in the pancreatic tail is most likely afflicted by a VIPoma.

Vasoactive intestinal peptide-secreting tumours (VIPomas) are  pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours that secrete excessive amounts of vasoactive intestinal peptides (VIP) which are responsible for the secretory watery diarrhoea and other symptoms. The patient commonly presents with severe intermittent watery diarrhoea leading to dehydration, and weakness from fluid and electrolyte losses.

Electrolyte abnormalities in VIPoma include:

* Metabolic acidosis and hypokalemia- due to a large amount of GI loss and bicarbonate wasting

* Hypochlorhydria- due to the direct gastric acid inhibitory effect of VIP

* Hypomagnesemia- due to severe diarrhoea

* Hyperglycemia- due to the increased glycogenolytic activity of VIP

* Hypercalcemia- due to dehydration, coincidental MEN1 syndrome, or secretion by the tumor of a calcitrophic peptide

Vasoactive intestinal peptide-secreting tumor (VIPoma) is also referred to as Verner–Morrison syndrome/ WDHA syndrome:

WDHA stands for:

* WD - Watery Diarrhea

* H – Hypokalemia

* A – Achlorhydria

Metastases commonly occurs in the liver, lymph nodes, bones, and kidney.

Diagnosis can be made by the demonstration of an elevated plasma VIP level (upto 250 to 500 pg/ml) and a history of large-volume diarrhea (> 5L/day). A CT scan localizes most VIPomas. EUS is the most sensitive imaging method.

While suspecting a case of VIPoma it is essential to conduct a VIP assay so as to confirm the presence of other tumors of neural crest origin such as neuroblastoma or pheochromocytoma.

The medical management of VIPoma:

*

Initial medical management is symptomatic with correction of fluids and electrolyte imbalance.

*

Somatostatin analogs like octreotide and lanreotide inhibit secretion of VIP and are used for symptomatic control.

*

Glucocorticoids are used in patients refractory to somatostatin analogs.

*

Interferon-alpha has also been used in patients in patients not responding to the above medications.

The surgical management of VIPoma:

* Complete resection is the treatment of choice for primary tumors and is usually a distal pancreatectomy. If the tumor cannot be excised completely, surgical debulkingmay be done

* Radiofrequency ablation and cryoablation

* Hepatic artery embolization is a palliative treatment measure in patients with unresectable hepatic metastases.

Pearl PF0939: Pancreatic Endocrine Neoplasms

Endocrine neoplasm

Syndrome

Glucagonoma

Mild diabetes mellitus, a characteristic skin rash (necrolytic migratory erythema), and anemia

Insulinoma

Gastrinoma

Peptic ulceration often unresponsive to therapy and in unusual locations such as the jejunum

Somatostatinoma

Diabetes mellitus, cholelithiasis, steatorrhea, and hypochlorhydria

VIPoma

Watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria, or WDHA syndrome

Pancreatic polypeptide-secreting endocrine tumors

Present as mass lesions as even high plasma levels of this hormone fail to cause symptoms

* Islet hyperplasia (previously known as nesidioblastosis) is seen in maternal diabetes, Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome , and rare mutations in the β-cell K+-channel protein or sulfonylurea receptor.

* In maternal diabetes, the fetal islets respond to hyperglycemia by increasing their size and number. In the postnatal period, these hyperactive islets may be responsible for serious episodes of hypoglycemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the Opening Snap (OS) in a patient of mitral stenosis?
options: OS is best heard with the bell of stethoscope
Intensity of OS becomes louder when the valve is calcified
OS moves closer to the second sound (S2) as the stenosis becomes more severe
OS is best heard at the second left intercostal space
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. OS moves closer to the second sound (S2) as the stenosis becomes more severe

The opening snap (OS) is a high-pitched early diastolic sound produced by the sudden tensing of a stenotic but still mobile mitral valve as it opens after the aortic component of the second heart sound (A2). It is a characteristic auscultatory finding in rheumatic mitral stenosis.

Why is C correct?

• Severe mitral stenosis → Higher left atrial pressure → Earlier mitral valve opening → Shorter A2–OS interval.
• Therefore, the opening snap moves closer to S2 as stenosis becomes more severe.

Why not the other options?

• A. OS is best heard with the bell of stethoscope: Incorrect. The opening snap is a high-pitched sound and is best heard with the diaphragm.
• B. Intensity of OS becomes louder when the valve is calcified: Incorrect. A heavily calcified and immobile valve produces a soft or absent opening snap.
• D. OS is best heard at the second left intercostal space: Incorrect. It is best heard just medial to the apex or at the left lower sternal border, not at the pulmonary area.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman is brought to the psychiatric outpatient department by a friend. She believes her boss is in love with her and is stalking her, but her friend denies these claims. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s belief that her boss is in love with her, despite a lack of evidence or direct interaction, is the defining symptom of Erotomania (also known as Clerambault syndrome) (Option D). This is a subtype of delusional disorder where the individual believes that another person, usually of higher social or professional status, is deeply in love with them. Megalomania (Option A) involves delusions of grandeur or extreme power. Delusion of reference (Option B) is the belief that neutral events or remarks have a special personal meaning. Delusion of control (Option C) is the belief that one's thoughts or movements are being directed by an external force. Because the patient’s fixed, false belief is specifically centered on a perceived romantic relationship with a person of higher status, erotomania is the definitive psychiatric diagnosis. Management typically involves antipsychotic medications and psychosocial interventions
questions.learning: The patient’s belief that her boss is in love with her, despite a lack of evidence or direct interaction, is the defining symptom of Erotomania (also known as Clerambault syndrome) (Option D).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following fluoroquinolone is not given in liver disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pefloxacin

Pefloxacin is mainly metabolized in the liver and hence avoided in patients with liver disease.

Quinolones with primarily hepatic metabolism include moxifloxacin, pefloxacin, and trovafloxacin (withdrawn from the market due to hepatotoxicity).

Quinolones primarily excreted by the kidneys include ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, norfloxacin, lomefloxacin, and ofloxacin.

questions.text: Identify the imaging modality.

Correct answer: A. Retrograde pyelogram

The image depicts a retrograde pyelogram.

Retrograde Pyelogram is particularly valuable when IVP/CT is contraindicated and excels at providing detailed imaging of the collecting system, especially for evaluating ureteral strictures and filling defects, making it especially useful in surgical planning.

Other Options:

It helps diagnose anterior urethral abnormalities. The following image shows an image of retrograde urethrogram contrast leakage at the membranous urethra.

Option C: Intravenous Pyelography (IVP) provides comprehensive visualization of the entire urinary collecting system, useful for detecting stones, tumors, and anatomical abnormalities, though it's becoming less common with the advent of CT urography and has limitations in patients with renal insufficiency or contrast allergies.

Option D: Antegrade Pyelography, performed through a nephrostomy tube, is particularly useful when retrograde access isn't possible and helps evaluate obstruction below the kidney, often being employed in patients with existing nephrostomy tubes. questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the recommended maximum time frame for cornea harvesting after death to ensure optimal transplant quality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 6 hours

Donor corneas are to be harvested within 6 hours of death.

Eye banks manage corneal and scleral tissue donation for transplantation. The process requires next-of-kin consent and involves screening donors for contraindications including infectious diseases, malignancies, and neurological conditions. Tissues must be harvested within 6-8 hours of death.

Two harvesting methods are used:

* Whole globe enucleation: Complete eyeball removal, stored in moist chamber bottles

* In situ corneoscleral rim excision: Direct corneal rim removal into storage medium

The process is regulated by the Transplantation of Organs and Tissues Act and coordinated by the National Organ and Tissue Transplant Organization. Eye banks conduct public education and place counselors in hospitals to improve donation rates through the Hospital Cornea Retrieval Program.
questions.learning: 6 hours Donor corneas are to be harvested within 6 hours of death. Eye banks manage corneal and scleral tissue donation for transplantation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs increases uric acid in urine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Probenecid

Probenecid is a uricosuric agent that promotes the excretion of uric acid.

Probenecid is used to decrease the body pool of urate in patients with chronic gout. The drug acts by inhibiting the organic anion transporter, particularly URAT-1 in the renal tubules that are involved in uric acid reabsorption. It is used as an adjuvant to allopurinol in chronic gout and hyperuricemia.

Probenecid increases urinary urate levels. Plenty of fluids are given to avoid urate calculi formation. Probenecid should not be used in gouty patients with nephrolithiasis or with overproduction of uric acid.

Probenecid inhibits penicillin's urinary excretion, prolonging penicillin action by enhancing and sustaining their blood levels. It inhibits the urinary excretion of other drugs such as cephalosporins, sulfonamides, methotrexate, and indomethacin. Aspirin blocks the uricosuric action of the drug.

Other options:

Option A: Colchicine acts by preventing the polymerization of microtubules by tubulin, this reduces neutrophil recruitment to inflamed tissue and also decreases the secretion of chemotactic factors by activated neutrophils. Overall it reduces the inflammatory response.

Option B: Febuxostat is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that prevents the conversion of xanthine to uric acid approved for the treatment of hyperuricemia in patients with gout.

Option D: Allopurinol by inhibiting the xanthine oxidase enzyme that prevents the conversion of xanthine to uric acid.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In an HIV-positive patient who presents with multiple dog bites, what is the appropriate management?
questions.explanation: HIV-positive patients are considered immunocompromised, and multiple dog bites are classified as Category III exposure. This requires a comprehensive approach: immediate wound management (washing with soap and running water for 15-20 minutes), the full rabies vaccine course, and the administration of Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG). Option A is insufficient because immunocompromised individuals may not mount a timely immune response, making RIG essential for immediate passive protection. RIG alone (Option B) does not provide the long-term protection afforded by the vaccine. Simple wound care (Option C) cannot prevent the virus from reaching the central nervous system. Because rabies is nearly 100% fatal once symptoms appear, the combined use of active and passive immunization is the mandatory standard of care for Category III bites

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What are the diagnostic criteria for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) as defined by the Modified Rotterdam Criteria? 1. Obesity 2. Delayed menstruation 3. Hirsutism 4. Insulin resistance
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2 and 3

Modified Rotterdam Criteria (2003)

Diagnosis of PCOS requires any 2 out of the following 3 criteria after excluding other causes.

| Criterion | Description

| --------- | -----------

| Oligo-ovulation / anovulation | Irregular or delayed menstruation

| Clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism | Hirsutism, acne, ↑ testosterone

| Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound | ≥20 follicles or ovarian volume ≥10 mL

Thus in the options:

• Delayed menstruation → represents oligo-ovulation
• Hirsutism → represents hyperandrogenism

Hence 2 and 3 are correct.

Polycystic Ovaries on Ultrasound

Typical ultrasound features:

• ≥20 follicles measuring 2–9 mm
• Peripheral arrangement called “string of pearls”
• Ovarian volume ≥10 mL

Clinical Hyperandrogenism (Hirsutism)

Hyperandrogenism may present as:

• Hirsutism
• Acne
• Alopecia

Assessment commonly done using Ferriman–Gallwey score.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly man with a history of Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery for obesity presents with episodes of dizziness, fatigue, and tremors occurring about two hours after eating a carbohydrate-rich meal. These postprandial symptoms are most likely caused by which underlying mechanism? 1. Hypoglycemia 2. Small volume of food intake 3. High osmotic load of food 4. Increased release of insulin 5. Increased release of glucagon
questions.explanation: The patient is experiencing Late Dumping Syndrome, a common complication after gastric bypass surgery. Unlike "Early" dumping, which occurs within 30 minutes due to osmotic shifts, Late Dumping occurs 1 to 3 hours after a meal. It is caused by the rapid transit of simple carbohydrates into the small intestine, triggering an exaggerated and rapid increase in insulin release (4) from the pancreas. This "overshoot" of insulin leads to reactive hypoglycemia (1), resulting in the characteristic tremors, dizziness, and fatigue. Option 3 (High osmotic load) is the primary cause of Early dumping syndrome. Option 2 (Small volume) and Option 5 (Glucagon) are not the drivers of this reactive metabolic state. Therefore, the specific timing and neuroglycopenic symptoms confirm that reactive hypoglycemia caused by hyperinsulinemia is the responsible mechanism. Management involves frequent, small, low-carbohydrate meals
questions.learning: The patient is experiencing Late Dumping Syndrome, a common complication after gastric bypass surgery. Unlike "Early" dumping, which occurs within 30 minutes due to osmotic shifts, Late Dumping occurs 1 to 3 hours after a meal.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not involved in the repair of DNA following double-stranded breaks?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. MSH2

MSH2 is involved in mismatch repair and is not involved in the repair of double-stranded DNA breaks as the repair involves the correction of a single mismatch base pair e.g. C to A, instead of T to A.

DNA mismatch repair proteins function as spell checkers during DNA replication by correcting the incorrect pairing. In HNPCC, the proofreading function of the mismatch repair systems (majorly MLH1 and MSH2) is lost, leading to the accumulation of errors throughout the genome. The genomes of these patients show microsatellite instability, which is characterized by changes in the length of short repeats.

Double-strand breaks (DSBs) in DNA pose a significant concern.  Genetic recombination events can give rise to chromosomal translocation, chromosomal breakage, and ultimately cellular demise. Double-strand breaks (DSBs) have the potential to undergo repair through two distinct mechanisms: homologous recombination and non-homologous end joining. Homologous recombination is observed in yeasts, whereas in mammals, non-homologous end joining predominates.

Non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) is a mechanism by which a group of proteins mediates the recognition, processing, and direct ligation of the ends of two DNA fragments where a double-strand break in DNA has occurred. This is in contrast to homologous repair (HR), another mechanism, where an undamaged homologous DNA template is required to replace an adjacent damaged one.

The type of repair depends on the phase of cell cycles:

Phase of the cell cycle
Repair mechanism

G0 /G1 Phase
Nonhomologous End Joining Repair

S, G2, M Phase
Homologous Repair

Other options:

Option A: The protein known as ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) serves as a crucial kinase that triggers a wide range of cellular stress responses through its signalling activity. The activation of ATM is induced by DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) and oxidative stress, resulting in the phosphorylation of a wide range of target proteins. Recent advancements in molecular biology have brought to light the participation of the ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) protein in a range of cellular mechanisms triggered by DNA damage. These mechanisms encompass the repair of double-strand breaks (DSBs), the halting of cell cycle progression through checkpoint activation, the initiation of programmed cell death (apoptosis), and the cessation of transcriptional activity. The compromised precision of repair resulting from the combinational failure of stress responses leads to heightened sensitivity to ionizing radiation (IR) in ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T) cells.

Option B: CtIP which is a DNA repair protein involved in Homologous Repair whose function is dependent on phosphorylation at serine 327 as well as the recruitment of BRCA 1.

Option D: The Ku heterodimer, consisting of Ku70 and Ku80 subunits, plays a pivotal role in the nonhomologous end-joining (NHEJ) pathway, which is responsible for the repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs). Ku protein mediates the binding of the damaged DNA fragment and orchestrates the recruitment of additional proteins to enable the subsequent processing and ligation of the broken DNA end.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Type 2 lepra reaction is caused by __________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Type III hypersensitivity reaction

Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) or type 2 lepra reaction is caused by type III hypersensitivity reaction which is immune-complex mediated.

Type 2 lepra reactions (ENL) are mainly seen in multibacillary disease; LL(50%)>BL(15%). They can occur before, during, or after treatment, and are commonly recurrent. These reactions are caused by immune complexes (type 3 hypersensitivity).
ENL presents with painful, erythematous nodules on the face and extensor surfaces of limbs. Systemic manifestations like fever, malaise, anorexia, neuritis, uveitis, dactylitis, arthritis, myositis, etc. can also be seen.

Treatment of type 2 lepra reactions includes high-dose steroids, thalidomide (drug of choice in young men with severe ENL), and clofazimine.

Type 1 lepra reaction, on the other hand, is caused by type IV hypersensitivity reaction i.e. cell-mediated immune inflammation within existing skin lesions.
questions.learning: Type III hypersensitivity reaction Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) or type 2 lepra reaction is caused by type III hypersensitivity reaction which is immune-complex mediated.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following treatments for a pregnant lady who has been exposed to a patient of chicken pox are correct? 1. Varicella-zoster immune globulin 2. Varicella-zoster vaccine 3. Acyclovir 4. Prednisolone Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 3 only

A susceptible pregnant woman exposed to varicella (chickenpox) should receive Varicella-zoster immune globulin (VZIG) as post-exposure prophylaxis to reduce disease severity. If she develops varicella infection, acyclovir is recommended, particularly if started within 24 hours of rash onset or in severe disease.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Varicella-zoster immune globulin (VZIG) ✔️ – Recommended after significant exposure in a non-immune pregnant woman.
• 2. Varicella-zoster vaccine ❌ – A live attenuated vaccine; contraindicated during pregnancy.
• 3. Acyclovir ✔️ – Used if the pregnant woman develops chickenpox, especially in moderate-to-severe disease.
• 4. Prednisolone ❌ – No role in routine post-exposure prophylaxis or treatment of maternal varicella.
questions.learning: 1 and 3 only A susceptible pregnant woman exposed to varicella (chickenpox) should receive Varicella-zoster immune globulin (VZIG) as post-exposure prophylaxis to reduce disease severity.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with oral cavity findings are seen in the image below. He is a smoker. What would you choose as your next step in the management of this patient?
options: Cessation of smoking and do biopsy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cessation of smoking and do biopsy

The patient, who is a chronic smoker, presenting with a wrinkled white patch on the ventral surface of his tongue is likely to have leukoplakia.  Confirmation of this diagnosis will require a biopsy of the lesion. Leukoplakia is a premalignant lesion, with a malignant potential of 1 - 17.5%, hence it is imperative that the patient is advised on cessation of smoking.

Leukoplakia is a premalignant condition of the oral cavity characterized by whitish patches or plaques that cannot be rubbed off.  They appear as small, well-circumscribed lesions and can extensively involve a large area of the oral mucosa.

Variants of leukoplakia are:

• Homogenous variant: Smooth white patch. Less asociation with malignancy.
•  Non-homogenous variants:

• Speckled leukoplakia is whitish lesions on an erythematous base. They have the highest risk of malignant transformation.
• Proliferative verrucous leukoplakia is rare and has a high risk for malignant transformation.
• Erosive (erythroleukoplakia) is when it is interspersed with erythroplakia and has erosions and fissures. This also has malignant potential.

Management includes smoking cessation and reduction in alcohol consumption. A biopsy should be done. A CO2 laser is often used for ablation.

A photographic record of the lesion is useful for long-term follow-up in cases of conservative treatment.

Given below is a list of premalignant lesions of the oral cavity with their risk of malignancy:

High-risk lesions
Medium risk lesions
Low-risk lesions

•  Speckled type is the most  aggressive

• Hypersensitive reaction to betel nut product.
• Other risk factors are - tobacco, chili, vitamin deficiency
• Clinical features - trismus, ankyloglossia, soreness, and burning sensation in the mouth.
• Management includes antioxidants, intralesional triamcinolone, and surgical excision.

• Management is topical corticosteroids.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements: • Statement 1- Contemplation – A person who smokes is thinking of quitting smoking • Statement 2- Precontemplation – A person is considering starting morning walks and the benefits to their health • Statement 3- Maintenance phase – A person quit smoking one year back and has not smoked since then • Statement 4- Action phase – A person with obesity says they can’t do anything, as it runs deep in their family
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Statement 1 and 3 are correct

The Stages of Change (Transtheoretical Model):

A behavioral change framework (Prochaska & DiClemente) describing readiness to change across sequential stages.

Stages of Change

• Precontemplation

• No intention to change
• Unaware / denial / resistance
• Example: “Smoking isn’t a problem for me.”

• Contemplation

• Aware of problem, thinking about change
• Ambivalence present
• Example: “I should quit, but it’s hard.”

• Preparation

• Intends to act soon
• Small initial steps taken
• Example: “I’ll quit next month; I’ve reduced cigarettes.”

• Action

• Active behavior change
• High effort and risk of relapse
• Example: Recently stopped smoking

• Maintenance

• Sustained change (>6 months)
• Focus on preventing relapse
• Example: Abstinent for months, avoiding triggers

• Relapse

• Return to old behavior
• Common and part of the cycle

Contemplation involves awareness and thinking about change (Statement 1 correct), while precontemplation reflects lack of intent to change; considering health benefits fits early contemplation rather than denial. (hence statement 2 is incorrect)

Maintenance refers to sustained behaviour change for >6 months, as in quitting smoking for one year (Statement 3 correct).

The action phase involves active behaviour change; expressing helplessness reflects precontemplation, making Statement 4 incorrect.
questions.learning: Statement 1 and 3 are correct — The Stages of Change (Transtheoretical Model): A behavioral change framework (Prochaska & DiClemente) describing readiness to change across sequential stages.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman was brought to the psychiatric OPD by her friend. The patient claims that her boss is in love with her and stalks her. The woman’s friend refutes her claims. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Erotomania

Erotomania is a delusional disorder where the patient believes someone is in love with him/her, against evidence to the contrary. It is also known as De Clérambault syndrome.

The lover in the delusion is often a person of higher social status. It is more common in women.

Pearl PF1258: Types of delusions

THE TYPES OF DELUSIONS

Delusion of control

False belief that a person’s will, thoughts, or feelings are being controlled by external forces.

Delusion of grandeur or Megalomania

Exaggerated conception of one’s importance, power, or identity.

Delusion of infidelity or morbid jealousy or Othello syndrome

False belief that one’s lover is unfaithful. Sometimes called pathological jealousy.

Delusion of love or erotomania

False belief that another person is in love with them. In De Clerambault syndrome, the woman believes that a man, frequently older and of higher status, is in love with her.

Delusion of misidentification

Capgras syndrome: Belief that a familiar person has been replaced by an exact double i.e. an impostor.

Fregoli syndrome: Person holds a delusional belief that different people are in fact a single person who changes his or her appearance or is in disguise.

Nihilistic delusion

False belief that oneself, others or the world, is non-existent or about to end. When nihilistic delusion is accompanied by ideas concerning bodily function failure e.g. putrefaction of intestine etc, it is called Cotard syndrome.

Delusion of infestation

False belief that one is infested with small but visible organisms. As a monosymptomatic delusional disorder, this is called Ekbom syndrome.

Delusion of persecution

The most common delusion. False belief of being harassed or persecuted.

Delusion of poverty

The person strongly believes they are financially incapacitated.

Delusion of reference

False belief that the behavior of others has a particular and unusual significance, usually of a negative nature. The person may falsely feel that others are talking about them (e.g. the people on television are talking to or about the person).

Delusion of self-accusation

False feeling of remorse and guilt. Seen in depression with psychotic features.
questions.learning: Erotomania Erotomania is a delusional disorder where the patient believes someone is in love with him/her, against evidence to the contrary. It is also known as De Clérambault syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: An elderly patient presents with increased frequency of breathing and weakness. ABG is given. What is the likely diagnosis? • pH = 7.3 • pCO₂ = 44 mmHg • pO₂ = 85 mmHg • HCO₃⁻ = 16 mEq/L • Na⁺ = 132 mEq/L • Cl⁻ = 86 mEq/L • Base excess = -12 mEq/L
options: Acute metabolic alkalosis with AG 16 mEq/L
Acute respiratory acidosis with AG 16 mEq/L
Acute metabolic acidosis with AG 30 mEq/L
Chronic Respiratory acidosis with AG 30 mEq/L
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute metabolic acidosis with AG 30 mEq/L

Low pH with markedly reduced HCO₃⁻ (16 mEq/L) indicates primary metabolic acidosis.

Anion gap = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) = 132 − (86 + 16) = 30 mEq/L, which is elevated.

Near-normal pCO₂ reflects early/partial respiratory compensation, confirming acute high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

| Parameter | Finding

| --------- | -------

| pH | ↓ (acidemia)

| HCO₃⁻ | ↓ → metabolic cause

| pCO₂ | not appropriately ↓

| AG | 30 (high)

Acidemia (↓ pH)

↓

Check HCO₃⁻ → LOW → Metabolic acidosis

↓

Calculate AG → HIGH (30)

↓

Check compensation (Winter’s formula)

↓

pCO₂ higher than expected → Acute / inadequate compensation

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the term for the number of maternal deaths occurring per 100,000 live births?
questions.explanation: The term used to define the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births is technically the Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR). By definition: Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR): Number of maternal deaths during pregnancy, childbirth, or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy per 100,000 live births However, there is a nomenclature issue in the options provided. Since “Maternal Mortality Ratio” is not listed, the intended and closest correct option is “Maternal mortality rate” (Option A). In many medical entrance and board examinations, the terms rate and ratio are often (though incorrectly) used interchangeably. Why other options are incorrect: 1. Under-5 Mortality Rate (B): Deaths of children under 5 years per 1,000 live births 2. Infant Mortality Rate (C): Deaths under 1 year of age per 1,000 live births 3. Perinatal Mortality Rate (D): Late fetal deaths + early neonatal deaths per 1,000 total births

questions.text: A girl diagnosed with schizophrenia presents to a Primary Health Centre (PHC) in India. Which Government of India (GOI)–provided online application is used to support mental health services in this setting?
questions.explanation: Tele-MANAS (Mental Health Assistance and Networking Across States) is the correct application launched by the Government of India. It is a 24/7 toll-free service (14416) designed to provide immediate mental health support and counseling to individuals in distress. It aims to bridge the mental health care gap across all states. U-WIN (Option B) is a platform for tracking immunizations. NIKUSHT (Option C) is a digital platform for monitoring leprosy or sickle cell disease. NIKSHAY (Option D) is the national surveillance and reporting system for tuberculosis management. Given that the patient requires mental health support for schizophrenia, Tele-MANAS is the only relevant technical platform provided by the GOI for this specific clinical need

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Identify the edges of the lesion given in the image?
questions.explanation: The image displays a characteristic Basal Cell Carcinoma (rodent ulcer), and the defining clinical feature of its margin is a rolled-out (or "pearly, rolled") edge. These raised, semi-translucent borders are a classic hallmark of this slow-growing malignancy. Everted edges (Option A) are characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma, where the tissue is growing outward. Sloping edges (Option C) are typical of healing venous ulcers. Punched-out edges (Option D) are seen in trophic or syphilitic ulcers, which appear deep and cleanly cut. Recognizing these edge characteristics is fundamental for the clinical diagnosis of chronic skin lesions. A rodent ulcer, while locally invasive, rarely metastasizes but can cause significant tissue destruction if left untreated. It typically occurs on sun-exposed areas of the head and neck. Definitive management involves wide local excision or Mohs micrographic surgery to ensure clear margins while preserving healthy tissue
