questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: You are a junior resident in the ICU. A senior doctor asks you to manage a mechanically ventilated patient whose arterial blood gases showed features of hypoventilation with respiratory acidosis. Which of the following parameters can you modulate to improve the condition of the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increase Respiratory Rate

Since this patient has features of hypoventilation and respiratory acidosis this is a case of type 2 respiratory failure and needs correction of hypoxia and hypercapnia. Thus, the respiratory rate should be increased, which increases ventilation and decreases the CO2 content, leading to improvement in the condition of this patient.

The most common ventilator mode to use in a newly intubated patient is ACMV(Assist Control Mode Ventilation).

The common terms used in association with a ventilator:

* Ventilation/minute ventilation is calculated as respiratory rate (RR) times tidal volume (Vt). In a mechanically ventilated patient, the CO2 content of the blood can be modified by changing the tidal volume or the respiratory rate.

* Tidal volume is the volume of air moved in and outside the lungs in each respiratory cycle.

* Oxygenation of the lungs can be changed by altering the fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2%) or the positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP).

*

FiO2 is the percentage of oxygen in the air mixture that is delivered to the patient.

* PEEP: The positive pressure that will remain in the airways at the end of the respiratory cycle.

* Peak pressure is a measure of airway resistance as well as compliance and includes the tubing and bronchial tree.

* Plateau pressures are a reflection of alveolar pressure and thus of lung compliance.

Initial ventilatory settings are as given below:

* Tidal volume - 4-6 ml/kg of IBW (Ideal Body Weight)

* Respiratory rate - 12 Breaths/ min

* FiO2 - 100% to begin with and titrated to lesser values to prevent oxygen toxicity

* PEEP - Begin with 5 cm H2O, titrate to 10 cm H2O (Carefully increased as high PEEP may impair ventricular filling in a patient with blunt chest trauma)

An ABG should be obtained 30 minutes after intubation and changes to the ventilator settings should be made in accordance with ABG findings. Peak and plateau pressures should be checked on the vent to assure there are no problems with airway resistance or alveolar pressure in order to prevent ventilator-induced lung injury.

Based on the ABG, hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and hyperventilation can be corrected by altering some ventilator settings.

* To increase the oxygenation either FiO2% or PEEP has to be increased. Raising the PEEP has a risk of barotrauma and hypotension while increased FiO2 can cause oxidative damage in the alveoli. A target of 92-94% should be maintained. A sudden drop of saturation can be caused by tube misplacement, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, atelectasis, or the development of mucus plugs.

* Hypercapnia can be managed by modifying alveolar ventilation which is dependent on tidal volume or the respiratory rate. Raising the rate or the tidal volume, will increase ventilation and decrease CO2. While increasing the rate, it will also increase the amount of dead space and can lead to the development of auto-PEEP.

Dynamic hyperinflation or auto-PEEP is a process in which some of the inhaled air is not fully exhaled at the end of the respiratory cycle. The accumulation of trapped air will increase pulmonary pressures and cause barotrauma and hypotension. To prevent and resolve auto-PEEP, enough time should be given for the air to leave the lungs during exhalation.

Note:

Causes of elevated peak pressure and normal plateau pressure: Kinked ET tube, Mucus plug, Bronchospasm.

Causes of elevated peak and elevated plateau pressure: Mainstem intubation, Pneumothorax, Atelectasis, Pulmonary edema, ARDS.
questions.learning: Increase Respiratory Rate Since this patient has features of hypoventilation and respiratory acidosis this is a case of type 2 respiratory failure and needs correction of hypoxia and hypercapnia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 23-year-old woman accompanied by her mother-in-law comes to the infertility clinic. She has been having regular intercourse for 6 months but is not able to conceive. What is the next best step?
options: Reassure and review the couple after 6 months
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reassure and review the couple after 6 months

The next best step would be to reassure and review the couple after 6 months.

The inability to conceive after 1 year of unprotected intercourse of reasonable frequency is described as infertility.

Infertility evaluation is offered to any couple that has failed to conceive after 1 year of regular unprotected intercourse. There is a decline in the conception rate and a rise in poor pregnancy outcomes in older women hence, the majority of experts concur that in women older than 35, evaluation may be considered after 6 months. Since the woman is 23 years old and has tried conceiving for only 6 months, it is advisable to review them in another 6 months if they fail to conceive.

Infertility workup includes the following if required:

(1) Ovulation and evaluation for the diminished ovarian reserve-

(2) Evaluation of Female reproductive tract abnormality-

• Hysterosalpingography
• Sonography
• Laparoscopy
• Hysteroscopy- The preferred way to diagnose intrauterine anomalies is an endoscopic assessment of the uterine cavity. Both an operating room and a doctor's office can be used for hysteroscopy. It has the ability to concurrently diagnose and treat the abnormalities.

(3) Semen analysis
questions.learning: Reassure and review the couple after 6 months — The next best step would be to reassure and review the couple after 6 months. The inability to conceive after 1 year of unprotected intercourse of reasonable frequency is described as infertility.

questions.text: Identify the following marked structures.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 - Involucrum, 2 - Cloacae, 3 - Sequestrum

In the given radiographs showing features of chronic osteomyelitis, the marked structures are as follows:

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Identify the given condition and its treatment.
options: Staphylococcal scalded syndrome with Inj cephalexin
questions.explanation: The clinical image demonstrates widespread erythema and superficial desquamation, which is the hallmark of Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS). SSSS is caused by an exfoliative toxin produced by Staphylococcus aureus, which causes the top layer of the epidermis to detach, creating a "scalded" appearance. Treatment requires intravenous (IV) antistaphylococcal antibiotics to target the systemic bacterial cause, alongside supportive care similar to burn management. Epidermolysis bullosa (Option B) is a genetic disorder of skin fragility rather than an infection. Impetigo bullosa (Option C) is a localized form of staphylococcal infection presenting with large blisters but not widespread peeling. Erythema multiforme (Option D) is a hypersensitivity reaction characterized by "target lesions". Therefore, given the extensive peeling and pediatric presentation, SSSS treated with appropriate antibiotics is the correct diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical image demonstrates widespread erythema and superficial desquamation, which is the hallmark of Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An elderly woman presents with a sudden onset of severe ocular pain, redness, and decreased vision. On examination, she has a hazy cornea, a fixed mid-dilated pupil, and a shallow anterior chamber. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute angle closure Glaucoma

Acute angle-closure glaucoma (AACG) is an ophthalmic emergency caused by sudden obstruction of aqueous outflow, leading to a rapid rise in intraocular pressure.

• Severe ocular pain + headache
• Red eye with hazy (edematous) cornea
• Fixed mid-dilated pupil
• Shallow anterior chamber
• Sudden decrease in vision ± halos

Pathophysiology: Closure of anterior chamber angle → blocked trabecular outflow → ↑ IOP

Why not others:

• Uveitis → constricted pupil, not mid-dilated
• Conjunctivitis → no vision loss or high IOP
• Open-angle glaucoma → painless, gradual

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female, married for the past 5 years, presents with complaints of inability to conceive despite regular intercourse. Physical examination is unremarkable. Semen analysis of the husband revealed no abnormalities. Hysterosalpingography reveals the following picture. The anomaly shown in the image below falls under which category of the american fertility society classification of mullerian duct anomalies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Class II

The image shows a hysterosalpingogram of a unicornuate uterus, which falls under Class II of Mullerian duct anomalies

In the unicornuate uterus, the formation of the uterus and fallopian tube occurs entirely from one Mullerian duct due to developmental arrest of other Mullerian ducts. On Hysterosalpingography, the endometrial cavity usually appears fusiform shape tapering at the apex and draining into a single Fallopian tube. The uterus generally appears shifted off the midline.

The AFS (American Fertility Society) classification of Mullerian duct anomalies is as follows:

* Class I—Mullerian agenesis or hypoplasia.

* Class II—Unicornuate uterus, with absent or defective development of one Mullerian duct.

* Class III—Uterus didelphys

* Class IV—Bicornuate uterus

* Class V—Septate uterus

* Class VI—Arcuate uterus

Infertility is defined as lack of conception despite 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse in women aged < 35 years old and despite 6 months of regular unprotected intercourse in women aged > 35 years old.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is the major contributor to the total energy intake, in terms of energy provided, in an average Indian diet?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Carbohydrates

Carbohydrates are the major source of energy in the average Indian diet, contributing approximately 60–70% of the total daily energy intake. They are the body’s preferred and most economical source of energy, providing 4 kcal/g.

High-Yield Pearls

• Carbohydrates provide 4 kcal/g and contribute 60–70% of total energy in a balanced Indian diet.
• Proteins provide 4 kcal/g and contribute about 10–15% of total energy.
• Fats provide 9 kcal/g and contribute about 20–30% of total energy.
• Vitamins do not provide energy; they function as regulators of metabolic processes.
questions.learning: Carbohydrates Carbohydrates are the major source of energy in the average Indian diet, contributing approximately 60–70% of the total daily energy intake.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the marked structure of the cochlear implant shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ground electrode

The marked structure in the radiology image of the cochlear implant is the ground electrode.

A cochlear implant is a medical device that uses electricity to stimulate the spiral ganglion cells of the auditory nerve to restore sensorineural hearing loss. It can be used in a patient with bilateral severe sensorineural hearing loss.

It converts sound to an electrical signal (transduction) and delivers this to the hearing nerve, which bypasses the damaged hearing apparatus. It cannot be used in patients with cochlear aplasia or without the VIIIth cranial nerve.

Cochlear implant:

• An electronic device for severe to profound SNHL and who cannot benefit from a hearing aid.
• Principle- surgery to place the electrode array within the scala tympani of the cochlea.
• Indication- bilateral severe to profound deafness
• Prerequisites- intact 8th nerve and higher auditory pathway
• Surgical approach- facial recess (posterior tympanotomy) approach
• The electrode of a cochlear implant is placed in the scala tympani. (Note: In the auditory brainstem implant, the site of the implant is the lateral recess of the 4th ventricle.)

The receiver-stimulator implanted during surgery (under the skin) and the electrode array (implanted in the scala tympani of the cochlea) are part of the internal component of the cochlear implant. The microphone, speech processor and transmitter are part of the external component of the cochlear implant, which remains outside the body.

Cochlear implants replace the non-functional transducer system of hair cells of the cochlea and convert the sound signal to electrical impulses, which directly stimulate the fibres of cranial nerve VIII.
questions.learning: Ground electrode — The marked structure in the radiology image of the cochlear implant is the ground electrode. A cochlear implant is a medical device that uses electricity to stimulate the spiral ganglion cells of the auditory nerve to restore…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with a history of COPD presents with acute worsening of dyspnea. Arterial blood gas analysis shows pH 7.24, pCO₂ 60 mmHg, pO₂ 52 mmHg, and HCO₃ [value not provided]. What is the most appropriate treatment option for this patient?
questions.explanation: Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV). The patient is in acute respiratory failure due to a COPD exacerbation. His ABG shows respiratory acidosis (pH 7.24, 60 mmHg) and hypoxemia ( 52 mmHg). For a COPD patient who is acidotic but still awake/stable, Non-invasive Positive Pressure Ventilation (NIPPV) (Option C) is the gold-standard first-line treatment. NIPPV reduces the work of breathing, improves gas exchange, and significantly lowers the need for invasive ventilation and hospital mortality. Endotracheal intubation (Option A) and invasive ventilation (Option B) are reserved for those who fail NIPPV or present in coma/arrest. Lung volume reduction surgery (Option D) is a chronic management option for end-stage emphysema, not for acute failure. Therefore, because NIPPV is highly effective at reversing the acidosis while avoiding the complications of an artificial airway, it is the definitive most appropriate choice. Clinicians must monitor the patient closely for improvement within the first few hours. .
questions.learning: Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV). The patient is in acute respiratory failure due to a COPD exacerbation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The distance walked in 6 minutes is an indirect measure of which of the following variables of the BODE Index which is used to assess the prognosis in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Exercise capacity

The BODE Index is a multidimensional prognostic scoring system used to predict mortality, hospitalization, and disease severity in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). It is a better predictor of prognosis than FEV₁ alone.

Components of the BODE Index

| Component | Assessment

| --------- | ----------

| B – Body Mass Index (BMI) | Nutritional status

| O – Airflow Obstruction | Post-bronchodilator FEV₁ (% predicted)

| D – Dyspnoea | Modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) dyspnoea scale

| E – Exercise Capacity | 6-minute walk distance (6MWD)

The 6-minute walk test (6MWT) measures the distance a patient can walk in 6 minutes, which is an indirect measure of exercise capacity and functional status.

• Lower 6-minute walk distance is associated with:

• Increased mortality
• More frequent COPD exacerbations
• Poorer quality of life

• A higher BODE score indicates worse prognosis.
questions.learning: Exercise capacity — The BODE Index is a multidimensional prognostic scoring system used to predict mortality, hospitalization, and disease severity in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient who has been diagnosed with multiple gastrointestinal polyps and carcinoma, with a positive family history/history of hereditary non-polyposis colon carcinoma has a defect in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mismatch repair

Mismatch repair will be defective in a patient with multiple gastrointestinal polyps and carcinoma, with a positive family history/history of hereditary non-polyposis colon carcinoma (HNPCC)

Mismatch repair is a DNA repair mechanism that corrects single-nucleotide mismatches, insertions, and deletions introduced by the DNA polymerase during DNA replication.

HNPCC or Lynch syndrome is an autosomal dominant genetic condition. It occurs due to defects in DNA mismatch repair genes like MLH1 and MSH2. The genomes of these patients show microsatellite instability. HNPCC is associated with a high risk of colon cancer. It may also be associated with a risk of developing carcinomas of the endometrium, stomach, small bowel, ovary, pancreas, and transitional cell carcinoma of the ureter and renal pelvis.

The diagnostic criteria for HNPCC are referred to as the Amsterdam criteria or the 3-2-1-0 rule. It includes:

• Three or more relatives with HNPCC-associated cancer (colorectal cancer, endometrial cancer, cancer of the small bowel, ureter, or renal pelvis), one of whom is a first-degree relative of the other two.
• At least two successive generations affected
• At least one case diagnosed before age 50 years
• Familial adenomatous polyposis excluded
• Tumors verified by pathologic examination.

Other options:

Option B: Patients with xeroderma pigmentosum have a defect in the nucleotide excision repair pathway.

Option C: Defect in base excision repair pathway is seen in patients with MUTYH-associated polyposis.

Option D:  Sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia are examples of diseases seen in patients with point mutations.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 27-year-old female patient presents with weight loss, anxiety, tachycardia, and restlessness. The resting pulse was 110 beats per minute. Which of the following tests should be done next to evaluate her condition further?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. TSH

TSH is the best initial screening test for suspected hyperthyroidism because it is the most sensitive indicator of thyroid function.

| Test | Role | When Used

| ---- | ---- | ---------

| TSH ⭐ | Initial screening | First test

| Free T4 | Confirm severity | After TSH

| Total T3 | Sometimes used | Less preferred

| Thyroid scan | Etiology | Later step

In thyrotoxicosis, TSH is characteristically suppressed due to negative feedback from elevated thyroid hormones. Free T4 or T3 are measured only after an abnormal TSH to confirm and classify severity. Thyroid scan is reserved for etiologic evaluation, not first-line screening.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following contributes to the latent period in a single muscle twitch? a. Excitation-contraction coupling b. Opening of sodium channels on NMJ c. Transmission of impulse from the site of stimulus to NMJ d. Pumping of calcium back to the sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. a, b, c

The latent period of a muscle twitch is the short delay (≈2–5 ms) between stimulus application and start of contraction.

This period includes all events before actual cross-bridge cycling begins. The latent period represents the time between stimulus and onset of contraction and includes electrical and coupling events before tension develops. It covers impulse transmission to the NMJ, opening of Na⁺ channels with depolarization, and excitation–contraction coupling with Ca²⁺ release. Pumping Ca²⁺ back into the SR occurs during relaxation, not latency. Hence a, b, and c contribute to the latent period.

Stimulus applied

↓

Impulse travels along motor nerve (c)

↓

Acetylcholine release at NMJ → Na⁺ channels open (b)

↓

End plate potential → Muscle action potential

↓

T-tubule depolarization

↓

Ca²⁺ release from SR (Excitation-Contraction Coupling) (a)

↓

Actin-myosin interaction begins → Contraction starts

Latent period reflects 3 physiological delays:

1. Neural delay

• Nerve conduction time

2. Synaptic delay (\~0.5 ms)

• ACh release, diffusion, receptor binding

3. E-C coupling delay

• T-tubule depolarization
• DHPR–RyR interaction
• Ca²⁺ release

Most important contributor: Excitation–contraction coupling
questions.learning: a, b, c The latent period of a muscle twitch is the short delay (≈2–5 ms) between stimulus application and start of contraction. This period includes all events before actual cross-bridge cycling begins.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What type of collagen is predominantly found in cartilage?
questions.explanation: Cartilage is a specialized connective tissue, and its extracellular matrix composition varies by type. However, hyaline cartilage, which is the most abundant type in the body, predominantly contains Type 2 collagen fibers. This specific collagen provides the structural framework necessary to resist compressive forces within joints, the nose, and the respiratory tract. In contrast, Type 1 collagen is the primary component of bone, skin, and tendons, offering high tensile strength. Type 10 collagen is associated specifically with hypertrophic chondrocytes during endochondral ossification, marking the transition from cartilage to bone during growth. Type 7 collagen forms anchoring fibrils that secure the epidermis to the dermis at the basement membrane zone. Understanding these distribution patterns is fundamental for histology and pathology, as genetic defects in Type 2 collagen synthesis lead to skeletal dysplasias and early-onset osteoarthritis. Therefore, while various minor collagens exist in the matrix, Type 2 remains the defining structural protein of the cartilaginous framework
questions.learning: Cartilage is a specialized connective tissue, and its extracellular matrix composition varies by type. However, hyaline cartilage, which is the most abundant type in the body, predominantly contains Type 2 collagen fibers.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 4-year-old child inhaled a small toy while playing. X-ray reveals the toy to be on the right side of the chest. Which of the following is the anatomical basis for these findings? 1. Right bronchus is in direct line with the trachea 2. Right bronchus is wider 3. Right bronchus is longer 4. Right lung has 3 lobes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 2

The right main bronchus is the most common site for aspiration of inhaled foreign bodies because it is wider, shorter, and more vertical (more in direct continuation with the trachea) than the left main bronchus. As a result, aspirated objects are more likely to enter the right bronchial tree.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Right bronchus is in direct line with the trachea
• 2. Right bronchus is wider

Why not the other options?

• 3. Right bronchus is longer: The right main bronchus is shorter, not longer.
• 4. Right lung has 3 lobes: Although true anatomically, the number of lobes does not influence the site of foreign body aspiration.
questions.learning: 1 and 2 The right main bronchus is the most common site for aspiration of inhaled foreign bodies because it is wider, shorter, and more vertical (more in direct continuation with the trachea) than the left main bronchus.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the emergency room with excruciating burning pain over the palms and soles, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and ringing sensation in the ears. On examination, he has thickening of lips, frontal bossing, corneal opacities, and skin lesions. This X-linked disorder is caused due to which enzyme deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. α-Galactosidase

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Fabry's disease, and it is caused by the deficiency of α-Galactosidase.

Fabry disease is an X-linked, multisystem, lysosomal storage disorder caused by mutations in the gene that codes for α-Galactosidase, resulting in decreased activity of the enzyme. This leads to accumulation of globotriaosylceramide. It is seen in both men and women (less severe).

It usually manifests in childhood or adolescence, with symptoms of severe agonizing pain in the palms of hands, soles of feet, and proximal extremities, called acroparesthesia, aggravated by changes in temperature, exercise, fatigue, or fever, and may last anywhere from a few minutes to many days.

There is a characteristic facial appearance of frontal bossing, thickening of the lips, and prominent supraorbital ridges. Angiokeratomas, as seen in the image above, are present, which are lesions that are dark-red to blue-black, flat or slightly raised, punctate, and usually seen between the umbilicus and the knees (called the 'bathing suit area') and the trunk.

Patients also have diarrhea, abdominal distension, heat intolerance, and tinnitus. Late presentations include renal failure and cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease, which are the leading causes of death in these patients.

Urinalysis shows proteinuria. An enzyme assay, genetic testing, or a skin or kidney biopsy showing glycolipid deposits helps establish the diagnosis.

Treatment is with enzyme replacement therapy (recombinant alpha-Gal A or migalastat).

Other options:

Option B: β-Glucosidase deficiency manifests as Gaucher disease, which gives rise to symptoms of hepatosplenomegaly, erosion of long bones and mental retardation in infants.

Option C: Sphingomyelinase deficiency manifests as Niemann-Pick disease, with patients presenting with symptoms of hepatosplenomegaly and mental retardation. It is usually fatal in early life.

Option D: Ceramidase deficiency manifests as Farber disease, characterized by dermatitis, hoarseness, skeletal deformities, and mental retardation. It is fatal in early life.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Skull of a dead person was found during investigation. Police asked the relatives to bring the photo of deceased. Which method is being used for identification of dead body?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Superimposition

Superimposition is a forensic identification technique used when skeletal remains (especially skull) are compared with antemortem photographs.

• The skull is superimposed over a photograph of the missing person
• Matching of facial landmarks (orbit, nasal aperture, jaw, teeth, contours) is assessed
• Helps determine whether the skull could belong to that individual

• Key use:

• When only skull or skeletal remains are available
• When photographs of the suspected individual are available

• Limitations:

• It is supportive, not confirmatory
• Cannot establish identity with absolute certainty (unlike DNA)

• Other Options:

Option A. Anthropometry → body measurements (obsolete)

Option B. Dactylography → fingerprints (requires soft tissue)

Option D. DNA fingerprinting → confirmatory but not based on photo comparison

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old man who is a known case of hypertension presented with multiple episodes of hematuria and loin pain. His elder brother passed away due to stroke at the age of 40. The ultrasound abdomen is shown below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease

This clinical scenario with a family history of stroke and USG showing a cystic appearance of the kidney is suggestive of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD).

ADPKD is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with mutations in the PKD1(chromosome 16) and PKD2 genes (chromosome 4).

The disease does not usually manifest before 30 years of age, and in some patients, it is never diagnosed. The progression of the disease is faster in males.

Hypertension is the most common presentation. Renal manifestations of ADPKD include:

• Flank/loin pain -  either due to hemorrhage inside cysts or due to renal stones (most commonly uric acid stones)
• Irregular upper quadrant renal mass
• Hematuria
• Uremia
• Renal failure (seen in 10–15% of the patients who receive hemodialysis)

The most common extrarenal manifestation is hepatic cysts, which are derived from the biliary epithelium. Other extra-renal manifestations of ADPKD:

• Pancreatic cysts
• Berry aneurysms (Rupture of cerebral aneurysms is an important cause of morbidity and The prevalence of intracranial aneurysms in patients with PKD is 40%.)
• Colonic diverticula
• Abdominal hernias
• Mitral valve prolapse

Screening cerebral angiography is strongly considered in all patients with PKD and a family history of cerebral aneurysm or subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Intravenous pyelography shows characteristic spider leg sign, as a result of stretched calyces due to multiple cysts. The nephrogram shows a swiss cheese appearance. On prenatal USG, the presence of either > 3 cysts in unilateral kidneys or > 2 cysts in each kidney is suggestive of PKD.

Treatment includes

• Surgical decompression is not a routine procedure performed in these patients. It may be required only in cases of very large cysts causing persistent pain and infected cysts.
• Analgesics
• Increased fluid intake

• Prevents renal stone formation
• Reduces growth of cysts by suppressing ADH release

• ACE inhibitors and ARBs

• Blood pressure control
• Slowing of cyst growth

• Tolvaptan (V2 receptor antagonist)

• Reduce pain and slow the decline in renal function

• Long-term dialysis
• Renal transplant

• Definitive management
• Pre-transplant nephrectomy may be required in patients with very large polycystic kidneys

Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) occurs secondary to a mutation of the PKHD1 gene. The severe form manifests in-utero or during infancy; milder cases can manifest later in childhood. 50% of affected newborns die in the first few days of life.

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is a relatively rare complication of ADPKD. There does not seem to be an increased frequency of RCC in these patients compared to the general population. However, when it occurs, it tends to be bilateral, multicentric, and of sarcomatoid type.

Tuberculosis kidney presents as putty kidney characterized by amorphous dystrophic calcification.
questions.learning: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease — This clinical scenario with a family history of stroke and USG showing a cystic appearance of the kidney is suggestive of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 16-year-old patient presents with diarrhoea and pellagra-like photosensitive skin eruptions for the last 5 years. Her vital examinations are normal. Urine analysis reveals an increase in the amino acid levels but normal levels of 5-hydroxyindole acetic acid (5-HIAA). What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hartnup disease

The above clinical history of a 16-year-old child presenting with diarrhoea and pellagra-like photosensitive skin eruptions with urine analysis showing an increase in the amino acid levels and normal 5-HIAA levels is suggestive of Hartnup disease.

Amino acids are reabsorbed in the kidneys in the proximal convoluted tubule. Aminoaciduria points towards a pathology.

Hartnup disease (pellagra-like dermatosis) is an autosomal recessive condition caused by a single defect in the renal and intestinal transport of neutral amino acids (eg, Tryptophan). Decreased intestinal absorption of tryptophan in conjunction with its increased renal loss leads to its reduced bioavailability. This hampers niacin synthesis, and Hartnup disorder can thus present with manifestations of niacin deficiency (pellagra) like diarrhoea, dermatitis, and dementia.

Clinical features:

* Most of the children are asymptomatic

* Symptomatic patients show cutaneous photosensitivity

* The skin becomes rough and red after moderate exposure to the sun, and with greater exposure, a pellagra-like rash may develop. The rash may be pruritic, and chronic eczema may also appear.

* Some patients may also have intermittent ataxia, manifested as an unsteady, wide-based gait, which usually lasts for a few days and recovers spontaneously.

The diagnosis of Hartnup disorder is established by typical clinical history and the presence of neutral amino acids in the urine.

The Obermeyer test will be positive for Hartnup disorder. The Obermeyer test detects the urinary excretion of indole compounds. Indole derivates such as indican are found in large amounts in patients due to bacterial breakdown of unabsorbed tryptophan in the intestines.

Urinary excretion of other amino acids remains normal, which differentiates it from causes of generalized aminoaciduria like Fanconi syndrome.

Treatment:

* Niacin or niacinamide supplements

* Nicotinamide for attacks

Other options:

Option A: In Carcinoid syndrome, there is an excess synthesis of serotonin. This consumes available tryptophan and leads to a deficiency of niacin and eventually pellagra-like symptoms. In carcinoid syndrome, excess serotonin is converted to 5-HIAA which is excreted in urine. This patient has normal levels of 5-HIAA.

Option B:  Nutritional pellagra can appear in patients with excessive maize-based diets. Maize has niacin in its unusable form. Additionally, they will not excrete amino acids in urine.

Option C: Fructosuria will present with fructose in urine instead of amino acids.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is this view called in which frontal sinus is seen best ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Caldwell's view

Caldwell view (Occipitofrontal view or nose-forehead position):

The view is taken with nose and forehead touching the film and X-ray beam is projected 15–20° caudally, as shown in the image above. Structures seen with Caldwell's view are:

* Frontal sinuses (seen best).

* Ethmoid sinuses.

* Maxillary sinuses.

* Frontal process of zygoma and zygomatic process of frontal bone.

* Superior margin of orbit and lamina papyracea.

* Superior orbital fissure.

* Foramen rotundum (inferolateral to superior orbital fissure).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the arrow-marked chamber?
questions.explanation: This is an axial CT scan of the thorax. On axial imaging, anatomical orientation is such that the anterior structures are at the top of the image, and the right side of the patient appears on the left side of the image. The arrow points to a chamber located anteriorly and somewhat toward the patient’s right side, which corresponds to the right ventricle (RV). The right ventricle forms the most anterior part of the heart and lies just behind the sternum, making it the chamber most commonly seen in the anterior position on CT. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Right atrium: Located more right-sided and slightly posterior, not the most anterior chamber. (B) Left atrium: Lies posteriorly, forming the base of the heart. (D) Left ventricle: Located more posterior and left-sided, forming the apex but not the most anterior structure. Thus, the arrow-marked chamber is the right ventricle
questions.learning: This is an axial CT scan of the thorax. On axial imaging, anatomical orientation is such that the anterior structures are at the top of the image, and the right side of the patient appears on the left side of the image.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A middle aged woman presents with complaints of hearing her own voice and breath sounds. On examination, the tympanic membrane was moving with respiration. What is the most likely cause of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rapid weight loss

The given clinical scenario where the patient hears her own voice and breath sounds is called autophony which is seen patulous eustachian tube.

Patulous eustachian tube is usually idiopathic where the tube is abnormally patent. But it is also seen in rapid weight loss, pregnancy especially the third trimester and patients with multiple sclerosis.

The eustachian tube valve is patulous and hence always open.This leads to the transfer of pressure changes in the nasal cavity to the middle ear and consequent movement of the tympanic membrane with respiration. This patent communication is the reason for hearing of own voice and breathing sounds

Treatment includes weight gain and administration of potassium iodide solution. In long-standing cases, specific treatment could include the cauterization of tubes or the insertion of the grommet.

Mass lesions of the nasal cavity may occlude the eustachian tube and cause fullness of the ear or otitis media, but won't cause any movement of tympanic membrane with respiration
questions.learning: Rapid weight loss — The given clinical scenario where the patient hears her own voice and breath sounds is called autophony which is seen patulous eustachian tube.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Chloride level in sweat is used in the diagnosis of which disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cystic fibrosis

The chloride level of sweat, known as the sweat test, is used to diagnose cystic fibrosis (CF). A sweat chloride level of >60 mmol/L is diagnostic of CF.

CF is an autosomal recessive disorder with a mutation in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane regulator (CFTR) gene on chromosome 7q.

The below image depicts the organs affected by CF:

Diagnostic tests include:
1. Immunoreactive trypsinogen for newborn screening of cystic fibrosis.
2. Sweat chloride test: Increased chloride concentration >60 mmol/L is diagnostic.
3. Genetic testing for CFTR gene mutations is the gold standard and should be done for all cases.
4. Nasal transepithelial potential difference can be estimated in equivocal cases.

Diagnostic criteria:
Presence of

• Clinical symptoms affecting at least one organ system (respiratory, gastrointestinal, or genitourinary) or
• Positive newborn screening or
• A sibling with cystic fibrosis.

Evidence of dysfunction of the CFTR gene by

• Two positive sweat chloride test results obtained on separate days or
• Identification of two CFTR mutations by genetic testing or
• An abnormal measurement of nasal potential difference.

Other options:

Option A: Phenylketonuria occurs due to the deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase, leading to elevated phenylalanine levels. Diagnosis is confirmed by measuring plasma phenylalanine concentration.

Option C: Gaucher disease is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by a deficiency of β-glucosidase. Diagnosis is confirmed by fibroblast/leukocyte β-glucosidase activity and gene mutations.

Option D: Osteogenesis imperfecta is a genetic connective tissue disorder due to defective type-1 collagen. DNA sequencing is the first diagnostic test.
questions.learning: Cystic fibrosis — The chloride level of sweat, known as the sweat test, is used to diagnose cystic fibrosis (CF). A sweat chloride level of >60 mmol/L is diagnostic of CF.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the structure in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Blastocyst

The arrow is pointing at Blastocyst.

Around the 4th/5th day of development, the morula becomes the blastocyst. Fluid passes into the morula from the uterine cavity and converts it to a blastocyst with a fluid-filled cavity called blastocoele. This fluid partially separates the cells of the inner cell mass from the outer cell mass.

Cell masses in the blastocyst:

* The outer cell mass is called the trophoblast and forms a major part of the placenta

* The inner cell mass is called the embryoblast and forms the embryo proper

The blastocyst normally implants in the functional layer of the uterine endometrium.

Timeline of implantation:

* 3-4 days after fertilization: The morula (12-16 cells) enters the uterus.

* 4th day after fertilization: The advanced morula reaches the uterine lumen.

* 4-5 days after fertilization: The early blastocyst stage is seen.

* 6-7 days after fertilization: The blastocyst implants in the uterus. Implantation corresponds to 20-22 days of the menstrual cycle.
questions.learning: Blastocyst — The arrow is pointing at Blastocyst. Around the 4th/5th day of development, the morula becomes the blastocyst.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A pregnant lady was diagnosed with Extensively Drug-Resistant TB. Which of the following drugs is unsafe in this lady?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Kanamycin

Aminoglycosides are unsafe in pregnancy and from the options Kanamycin, an Aminoglycoside is not used.

Antibiotics safe in pregnancy include:

* Penicillin group

* Cephalosporins

* Erythromycin

* Metronidazole (except in the 1st trimester)

Antibiotics unsafe in pregnancy include:

* Tetracycline

* Aminoglycoside

* Chloramphenicol

* Metronidazole(in the first trimester)

* Fluoroquinolones

Pearl PF0266: ATT Regimen for TB Patients

As per the latest recommendations from National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP), treatment of TB is now based primarily on drug susceptibility testing. This is irrespective of new cases, previously treated cases or recurrent TB cases.
All cases of TB are treated with Drug Sensitive TB Regimen, as long as the patient is sensitive to isoniazid and rifampicin. (No classification into category I or II)

Classification based on drug resistance

* Mono-resistant (MR): A TB patient, who is resistant to one 1st line anti-TB drug only.

* Poly-Drug Resistant (PDR): A TB patient, who is resistant to more than one 1st line anti-TB drug, other than Rifampicin.

* Rifampicin Resistant (RR): A TB patient, who is resistant to rifampicin with or without resistance to other drugs. Patients, who have rifampicin resistance, should be managed as if they are an MDR TB case.

* Multi Drug Resistant (MDR): A TB patient, who is resistant to both isoniazid and rifampicin.

* Extensively Drug Resistant (XDR): A MDR TB patient who is additionally resistant to a fluoroquinolone (ofloxacin, levofloxacin, or moxifloxacin) and a second-line injectable anti TB drug (kanamycin, amikacin, or capreomycin).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A neonate presents with forceful, non-bilious vomiting and visible gastric peristalsis. A barium meal study is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presentation of forceful (projectile) non-bilious vomiting in a neonate (typically at 3–6 weeks of age), along with visible gastric peristalsis (stomach movements), is classic for Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (CHPS). The "non-bilious" nature of the vomit is critical as it indicates the obstruction is proximal to the second part of the duodenum. The barium meal image provides the definitive diagnosis, showing the "string sign"—the elongated, narrow pyloric canal. Duodenal atresia (Option D) would show bilious vomiting and a "double bubble" on X-ray. Jejunal atresia (Option C) also causes bilious vomiting and distal obstruction. Hirschsprung's disease (Option A) causes low intestinal obstruction and delayed meconium passage . CHPS is also associated with a palpable "olive-shaped" mass in the epigastrium and hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. Surgical management involves a Ramstedt’s pyloromyotomy
questions.learning: The presentation of forceful (projectile) non-bilious vomiting in a neonate (typically at 3–6 weeks of age), along with visible gastric peristalsis (stomach movements), is classic for Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (CHPS).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which classification is used for Barrett esophagus?
questions.explanation: The Prague C & M criteria is the internationally recognized endoscopic classification system used to standardize the reporting of Barrett's esophagus. In this system, "C" represents the circumferential extent of the metaplastic mucosa, and "M" represents the maximal extent (including "tongues" of mucosa) from the gastroesophageal junction. This allows for accurate monitoring and surveillance of the disease. Savary-Miller classification (Option B) is used to grade the severity of reflux esophagitis based on erosions. Johnson classification (Option C) categorizes types of gastric ulcers. Forrest classification (Option D) is used in the setting of acute upper GI bleeding to categorize peptic ulcers based on their bleeding stigmata and to predict the risk of rebleeding. Therefore, for the specific anatomical measurement of Barrett's mucosa, the Prague classification is the only correct choice
questions.learning: The Prague C & M criteria is the internationally recognized endoscopic classification system used to standardize the reporting of Barrett's esophagus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old chronic smoker came to the medicine outpatient department with complaints of upper chest discomfort and drooping of an eyelid. He also complained of pain radiating to the upper arm and a tingling sensation in the 4th and 5th digits of his right hand. The chest X-ray is given below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pancoast tumor

Pancoast's tumor is the most likely diagnosis in this patient.

Pancoast syndrome/superior sulcus tumor results from a local extension of a tumor growing in the apex of the lung, with the involvement of C8, T1, and T2 nerve roots, stellate ganglion, and the chest wall. It presents with pain that radiates to the ulnar distribution of the arm, often with the destruction of the 1st and 2nd ribs. Patients with the central or endobronchial growth of the primary tumor may present with a cough, hemoptysis, wheeze, stridor, dyspnea, or post-obstructive pneumonitis.

Regional spread can cause

• Tracheal obstruction
• Esophageal compression with dysphagia
• Recurrent laryngeal paralysis with hoarseness
• Phrenic nerve palsy with the elevation of the hemidiaphragm and dyspnea
• Sympathetic nerve paralysis with Horner’s syndrome (enophthalmos, ptosis, miosis, and anhydrosis)

Investigations in Pancoast tumor:

• MRI > CT is the investigation of choice for superior sulcus tumor/Pancoast tumor as the associated soft tissue infiltration, the extent of which can be best visualized using an MRI.
• FDG-PET scan shows high uptake by the tumor cells. FDG is taken up by all metabolizing cells but more avidly by cancer cells.
• Bronchoscopy can be done in endobronchial tumors to obtain a tissue diagnosis.

The image below shows the management of the Pancoast tumor.

Other options:

Option B: Pneumonia patients usually present with fever, cough, chills, tachycardia, and/or sweats. Cough may be nonproductive or productive of mucoid, purulent, or blood-tinged sputum. Other symptoms may include fatigue, headache, myalgias, and arthralgias.

Option C: Patients with superior vena cava obstruction usually present with neck and facial swelling, dyspnea, and cough. Symptoms may aggravate while bending forward or lying. The characteristic physical findings are dilated neck veins, cyanosis, and edema of the face, arms, and chest. Facial swelling and plethora are typically exacerbated when the patient is supine.

Option D: Aspergilloma (fungal ball) is a late manifestation of chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis, but some patients are asymptomatic. Signs and symptoms include cough (sometimes productive), hemoptysis, wheezing, and mild fatigue. More significant signs and symptoms are associated with chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following is true statement about Korsakoff syndrome?
options: Triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia
Loss of long term memory but intact personality
Anterograde amnesia with loss of recent memory
Loss of implicit memory and immediate recall
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anterograde amnesia with loss of recent memory

In Korsakoff's psychosis, there is anterograde amnesia with loss of recent memory.

Korsakoff's syndrome is a chronic amnestic syndrome that can follow Wernicke's syndrome. It is caused by thiamine deficiency that is associated with chronic alcohol abuse. The typical feature of this disease is anterograde amnesia with loss of recent memory in an alert and responsive patient. Patients with Korsakoff's syndrome also typically have a change in personality, with a lack of initiative, reduced spontaneity, and a lack of interest.

The treatment is with 100 mg of thiamine orally for 3-12 months. Despite adequate treatment and nutritional support, very few of the patients fully recover. With treatment, patients may remain amnestic for up to 3 months, and then improve gradually during the next year.

Prolonged use of alcohol causes alcohol-induced persisting amnestic disorder with loss of short-term memory. When the symptoms are acute, it is called Wernicke's encephalopathy and when chronic, it leads to Korsakoff's syndrome. These conditions are caused due to thiamine deficiency and when they occur together, they are called Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

Other options

Option A -Triad of confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia is seen in Wernicke's encephalopathy. There may also be vestibular dysfunction. Wernicke's encephalopathy is completely reversible. The treatment is parenteral administration of 100 mg thiamine for 1-2 weeks.

Option B - Personality is affected in Korsakoff's syndrome. Recent memory is affected more compared to long-term memory.

Option D - Implicit memory refers to memory that does not require conscious recollection. Implicit aspects of memory are preserved, however, some studies conclude that implicit memory may be intact or impaired depending on the specific task parameters.
questions.learning: Anterograde amnesia with loss of recent memory — In Korsakoff's psychosis, there is anterograde amnesia with loss of recent memory. Korsakoff's syndrome is a chronic amnestic syndrome that can follow Wernicke's syndrome.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with sore throat starts developing skin lesions as in the image below. Which of the following is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Guttate psoriasis is a distinct form of psoriasis characterized by the sudden eruption of small, drop-like, scaly papules and plaques across the trunk and limbs. It is strongly associated with a preceding Group A Streptococcal infection (such as a sore throat or tonsillitis) roughly 2–3 weeks prior. The word "guttate" is derived from the Latin word for "drop." Pustular psoriasis (Option B) involves sterile pustules and is a much more severe, potentially systemic condition. Erythrodermic psoriasis (Option C) involves generalized redness and scaling of over 90% of the body surface area and is a medical emergency. Inverse psoriasis (Option D) occurs in skin folds (axillae, groin) and lacks the characteristic "drop" distribution. In many children and young adults, guttate psoriasis may resolve spontaneously or evolve into the more common plaque-type psoriasis. Treatment usually involves management of the underlying infection and topical steroids or phototherapy
questions.learning: Guttate psoriasis is a distinct form of psoriasis characterized by the sudden eruption of small, drop-like, scaly papules and plaques across the trunk and limbs.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer reports fever, malaise, and diarrhoea. There is a history of contact with livestock. Which of the following organisms is most likely to be the cause of the disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Coxiella burnetii

The most likely diagnosis is Q fever, which is caused by Coxiella burnetii.

The given clinical vignette describes a farmer with fever, malaise and diarrhoea along with previous exposure to livestock. This implies that the illness may be zoonosis-associated.

Q fever, or query fever, is caused by the pathogen Coxiella burnetii, which is a small, pleomorphic, gram-negative coccobacillus that was previously thought to be a Rickettsia but now has its own genus. It can be found in ticks, but it is a zoonosis transmitted to humans either through inhalation of aerosols or through contaminated milk.

It is an occupational hazard among abattoir workers, shepherds, cowherds, and other individuals in close contact with animals, especially during or immediately after their parturition. Acute Q-fever presents with nonspecific signs and symptoms, such as fever, cough, vomiting, diarrhoea, photophobia, pneumonia, and less commonly, anaemia, myocarditis, etc.

The disease can result in a state of chronic fatigue called "Q-fever fatigue syndrome". Chronic Q fever tends to occur months or years after the initial infection and can manifest as Q fever endocarditis, infected prostheses, infected aneurysms, and bone infections.

On TEE, endothelium-covered nodules are seen as vegetations on the valves, and new-onset valve regurgitation may be seen. Diagnosis requires a high index of clinical suspicion due to non-specific features and must be considered in all cases of culture-negative endocarditis.

Diagnostic methods include culture, which requires a level 3 biosafety cabinet and hence is not done in routine practice, or DNA detection using PCR. IFA (indirect fluorescent antibody test) is the most preferred test that identifies antibodies and can differentiate acute and chronic infections.

The treatment of choice is with doxycycline, which may be substituted for trimethoprim-sulphamethoxazole in pregnancy. Doxycycline is given for acute Q fever as 100 mg BD for 14 days. For chronic Q fever, doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine are given. Minimum treatment for native valve endocarditis is 18 months.

Due to the low minimum infective dose of Coxiella, it is a bioterrorism agent, Category B.

Other Options:

Option B: Rickettsia rickettsii is the causative agent for Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever (RMSF). Ticks act as a vector.

Option C: Endemic typhus is caused by Rickettsia typhi and transmitted by Xenopsylla, the flea. The reservoir of the infection is rats. It is a mild, sporadic fever that is not of great public health importance. The disease presents with fever and chills. A characteristic rash appears on the fourth or fifth day, which starts on the trunk and spreads over the limbs but spares the face, palms and soles. By the second week, the patient becomes stuporous and delirious.

Option D: Scrub typhus, also known as chigger-borne typhus, is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi. The vector is a trombiculid mite.
questions.learning: Coxiella burnetii — The most likely diagnosis is Q fever, which is caused by Coxiella burnetii. The given clinical vignette describes a farmer with fever, malaise and diarrhoea along with previous exposure to livestock.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 20-year-old female complained of fatigue for the past 1 year along with incidences of bleeding gums. Examination revealed massive splenomegaly and her hb level was noted to be 8gm/dl. Immature cells were seen in the peripheral smear. Her blood workup showed a Total leucocyte count (TLC) of 1,50,000/microL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CML

The clinical presentation with fatigue, bleeding gums, massive splenomegaly, and peripheral blood smear findings are suggestive of chronic myelogenous leukemia(CML).

Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative disorder with the peak incidence in the fifth to sixth decade of life. The chimeric BCR-ABL gene is created by a reciprocal (9;22)(q34;q11) translocation(Philadelphia chromosome). This BCR-ABL gene distinguishes CML from other myeloproliferative disorders and is detected by fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) or polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

Clinical features:

Mild to moderate anemia and hypermetabolism, fatigability, weakness, weight loss, and anorexia. Dragging sensation in the abdomen caused by splenomegaly, or the acute onset of left upper quadrant pain due to splenic infarction. The spleen is often greatly enlarged as a result of extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis. Extramedullary hematopoiesis can also produce mild hepatomegaly and lymphadenopathy.

Peripheral blood:

* Leukocytosis with leukocyte count, often exceeding 100,000 cells/mm3, which consists predominantly of neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils, and basophils.

* Blasts are usually less than 10% of the circulating cells.

* Platelet count is usually increased

Bone Marrow:

* Markedly hypercellular marrow because of massively increased numbers of maturing granulocytic precursors. There is usually an elevated proportion of eosinophils and basophils.

* There is also an increase in megakaryocytes which usually include small, dysplastic forms and erythroid progenitors are present in normal or mildly decreased numbers. Typically there is an increased reticulin deposition, but overt marrow fibrosis is rare early in the course.

Sea-blue histiocytes - These are scattered macrophages with abundant wrinkled,green-blue cytoplasm

Other options:
Acute leukemias have a presence of immature blast cells in the bone marrow and peripheral smear usually (>20%) which is not seen in this patient.

ALL lymphoblast cells have Tdt positive which is due to DNA polymerase. These cells can be B cell or T cell subtype. They are distinguished by cell surface markers. CD 10, 19, 20 are positive on B cells while CD2-8 are positive on T cell ALL.

AML has positive staining for myeloperoxidase and auer rods are seen in the cytoplasm.
CLL is a disease seen in elderly patients(>65) and peripheral smear will show smudge cells.
questions.learning: CML — The clinical presentation with fatigue, bleeding gums, massive splenomegaly, and peripheral blood smear findings are suggestive of chronic myelogenous leukemia(CML).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which nerve defect causes lagophthalmos?
questions.explanation: Lagophthalmos refers to the inability to close the eyelids completely, which leads to corneal exposure and potential ulceration. This condition is primarily caused by paralysis of the orbicularis oculi muscle, which is the muscle responsible for eyelid closure. The orbicularis oculi is innervated by the 7th cranial nerve (facial nerve). Therefore, facial nerve palsy is the most common cause of lagophthalmos. The 6th nerve (Option B) innervates the lateral rectus muscle, and its palsy results in medial strabismus. The 4th nerve (Option C) supplies the superior oblique muscle, and its defect causes vertical diplopia. The 5th nerve (Option D) provides sensory innervation to the face and motor innervation to the muscles of mastication, but it does not control eyelid closure. Clinical management of lagophthalmos focuses on ocular surface protection using lubricants, moisture chambers, or surgical procedures like tarsorrhaphy to prevent exposure keratopathy and permanent vision loss

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which segment of the vertebrae is involved in a patient presenting with pain in the back of the thigh and the leg after lifting heavy weight?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. S1

Pain radiating along the back of the thigh and posterior leg corresponds to the S1 dermatome, classically seen in sciatica.

S1 root involvement commonly occurs with L5–S1 disc herniation, affecting the Achilles reflex.

L4 and L5 involve anterior/anterolateral leg regions, while S2 pain is more perineal/posterior thigh only.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old athlete woman with secondary amenorrhea. Biochemical evaluation reveals LH=0.3, FSH=2, BMI 17.5. She likely suffers from which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism

linical clues from the question

• 24-year-old athlete
• Secondary amenorrhea
• Low LH (0.3)
• Low FSH (2)
• Low BMI (17.5)

These findings indicate suppression of the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian (HPO) axis.

This presentation is classic for Functional Hypothalamic Amenorrhea, a form of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

It occurs commonly in:

• Athletes
• Women with low body weight
• Excess physical exercise
• Stress or eating disorders

This condition is commonly part of the Female Athlete Triad.

The triad includes:

| Component | Explanation

| --------- | -----------

| Low energy availability | Excess exercise / inadequate calories

| Amenorrhea | Hypothalamic suppression

| Osteoporosis | Low estrogen levels

| Type | LH | FSH | Example

| ---- | --- | --- | -------

| Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism | ↓ | ↓ | Hypothalamic amenorrhea

| Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism | ↑ | ↑ | Ovarian failure

| Normogonadotropic | Normal | Normal | PCOS

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department for evaluation of cyanosis. He became fussy and sweaty while taking his bottle, and his lips "turned blue" for several minutes during the feeding. The infant has had similar episodes during feeding and crying, but these resolved quickly. The patient was born at 39 weeks gestation, and his birth weight was average for gestational age. His weight gain has been slow, currently at the 5th percentile. On examination, the infant is ill-appearing, agitated, cyanotic, and tachypneic. Cardiac auscultation reveals a grade 2/6 crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border and a single second heart sound. The patient is placed in a knee-chest position immediately. This maneuver improves the patient’s condition predominantly by which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased systemic vascular resistance

This infant’s episodic cyanosis during feeding or crying that improves with the knee-chest position is characteristic of a hypercyanotic (“tet”) spell seen in Tetralogy of Fallot.

During a tet spell:

• Increased right-to-left shunting across the ventricular septal defect occurs due to right ventricular outflow obstruction.
• This allows deoxygenated blood to bypass the lungs and enter systemic circulation, causing sudden cyanosis.

Knee-chest position mechanism:

• Compresses the femoral arteries → increases systemic vascular resistance (SVR).
• Higher SVR reduces right-to-left shunting across the VSD.
• More blood is directed toward the pulmonary circulation for oxygenation, improving cyanosis.
questions.learning: Increased systemic vascular resistance — This infant’s episodic cyanosis during feeding or crying that improves with the knee-chest position is characteristic of a hypercyanotic (“tet”) spell seen in Tetralogy of Fallot.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: During administration of an anesthetic block for ophthalmic surgery, which of the following extraocular muscles is least likely to be affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Superior oblique (SO)

Retrobulbar and peribulbar anaesthesia work by depositing local anaesthetic into the intraconal space — the cone bounded by the four recti and their intermuscular septa, with its apex at the annulus of Zinn. Akinesia therefore follows a simple rule:

A muscle is blocked if its nerve enters the orbit through the annulus of Zinn.

The muscle's own position is largely irrelevant. What matters is whether its motor nerve is bathed in the drug.

Applying the rule

| Nerve | Passes through annulus of Zinn? | Muscles supplied | Effect of block

| ----- | ------------------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------

| CN III (superior division) | Inside | SR, LPS | Akinetic + ptosis

| CN III (inferior division) | Inside | MR, IR, IO, sphincter pupillae | Akinetic + mydriasis

| CN VI | Inside (lies deepest in cone, on LR's ocular surface) | LR | Akinetic — earliest and most reliable

| CN IV | OUTSIDE — enters via the widest, most superolateral part of the SOF, then runs medially along the orbital roof, extraconally, to reach SO from above | SO | Spared longest ✔

CN IV is also the most slender cranial nerve and the only one that reaches its muscle without ever entering the cone. The anaesthetic simply never meets it in adequate concentration.

The bedside proof

This isn't theoretical — it produces a specific, observable sign:

In an eye with an otherwise complete retrobulbar block, ask the patient to look down-and-in, or watch the conjunctival vessels: intorsion persists while all other movement is abolished.

That residual intorsion is the superior oblique announcing that CN IV was missed. It is the single most testable correlate of this question.
questions.learning: Superior oblique (SO) Retrobulbar and peribulbar anaesthesia work by depositing local anaesthetic into the intraconal space — the cone bounded by the four recti and their intermuscular septa, with its apex at the annulus of Zinn.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In which condition is Grey-Turner's sign observed?
questions.explanation: Grey-Turner's sign is a clinical sign characterized by ecchymosis (bluish discoloration or bruising) of the flanks. It is a classic indicator of severe Acute Pancreatitis (Option B), specifically the hemorrhagic variety. This bruising results from blood tracked from the retroperitoneum through the transversalis fascia into the subcutaneous tissue of the abdominal wall. Acute appendicitis (Option A), cholecystitis (Option C), and hepatitis (Option D) involve different inflammatory pathways and do not typically lead to the massive retroperitoneal hemorrhage required to produce this sign . Another related sign is Cullen's sign, which involves bruising around the umbilicus. The presence of Grey-Turner's sign signifies a poor prognosis and a high severity of the disease. Therefore, its identification is critical for the risk stratification of patients with acute abdominal pain. It remains the classic pedagogical clinical finding associated with severe, necrotizing pancreatitis in medical board examinations
questions.learning: Grey-Turner's sign is a clinical sign characterized by ecchymosis (bluish discoloration or bruising) of the flanks. It is a classic indicator of severe Acute Pancreatitis (Option B), specifically the hemorrhagic variety.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents to the outpatient department with weakness and fatigue. Laboratory tests reveal low hemoglobin and a low reticulocyte count, while white blood cell and platelet counts are normal. Bone marrow examination shows a selective decrease in erythroid precursors. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: As established in Question 42, the combination of anemia (low Hb), an inadequate bone marrow response (low reticulocyte count), and normal WBC/platelet counts strongly points to a specific marrow failure. The definitive histological finding of a selective decrease in Erythroid precursors in the bone marrow confirms the diagnosis of Pure Red Cell Aplasia (PRCA). Aplastic anemia (Option A) would show a decrease in all cell lines (pancytopenia) and a "fatty" marrow. Iron deficiency anemia (Option C) would typically show microcytosis and absent iron stores, but not a total selective absence of red cell precursors. Hemolytic anemia (Option D) would show a high reticulocyte count as the marrow tries to compensate. PRCA can be congenital (Diamond-Blackfan anemia) or acquired. Acquired PRCA is often an autoimmune condition and is famously associated with thymomas; surgical removal of the thymoma can sometimes result in remission of the anemia. This selective failure is a high-yield concept in hematology
questions.learning: As established in Question 42, the combination of anemia (low Hb), an inadequate bone marrow response (low reticulocyte count), and normal WBC/platelet counts strongly points to a specific marrow failure.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A disease has an incubation period of 3-14 days. It has a median incubation of 10 days. A person had to travel abroad and he was not vaccinated. As the disease is of international significance, how long will he have to be quarantined?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 14 days

A person who is not vaccinated and has been exposed to a disease of international significance (like COVID) with an incubation period of 3-14 days should be quarantined for 14 days(longest incubation period).

Quarantine is defined as the limitation of freedom of movement of well-persons or animals, exposed to a communicable disease for a period of time not longer than the longest usual incubation period, to prevent contact with those not exposed. This is done to prevent the potential spread of the disease during its incubation period, which is the time between exposure and the onset of symptoms.

The quarantined person:

• Should stay in a well-ventilated single room and stay away from high-risk individuals
• Should not attend any religious or social gatherings
• Must wash hands often
• Their surroundings must be disinfected with 1% sodium hypochlorite solution

In case the person being quarantined becomes symptomatic, all his contacts should be home quarantined for 14 days and followed up for another 14 days or till the report turns out negative on lab testing.

Note: The median incubation period refers to the time between exposure to a pathogen and the onset of symptoms in 50% of cases. And isolation is the separation and restriction of movements or activities of persons who are sick, to prevent the transmission of disease.
questions.learning: 14 days A person who is not vaccinated and has been exposed to a disease of international significance (like COVID) with an incubation period of 3-14 days should be quarantined for 14 days(longest incubation period).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Detoxification of Xenobiotics for phase 1 reaction (Hydroxylation) require monooxygenase/cytochrome P-450 along with:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. NADPH

Phase I detoxification (functionalization reactions) of xenobiotics mainly involves oxidation reactions such as hydroxylation, catalyzed by the cytochrome P450 monooxygenase system present in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of liver cells.

In this system, NADPH acts as the reducing agent and provides electrons through NADPH–cytochrome P450 reductase, which allows molecular oxygen to be split, with one oxygen atom incorporated into the substrate (hydroxylation) and the other reduced to water.

Why other options are incorrect:

• NADH: Mainly involved in mitochondrial electron transport and not the primary reducing agent for cytochrome P450 reactions.
• FAD / FADH₂: These act as prosthetic groups in some enzymes but are not the direct electron donors for the cytochrome P450 monooxygenase system.
questions.learning: NADPH Phase I detoxification (functionalization reactions) of xenobiotics mainly involves oxidation reactions such as hydroxylation, catalyzed by the cytochrome P450 monooxygenase system present in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of liver cells.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man with a history of using contact lenses, presented with pain, redness and purulent discharge from his right eye. A greyish-white serpiginous ulcer was noted over the lower third of the cornea. The anterior chamber showed a 4 mm hypopyon and a moderate flare reaction. What is the most likely diagnosis ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bacterial corneal ulcer

Hypopyon corneal ulcer with a characteristic serpiginous description (ulcus serpens) is typically caused by Pneumococcus. The bacterial hypopyon is sterile.

Ulcus serpens is a greyish-white or yellowish disc-shaped ulcer occurring near the centre of the cornea. The ulcer has a tendency to creep over the cornea in a serpiginous fashion.

Risk factors include both surgical and non-surgical ocular trauma, dry eye, chronic corneal disease, immune alterations and contact lenses.

An examination may reveal the following signs:

* Swelling of lids and blepharospasm

* Conjunctival hyperemia

* Ciliary congestion, hypopyon and anterior chamber flare reaction

* Iridocyclitis

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is pegloticase used for?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chronic gout

Pegloticase is used in the treatment of chronic gout.

Pegloticase is a pegylated uricase (urate oxidase). It catalyzes the enzymatic oxidation of uric acid into allantoin, which is a more soluble and inactive metabolite.

It is used in the treatment of severe, refractory chronic gout or in cases where other urate-lowering therapies are contraindicated.
questions.learning: Chronic gout Pegloticase is used in the treatment of chronic gout. Pegloticase is a pegylated uricase (urate oxidase).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: A 44-year-old male presented with cough. Chest X-ray revealed pleural effusion. Thoracentesis was done, and the following was observed. Pleural fluid protein to serum protein ratio was 0.6. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pleural TB

A pleural fluid protein-to-serum protein ratio of 0.6 fulfills Light’s criteria for an exudative effusion.

Tuberculous pleural effusion is classically exudative, with high protein content due to increased capillary permeability.

Cirrhosis, CHF, and nephrotic syndrome cause transudative effusions with low protein ratios.

| Feature | Exudate | Transudate

| ------- | ------- | ----------

| Protein ratio | >0.5 | <0.5

| LDH | High | Low

| Cause | Inflammation | Pressure imbalance

| Example | TB, malignancy | CHF, cirrhosis

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Calcium binds to which of the following proteins during smooth muscle contraction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Calmodulin

Calcium binds to calmodulin during smooth muscle contraction.

Increased cytoplasmic Ca2+ binds to and activates calcium-binding proteins (calmodulin, troponin) or activates protein kinases (or phospholipase C) to bring about physiological effects.

Calmodulin is structurally and functionally related to troponin. In place of troponin, smooth muscle cells contain a large amount of the regulatory protein calmodulin; it is different in the manner in which it initiates contraction. Calmodulin initiates contraction by activating the myosin light chain kinase. Troponin, on the other hand, initiates contraction by causing a conformational change in the tropomyosin molecule which then uncovers the active sites on the actin filament.

The sequence of events in smooth muscle contraction:

* Binding of acetylcholine to muscarinic receptors

* Increased influx of Ca2+ into the cell

* Activation of calmodulin-dependent myosin light chain kinase

* Myosin phosphorylation

* Increased myosin ATPase activity and binding of myosin to actin

Actin, myosin, and tropomyosin are present in both skeletal muscle and smooth muscle.

Other options :

Option B: Actin is a protein that makes up microfilaments. Microfilaments are present in the outer zone of the cytoplasm and provide support to the cell membrane. In muscle cells, a specialized arrangement of actin provides the mechanism for muscle contraction.

Option C: Myosin is the major contractile protein found in muscle cells. Its specialized arrangement with actin is essential for muscle contraction. It does not play a role in axonal transport.

Option D: Troponin molecules are small globular units located at intervals along with the tropomyosin molecules. Each of the three troponin subunits has a unique function:

* Troponin T binds the troponin components to tropomyosin.

* Troponin I inhibits the interaction of myosin with actin.

* Troponin C contains the binding sites for the Ca 2+ that help to initiate contraction.

Pearl PF0509: Sarcomere
questions.learning: Calmodulin Calcium binds to calmodulin during smooth muscle contraction. Increased cytoplasmic Ca2+ binds to and activates calcium-binding proteins (calmodulin, troponin) or activates protein kinases (or phospholipase C) to bring about physiological effects.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
The most commonly occurring complication of TPN in a sepsis patient in ICU:

TPN - Total Parenteral Nutrition

ICU - Intensive Care Unit
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hyperglycemia

The most commonly occurring complication of TPN in a sepsis patient in the ICU is hyperglycemia.

To monitor or prevent complications in patients on TPN, the following steps may be taken:

• Infections

• Monitor the development of glucose intolerance as it is the earliest sign of systemic sepsis. (Note: glucose intolerance- glucose not processed effectively, leading to hyperglycemia)
• Use subclavian vein preferably

• Metabolic complications

• BUN and LFTs weekly
• Serum electrolytes every 2-3 days

• Intestinal atrophy

• Provide at least some nutrients enterally if feasible

TPN also referred to as central parenteral nutrition is used for patients who can't absorb nutrients through their digestive tract, often due to conditions like short bowel syndrome from extensive intestinal resection or fistulas. It can also be temporary until other feeding methods, like a nasojejunal tube, are established.

TPN typically comes in a 3-liter bag with a lipid emulsion, amino acids, glucose, electrolytes, and vitamins. The energy provided is about 150–250 kcal per gram of protein nitrogen, with 30–50% from fat. Folic acid is added weekly, with other vitamins given daily, and long-term TPN may require vitamin B12 supplementation.
