questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old child was brought to the clinic by her mother with reduced hearing for the past 2-3 months. The otoscopy finding is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myringitis bullosa

The given clinical scenario of a child presenting with hearing loss for the past 2-3 months and vesicles in the superficial layer of the tympanic membrane is suggestive of myringitis bullosa.

Bullous myringitis (myringitis bullosa haemorrhagica) is the finding of vesicles in the superficial layer of the tympanic membrane without affecting the contents of the external or middle ear. If the middle ear becomes involved, this would be consistent with acute otitis media. It occurs due to infection by influenza virus or by Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Bloody otorrhea can occur when a bulla rupture and is referred to as bullous hemorrhagic myringitis.

Option B: Serous otitis media is also known as secretory otitis media or mucoid otitis media or glue ear. It is characterized by the accumulation of nonpurulent effusion in the middle ear cleft.

It is often seen in children 5-8 years of age. They present with hearing loss not exceeding 40 dB, which is insidious in onset. Speech may be delayed and defective due to hearing loss. Mild earaches with a history of upper respiratory tract infection are usually seen.

On otoscopy,

* Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex

* Thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus

* If the tympanic membrane is transparent fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen

The tuning fork test reveals a conductive type of hearing loss. X-ray mastoid reveals clouding of air cells.

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

* Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, antibiotics, and middle ear aeration techniques.

* Surgical management includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid, grommet insertion, tympanotomy, or cortical mastoidectomy.

Option C: Acute otitis media is an acute infection of the middle ear by pyogenic organisms. It presents with marked earache and hearing loss is seen in later stages. Otoscopy shows a red and bulging tympanic membrane.

Option D: Myringitis granulosa is characterized by granulations on the outer surface of the tympanic membrane. It is associated with long-standing foreign body, wax impaction, and external ear infection.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which part of the fallopian tube is most commonly involved in genital tuberculosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ampulla

The ampullary part of the fallopian tube is most commonly involved in genital tuberculosis.

Fallopian tube in genital tuberculosis:

The fallopian tubes are almost always involved in genital tuberculosis. The lesions are generally bilateral. The mode of spread of disease is hematogenous, arising from a primary infective focus in the lung.

The ampulla is most commonly affected while the fimbriae and interstitium are spared.

Hysterosalpingography may reveal the following:

* Tobacco pouch appearance of hydrosalpinx and pyosalpinx

* Lead pipe appearance (rigid, nonperistaltic pipe)

* Beading and variation due to filling defects

* Calcification of the tube

* Cornual block

* Jagged fluffiness of tubal outline

Hysteroscopy will reveal the presence of synechiae, partial obliteration of the cavity, the golf-hole appearance of the tubal ostia, and presence of ulcers.
questions.learning: Ampulla — The ampullary part of the fallopian tube is most commonly involved in genital tuberculosis. Fallopian tube in genital tuberculosis: The fallopian tubes are almost always involved in genital tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old man presents with chronic low back pain, unexplained weight loss, and progressively worsening urinary symptoms. Imaging of the spine reveals osteoblastic lesions. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of advanced age, urinary symptoms (retention requiring catheterization), and osteoblastic (bone-forming) spinal lesions is pathognomonic for metastatic Prostate Cancer. Unlike most cancers that cause osteolytic (bone-destroying) lesions, prostate cancer classically stimulates osteoblasts, leading to dense white spots on X-ray. Benign Prostatic Hypertrophy (Option A) causes urinary symptoms but never causes weight loss or bone metastases. Carcinoma of the Bladder (Option B) usually presents with painless hematuria rather than primary bone pain. Renal Cell Cancer (Option D) typically produces large osteolytic lesions. Although the patient's PSA of 5.2 ng/ml is only mildly elevated (standard cutoff is 4.0), it does not rule out malignancy in the presence of metastatic evidence. Further evaluation should include a digital rectal examination and a transrectal ultrasound-guided (TRUS) biopsy. Prostate cancer is the leading cause of osteoblastic metastases in elderly men
questions.learning: The combination of advanced age, urinary symptoms (retention requiring catheterization), and osteoblastic (bone-forming) spinal lesions is pathognomonic for metastatic Prostate Cancer.
